items.text: Efes'e hoş geldiniz. İzmir'in topraklarında, MÖ 10. yüzyıla uzanan bir kentin sokaklarındasınız. Burası antik dünyanın en iyi korunmuş Roma kentlerinden biri. Ve birazdan karşınıza çıkacak olan Celsus Kütüphanesi, Efes'i dünyaca ünlü yapan o mermer cephe. Hazırsanız, yürümeye başlayalım.
items.speech: Efes'e hoş geldiniz. İzmir'in topraklarında, milattan önce 10. yüzyıla uzanan bir kentin sokaklarındasınız. Burası antik dünyanın en iyi korunmuş Roma kentlerinden biri. Ve birazdan karşınıza çıkacak olan Celsus Kütüphanesi, Efes'i dünyaca ünlü yapan o mermer cephe. Hazırsanız, yürümeye başlayalım.

items.text: Efes'in hikâyesi bir tanrıçayla başlar. İyonlar bu kenti kurduğunda, kalbinde Artemis Tapınağı vardı ve o tapınak Efes'i bütün Ege'nin dinî merkezi yaptı. Sonra Roma geldi. Efes, Asia eyaletinin başkenti oldu; sokaklarında 200 binden fazla insan yaşıyordu. Peki bu görkem nasıl sona erdi? Bir savaşla değil… sessizce. Alüvyon limanı yavaş yavaş doldurdu, gemiler gelmez oldu ve Efes önemini yitirdi.

items.text: Şimdi Celsus Kütüphanesi'nin önündesiniz. Başınızı kaldırıp bu mermer cepheye bakın. Çoğu ziyaretçi burayı yalnızca bir kütüphane sanır; oysa bu cephe aynı zamanda bir mezar anıtının yüzüdür. Celsus'un lahdi hâlâ, apsisin altındaki odada yatıyor. Gördüğünüz cephe 1970-78 yılları arasında taş taş yeniden dikildi. Uygulamadaki model de onu tam yüksekliğiyle, arkasındaki salonu ise duvarların bugün ayakta kaldığı yüksekliğe kadar gösteriyor.

items.text: Ve işte Büyük Tiyatro. Antik dünyanın en büyük tiyatrolarından biri. Panayır Dağı'nın yamacına oyulmuş üç katlı oturma basamakları, liman caddesinin ucundan Roma sahne binasına bakıyor. Burada yalnızca oyunlar oynanmadı: Elçilerin İşleri'nde anlatılan gümüşçüler ayaklanması da bu basamaklarda yaşandı. Bir an durun ve binlerce sesin aynı anda yükseldiğini hayal edin.

items.text: Kuretler Caddesi'nin karşısındaki yamaçta, Efes'in en zenginlerinin evleri duruyor: Yamaç Evler. Altı lüks konut… Yerlerde mozaikler, duvarlarda freskler. Ama asıl şaşırtıcı olan konfor: tabandan ısıtma, kapalı kanalizasyon, hatta cam pencereler. Üstelik MS 1. yüzyılda. Bir Roma zengininin evinin içini bu kadar yakından görebileceğiniz başka bir yer yok. Modelde, peristilli avlusuyla bu konutlardan birinin içine girebilirsiniz.

Plinius'a göre 36 sütunun kaidesi kabartmalarla süslüydü. Bugün o ormandan geriye, yerinde yükselen tek bir sütun kaldı. Modelde gördüğünüz, MÖ 4. yüzyılda yeniden inşa edilen üçüncü tapınak.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Artemis Tapınağı Dünyanın Yedi Harikası'ndan biriydi; bugün ayakta yalnızca tek bir sütunu var. Büyük Tiyatro tam 24.000 kişilikti. Elçilerin İşleri'ne göre, Aziz Pavlus'a karşı iki saat boyunca 'Efeslilerin Artemis'i uludur!' diye bağırılan o gösteri de burada yapıldı. Yamaç Evler'de tabandan ve duvardan ısıtma, kapalı kanalizasyon ve cam pencereler vardı; hem de MS 1. yüzyılda. Ve son bir sır: Efes bir liman kentiydi. Küçük Menderes'in taşıdığı alüvyon limanı doldurdu; bugün deniz, bu kalıntılardan 5 km uzakta.

items.text: Welcome to Ephesus. You are standing in the streets of a city in İzmir province whose story reaches back to the 10th century BC. This is one of the best-preserved Roman cities of antiquity — and just ahead waits the marble façade that made it famous: the Library of Celsus. Shall we begin?
items.speech: Welcome to Ephesus. You are standing in the streets of a city in İzmir province whose story reaches back to the 10th century BC. This is one of the best-preserved Roman cities of antiquity, and just ahead waits the marble façade that made it famous: the Library of Celsus. Shall we begin?

items.text: The story of Ephesus begins with a goddess. When Ionian settlers founded the city, it grew around the Temple of Artemis. Then came Rome. Ephesus became capital of the province of Asia, home to over 200,000 people. So how did all this splendour end? Not with a battle, but quietly: silt crept into the harbour, the ships stopped coming, and the city slowly declined.

items.text: You are now in front of the Library of Celsus. Look up at this marble façade. Most visitors take it for a library alone, but it is also the face of a tomb: Celsus' sarcophagus still lies in the chamber beneath the apse. The front you see was re-erected stone by stone in 1970-78. The model in the app shows it at its full height, and the hall behind it only as high as its walls survive.

items.text: And here is the Great Theatre, one of the largest theatres of antiquity. Its three-tiered cavea is cut into the slope of Mount Pion, looking down the Harbour Street at a Roman stage building. Plays were not the only drama here: the riot of the silversmiths in the Acts of the Apostles took place on these very tiers. Pause for a moment and imagine thousands of voices rising at once.

items.text: On the slope opposite Curetes Street stand the homes of the city's wealthiest: the Terrace Houses. Six luxury residences, their floors in mosaic and their walls in fresco. What astonishes most is the comfort — underfloor heating, enclosed drains, even glazed windows, all in the first century AD. Nowhere else shows so clearly what a rich Roman's house was actually like. In the model you can step inside one unit, around its colonnaded court.

items.text: Now to the city's most sacred place: the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders. Picture a marble forest 137 metres long, raised on marshy ground. Pliny tells us 36 of its columns were carved in relief at the base. Of that forest, a single column, re-erected from fragments, stands today. The model shows the third temple, rebuilt in the 4th century BC.

items.text: Curetes Street is the main colonnaded street of Ephesus, running from the Library of Celsus to the theatre, lined with monuments and statues. As you walk these stones, think of the crowds who passed this way centuries ago.

items.text: Did you know? The Temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders; a single re-erected column remains today. The Great Theatre seated 24,000 people. According to Acts, the two-hour chant of 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' against Saint Paul filled this very bowl. The Terrace Houses had underfloor and wall heating, enclosed drains and glazed windows — in the first century AD. And one last secret: Ephesus was a port. Silt from the Küçük Menderes filled the harbour, and today the sea lies 5 km from the ruins.

items.text: This brings our journey through Ephesus to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.

items.text: Willkommen beim Audioguide für Ephesos in der Provinz İzmir. Epoche: 10. Jahrhundert v. Chr. Eine der am besten erhaltenen römischen Städte der Antike, berühmt für die Celsus-Bibliothek.
items.speech: Willkommen beim Audioguide für Ephesos in der Provinz İzmir. Epoche: 10. Jahrhundert vor Christus Eine der am besten erhaltenen römischen Städte der Antike, berühmt für die Celsus-Bibliothek.

items.text: Von ionischen Siedlern gegründet, wuchs die Stadt rund um den Tempel der Artemis. Unter Rom wurde sie mit über 200.000 Einwohnern Hauptstadt der Provinz Asia und verlor dann an Bedeutung, als ihr Hafen verlandete.

items.text: Celsus-Bibliothek. Die Marmorfront in Ephesos ist nicht die Fassade einer Bibliothek, sondern die eines Grabmals: Der Sarkophag des Celsus liegt noch immer in der Kammer unter der Apsis. Das Modell zeigt die 1970–78 wieder aufgerichtete Fassade in voller Höhe und die Halle dahinter nur so hoch, wie ihre Mauern erhalten sind.

items.text: Hanghäuser. Sechs Luxuswohnhäuser am Hang gegenüber der Kuretenstraße, ihre Böden mit Mosaiken, ihre Wände mit Fresken. Mit Fußbodenheizung, geschlossenen Abwasserkanälen und verglasten Fenstern sind sie der einzige Ort, der zeigt, wie das Haus eines reichen Römers im ersten Jahrhundert n. Chr. tatsächlich aussah. Das Modell zeigt das Innere einer Wohneinheit rund um ihren Säulenhof.

items.text: Tempel der Artemis. Eines der Sieben Weltwunder, von dem heute eine einzige, aus Fragmenten wieder aufgerichtete Säule steht: ein 137 Meter langer Wald aus Marmor, errichtet auf sumpfigem Boden. Laut Plinius waren 36 der Säulen am Fuß mit Reliefs verziert. Das Modell zeigt den dritten Tempel, der im 4. Jahrhundert v. Chr. neu errichtet wurde.

items.text: Kuretenstraße. Die von Säulen gesäumte Hauptstraße, die die Celsus-Bibliothek mit dem Theater verbindet, gesäumt von Monumenten und Statuen.

items.text: Wussten Sie schon? Der Tempel der Artemis war eines der Sieben Weltwunder; heute steht von ihm nur noch eine einzige, wieder aufgerichtete Säule. Das Große Theater bot 24.000 Menschen Platz. Laut der Apostelgeschichte erfüllte der zweistündige Ruf „Groß ist die Artemis der Epheser!“ gegen den Apostel Paulus dieses Rund. Die Hanghäuser hatten Fußboden- und Wandheizung, geschlossene Abwasserkanäle und verglaste Fenster – im ersten Jahrhundert n. Chr. Ephesos war eine Hafenstadt. Schlamm des Küçük Menderes füllte den Hafen, und heute liegt das Meer 5 km von den Ruinen entfernt.

items.text: Добро пожаловать в аудиогид: Эфес, провинция Измир. Период: X век до н. э. Один из наиболее сохранившихся римских городов античности, знаменитый библиотекой Цельса.
items.speech: Добро пожаловать в аудиогид: Эфес, провинция Измир. Период: X век до нашей эры Один из наиболее сохранившихся римских городов античности, знаменитый библиотекой Цельса.

items.text: Основанный ионийскими переселенцами, город вырос вокруг храма Артемиды. При римлянах он стал столицей провинции Азия с населением более 200 000 человек, а затем пришёл в упадок, когда его гавань занесло илом.

items.text: Библиотека Цельса. Мраморный фасад в Эфесе — это лицо не библиотеки, а гробницы: саркофаг Цельса до сих пор покоится в камере под апсидой. Модель показывает фасад, заново возведённый в 1970–78 годах, во всю высоту, а зал за ним — лишь на ту высоту, на которую сохранились его стены.

items.text: Большой театр. Один из крупнейших театров античности: трёхъярусная кавея, высеченная в склоне горы Пион, обращена вдоль Портовой улицы к римскому сценическому зданию. Именно здесь происходит бунт серебряных дел мастеров, описанный в Деяниях апостолов.

items.text: Террасные дома. Шесть роскошных жилищ на склоне напротив улицы Куретов, с мозаичными полами и расписанными фресками стенами. С подпольным отоплением, закрытой канализацией и застеклёнными окнами они — единственное место, которое показывает, каким на самом деле был дом богатого римлянина в I веке н. э. Модель показывает интерьер одного из домов вокруг его двора с колоннадой.
items.speech: Террасные дома. Шесть роскошных жилищ на склоне напротив улицы Куретов, с мозаичными полами и расписанными фресками стенами. С подпольным отоплением, закрытой канализацией и застеклёнными окнами они, единственное место, которое показывает, каким на самом деле был дом богатого римлянина в I веке нашей эры Модель показывает интерьер одного из домов вокруг его двора с колоннадой.

items.text: Храм Артемиды. Одно из семи чудес света, от которого сегодня стоит лишь одна колонна, вновь собранная из фрагментов: мраморный лес длиной 137 метров, возведённый на болотистой почве. По словам Плиния, 36 колонн были украшены рельефами у основания. Модель показывает третий храм, отстроенный заново в IV веке до н. э.

items.text: А вы знали? Храм Артемиды был одним из семи чудес света; сегодня от него осталась лишь одна заново установленная колонна. Большой театр вмещал 24 000 зрителей. Согласно Деяниям апостолов, двухчасовой крик «Велика Артемида Ефесская!», направленный против святого Павла, наполнял эту чашу. В террасных домах были подпольное и настенное отопление, закрытая канализация и застеклённые окна — в I веке н. э. Эфес был портом. Наносы реки Кючюк-Мендерес заполнили гавань, и теперь море находится в 5 км от руин.

items.text: Pergamon was a royal capital set high on a steep acropolis. This ancient city in İzmir province takes us back to the 3rd century BC, and it is home to the steepest theatre of the ancient world. Ready to climb into its story?

items.text: Pergamon was the capital of the Attalid dynasty, and its library of 200,000 scrolls gave a whole writing material its name: parchment. Then, in 133 BC, the city was bequeathed to Rome. Under its new masters it became famous for a very different kind of place: the Asklepion, its healing centre.
items.speech: Pergamon was the capital of the Attalid dynasty, and its library of 200,000 scrolls gave a whole writing material its name: parchment. Then, in 133 BC, the city was bequeathed to Rome. items.text: You are now on the Great Altar terrace. It was less an altar than a stage: the 113-metre Gigantomachy frieze wrapped the building in a battle told in stone. Between 1878 and 1886 it was dismantled and shipped to Berlin. What stands at Pergamon now is the terrace and the footings. Pause for a moment and picture that stone battle once circling this very spot.

items.text: Here stands the Red Basilica, the great brick complex of Pergamon. Step back and take in its scale, and imagine it in another age, when this was a sanctuary of the Egyptian gods.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Acropolis and the Temple of Trajan, and save time for the Asklepion, where healing was the city's art.

items.text: Did you know? The word 'parchment' comes from Pergamon: when Egypt cut off the papyrus, the city perfected treated skins instead. The acropolis theatre is the steepest of the ancient world, with 80 rows pitched almost like a cliff and seating for 10,000. At the Asklepion, treatment meant dream interpretation, water cures and theatre, and Galen, the physician, trained here. As for the Great Altar, it was dismantled and shipped to Berlin between 1878 and 1886; it is the building the Pergamon Museum is named after.

items.text: Wussten Sie schon? Das Wort „Pergament“ stammt von Pergamon: Als Ägypten die Papyruslieferungen einstellte, perfektionierte die Stadt die Verarbeitung von Tierhäuten. Das Theater der Akropolis ist das steilste der antiken Welt: 80 Reihen, fast wie eine Klippe geneigt, mit Platz für 10.000 Menschen. Im Asklepieion bestand die Behandlung aus Traumdeutung, Wasserkuren und Theater. Der Arzt Galen wurde hier ausgebildet. Der Große Altar wurde zwischen 1878 und 1886 abgebaut und nach Berlin verschifft; nach ihm ist das Pergamonmuseum benannt.

items.text: Here in Aydın province lies Aphrodisias, an ancient city whose story reaches back to the 2nd century BC. It is a Roman city that stood beside its own marble quarries, and it became famous for its school of sculpture.

items.text: Aphrodisias grew around the cult of Aphrodite, and its loyalty to Rome was rewarded with exemption from tax. Its sculptors worked the local marble and sent their statues across the empire. Imagine the ring of chisels from the workshops of this city.

items.text: Did you know? The 30,000-seat stadium is the best-preserved stadium surviving from antiquity, and both of its curved ends are still standing. items.text: Выросший вокруг культа Афродиты, город получил освобождение от налогов за верность Риму. Его скульпторы, работавшие с местным мрамором, поставляли статуи по всей империи.

items.text: Hierapolis'i Bergama kralları kurdu. Kentin talihini belirleyen şey, topraktan çıkan sıcak sulardı: bu kaynaklar sayesinde Hierapolis bir şifa merkezine dönüştü. Ama aynı toprak sarsıntılar da getirdi. Depremlerle yıkılan kent, Roma döneminde yeniden inşa edildi.

Bir de Plutonion var, nam-ı diğer 'Cehennem Kapısı': yerin altından buraya karbondioksit sızar. Kurban hayvanları ölürken rahiplerin sağ kalması mucize sayılırdı. Sırrı ise şuydu: gaz yerde birikir, ayakta duran insanın başı bulutun üstünde kalır. Hierapolis'in nekropolü, 1200'den fazla mezarıyla Anadolu'nun en büyüğü. items.text: Above the travertines of Pamukkale, in Denizli province, lies a city of healing and of the dead. This is Hierapolis, whose story begins in the 2nd century BC: a spa and a necropolis city in one.

items.text: Hierapolis was founded by the kings of Pergamon, and its hot springs made it a centre of healing. Earthquakes destroyed it, but the city rose again, rebuilt in grand Roman style.

items.text: You are now at the Theatre, cut into the slope above the travertines of Pamukkale. It held 15,000 spectators. Look at the stage front: three ranks of columns deep, it survives in large part and was re-erected between 2004 and 2014. Pause for a moment and imagine every seat filled.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Antique Pool, the Necropolis, Frontinus Street and the Temple of Apollo.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Antique Pool, the Necropolis, Frontinus Street and the Temple of Apollo.

items.text: Did you know? The columns lying in the Antique Pool fell there during an earthquake in the 7th century. Then there is the Plutonion, the 'Gate to Hell', which leaks carbon dioxide from below. Sacrificial animals died there while the priests survived, because the gas pools at ground level, leaving a standing man's head above the cloud. The necropolis, with more than 1,200 tombs, is the largest in Anatolia. Many who came to the hot springs for a cure never left.

items.text: Wussten Sie schon? Die Säulen, die im Antiken Becken liegen, stürzten bei einem Erdbeben im 7. Jahrhundert hinein. Aus dem Plutonion, dem „Tor zur Hölle“, entweicht Kohlendioxid aus der Tiefe. Die Opfertiere starben, während die Priester überlebten: Das Gas sammelt sich am Boden, sodass der Kopf eines stehenden Menschen über der Wolke bleibt. Ihre Nekropole mit mehr als 1.200 Gräbern ist die größte Anatoliens. Viele, die zur Heilung an die heißen Quellen kamen, kehrten nie zurück.

Жертвенные животные погибали, а жрецы оставались в живых: газ скапливается у самой земли, и голова стоящего человека остаётся над облаком. items.text: Aydın'da, antik Milet'in kalıntıları arasındasınız. Hikâyesi MÖ 15. yüzyıla uzanan bu liman kenti, iki büyük fikrin doğduğu yer sayılır: ızgara planlı kent tasarımı ve felsefe. Bu sokaklarda yürürken, düşüncenin de burada yola çıktığını aklınızda tutun.

items.text: Milet'in dört limanı vardı ve bu limanlar onu Akdeniz ticaretinin merkezi yaptı. Buradan yola çıkanlar 90'dan fazla koloni kurdu. Sonra Persler geldi ve kenti yıktı. Ama Milet yeniden kuruldu: bu kez Hippodamos'un ızgara planına göre, dümdüz sokaklarla.

items.text: Şimdi Büyük Tiyatro'nun önündesiniz, Anadolu'nun en büyük tiyatrolarından birinin. Caveası 140 metreye yakın çapıyla yamaca yaslanmış ve bir stadyum gibi önünüzde açılıyor. İlk olarak MÖ 250-225'te Yunan mimarlarınca kuruldu. Roma döneminde, MS 68-96'da, üç katlı taş bir sahne binası eklenerek yeniden inşa edildi. O sahne duvarına bakın: arkasındaki işlikleriyle birlikte bugün en bütün kalmış örneklerden biri.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Bu liman kenti bugün denizden 8 km uzakta; Menderes Nehri limanları tamamen doldurdu. Tiyatrosu 15.000 kişilikti ve Ege'nin en büyüklerinden biridir; ön sırada imparator locasının sütun yuvalarını hâlâ görebilirsiniz. Thales, Anaksimandros ve Anaksimenes bu kentten çıktı. Yani Batı felsefesinin ilk üç adı, aynı limanın insanlarıydı. Ve son olarak: kentin anıtsal Pazar Kapısı 1907-08'de parça parça Berlin'e taşındı ve orada yeniden dikildi.

items.text: Welcome to Miletus, an ancient city in Aydın province whose story reaches back to the 15th century BC. This was a harbour city, and a remarkable one: here grid-plan urbanism was born, and here philosophy took its first steps.
items.speech: Welcome to Miletus, an ancient city in Aydın province whose story reaches back to the 15th century BC. This was a harbour city, and a remarkable one: here grid-plan urbanism was born, and here philosophy took its first steps.

items.text: Imagine a city with not one harbour but four. From them Miletus dominated Mediterranean trade and founded over 90 colonies. Then the Persians destroyed it. Yet the city rose again, rebuilt on the grid plan of Hippodamus.
items.speech: Imagine a city with not one harbour but four. From them Miletus dominated Mediterranean trade and founded over 90 colonies. Then the Persians destroyed it. Yet the city rose again, rebuilt on the grid plan of Hippodamus.

items.text: You are now in front of the Great Theatre, one of the largest theatres in Anatolia. Its cavea, nearly 140 m across, opens like a stadium set against the hillside. Greek architects built it in 250-225 BC; under Rome, in AD 68-96, it was rebuilt with a three-storey stone stage building. That front still survives, with the workshops behind it, and it is among the most complete anywhere.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Baths of Faustina, the Bouleuterion and the İlyas Bey Mosque.

items.text: Did you know? The city now lies 8 km inland: the Meander river filled in all four of its harbours. The theatre held 15,000 people and is among the largest in the Aegean, and in the front row you can still see the sockets for the emperor's box. Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes all came from here — the first three names in Western philosophy shared one harbour. And the monumental Market Gate? It was shipped piece by piece to Berlin in 1907-08 and re-erected there.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Tapınağın duvarlarında hâlâ inşaat çizimleri, yani mimari şablonlar görülebiliyor. Apollon Tapınağı 122 sütunlu tasarlandı, yaklaşık 500 yıl inşa edildi ve hiçbir zaman tamamlanamadı. Sütunları tam 19,7 metre yüksekliğinde; bu da onu Yunan dünyasının en büyük tapınaklarından biri yapıyor. Burası bir kehanet merkeziydi ve Milet'e 17 kilometrelik bir Kutsal Yol'la bağlıydı. Hacılar bu yolu yürüyerek gelirdi.

items.text: Enter Didyma, a sanctuary in Aydın province whose story begins in the 8th century BC. This was the oracle sanctuary of Apollo, and its temple is one of the largest in Anatolia. Prepare to feel very small.

items.text: A sacred way linked Didyma to Miletus, and this was a major oracle. After Alexander's visit, work began on a colossal temple — but it was never finished.
items.speech: A sacred way linked Didyma to Miletus, and this was a major oracle. After Alexander's visit, work began on a colossal temple, but it was never finished.

items.text: You are now standing before the Temple of Apollo, one of the largest temples ever attempted. It was some 500 years in the building, and still never finished. And here is a surprise: it never had a roof. Behind the forest of columns lay an open court, holding the oracle spring and the laurel tree.

items.text: Did you know? Construction drawings used by the ancient architects can still be seen on the temple walls. The Temple of Apollo was designed with 122 columns, built over some 500 years, and never finished. Its columns stand 19.7 metres tall, making it one of the largest temples in the Greek world. And it was an oracle, linked to Miletus by a 17-kilometre Sacred Way that pilgrims walked.

items.text: You are standing in Priene, an ancient city in Aydın province from the 4th century BC. This compact Ionian city sits on Mount Mycale, and its grid plan survives intact.
items.speech: You are standing in Priene, an ancient city in Aydın province from the 4th century BC. This compact Ionian city sits on Mount Mycale, and its grid plan survives intact.

items.text: Priene was refounded in the Hellenistic period. Because it escaped major Roman rebuilding, what you see here is the purest surviving example of classical town planning.
items.speech: Priene was refounded in the Hellenistic period. Because it escaped major Roman rebuilding, what you see here is the purest surviving example of classical town planning.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Temple of Athena and the Bouleuterion, then the Theatre and the Ekklesiasterion.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Temple of Athena and the Bouleuterion, then the Theatre and the Ekklesiasterion.

items.text: Did you know? The marble armchairs in the theatre's front row were reserved for city dignitaries. Priene is the best-preserved grid-plan city of antiquity, laid out in squares on a steep slope as if the ground were flat. Pytheos, architect of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, built the Temple of Athena, and Alexander the Great paid for it; the dedication inscription is now in the British Museum. And the council house seated 640, very nearly the city's entire adult male citizenry at once.

items.text: You are in Sardis, an ancient city in Manisa province dating from the 7th century BC. This was the capital of the Lydian kingdom, where the world's first coins were struck.

items.text: Sardis was famed for the wealth of King Croesus. It was the western terminus of the Persian Royal Road, and it was later revived by Rome, with a huge synagogue and gymnasium.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Temple of Artemis, the Gymnasium and the Synagogue, then look for the Mint workshop and the Bin Tepe tumuli.

items.text: Did you know? The phrase 'rich as Croesus' comes from this city's Lydian king. The Sardis synagogue is the largest known from the ancient world — and it sits inside a sports complex. The gold came from the Pactolus stream, where King Midas was said to have washed away his golden touch.

items.text: This brings our journey through Sardis to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.

items.text: You are walking into Laodicea, an ancient city in Denizli province, founded in the 3rd century BC. This was a wealthy trading city of the Lycus valley, with two theatres and broad avenues.

items.text: The Seleucid king Antiochus II founded the city for his wife Laodice. It grew rich on textiles and banking, and it was home to one of the Seven Churches.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss Syria Street, the West Theatre, the Laodicea Church and the water distribution terminal.

items.text: Did you know? After the earthquake of AD 60, the city refused Roman aid and rebuilt itself with its own money — a detail Tacitus thought worth recording. Laodicea was one of the seven churches of Revelation. Its rebuke, 'neither cold nor hot', is thought to play on the water that arrived lukewarm through kilometres of aqueduct. And the city had two theatres, a stadium, and one of the largest ancient water-distribution terminals in Anatolia.

items.text: This is Halicarnassus, an ancient city in Muğla province whose story reaches back to the 11th century BC. It was the Carian capital, and here once stood the Mausoleum, one of the Seven Wonders.
items.speech: This is Halicarnassus, an ancient city in Muğla province whose story reaches back to the 11th century BC. It was the Carian capital, and here once stood the Mausoleum, one of the Seven Wonders.

items.text: Satrap Mausolus made this city his capital. When he died, his sister and wife Artemisia completed his colossal tomb. But it did not stand forever: earthquakes toppled it, and its stones were later quarried for the castle.

Antik kaynaklara göre burada bir gözlemevi kurmuştu; kentte gözlemevi olduğu düşünülen yapı bugün onun adıyla anılıyor. Praksiteles'in Knidos Aphroditi ise Yunan sanatının ilk büyük çıplak kadın heykeliydi; sırf onu görmek için kente gelenler oldu. Kentin iki limanı vardı ve bunlardan biri askerîydi. İki denizin buluştuğu bu burunda kurulduğu için, gemiler rüzgârı beklemek üzere buraya sığınırdı.

items.text: You have reached Knidos, an ancient city in Muğla province from the 4th century BC. At the very tip of the Datça peninsula, this city of science and art had not one harbour but two.

items.text: Knidos was set where the Aegean meets the Mediterranean, so for ships it was an obligatory stop. But many came for something else: Praxiteles' Aphrodite drew visitors from across the ancient world.
items.speech: Knidos was set where the Aegean meets the Mediterranean, so for ships it was an obligatory stop. But many came for something else: Praxiteles' Aphrodite drew visitors from across the ancient world.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Round Temple of Aphrodite and the Theatre, then the Sundial terrace and the Twin harbours.

items.text: Did you know? The astronomer Eudoxus came from Knidos. According to ancient sources he built an observatory here and measured the year with striking accuracy, and the structure thought to be that observatory carries his name. Praxiteles' Aphrodite of Knidos was the first monumental female nude in Greek art; people sailed here simply to see it. The city had two harbours, one of them naval. Built on the cape where two seas meet, it was where ships waited out the wind.

items.text: Beneath the streets of İzmir lies its forerunner: Smyrna, an ancient city in İzmir province whose story runs from the 3rd millennium BC to today. It is famed above all for the Roman agora at the foot of Kadifekale, and that is where our walk begins.

items.text: In the 4th century BC a new chapter opened, when Alexander's general Lysimachus founded New Smyrna around Kadifekale. Then disaster struck: an earthquake in AD 178 destroyed the city. Yet Smyrna rose again, and its agora was rebuilt under Emperor Marcus Aurelius.

items.text: You are now standing in the Roman Agora. In Roman times this square was the city's commercial and administrative centre. Imagine merchants and officials crossing paths right where you stand.

items.text: Before you is the Gate of Faustina, the monumental gate in the agora of Smyrna. It was dedicated to Faustina, wife of Emperor Marcus Aurelius.

items.text: Now look at the agora columns. These are the remains of the stoas and public buildings that once surrounded the square. Let your imagination fill in the buildings around them.

items.text: And finally, Kadifekale: the acropolis of ancient Smyrna, set atop the hill that overlooks İzmir. The old city and the new still share this view.

items.text: As you wander through the agora, don't miss the Basilica, and take your time there.
items.speech: As you wander through the agora, don't miss the Basilica, and take your time there.

items.text: Did you know? Smyrna was one of the Seven Churches of Revelation, and one that has survived to the present day. It was also one of seven cities claiming to be Homer's birthplace, and the one with the strongest claim. After the earthquake of AD 178, the agora's three-storey basilica was rebuilt with a donation from the empress Faustina. And in the fourth century BC the city moved, on Alexander's orders, to the slopes of today's Kadifekale; İzmir still sits on that plan.

items.text: Near Milas, in Muğla province, lies Euromus, an ancient Carian city whose story runs from the 6th century BC to the 4th century AD. It is famous above all for one sight: its standing Temple of Zeus.
items.speech: Near Milas, in Muğla province, lies Euromus, an ancient Carian city whose story runs from the 6th century BC to the 4th century AD. It is famous above all for one sight: its standing Temple of Zeus.

items.text: From the 6th century BC the city developed within the Carian world, and it passed through Persian and then Roman rule. Its great treasure is the Temple of Zeus Lepsinos, one of the best-preserved colonnaded temples in Anatolia.
items.speech: From the 6th century BC the city developed within the Carian world, and it passed through Persian and then Roman rule. Its great treasure is the Temple of Zeus Lepsinos, one of the best-preserved colonnaded temples in Anatolia.

items.text: You are now before the Temple of Zeus Lepsinos, the temple of Zeus at Euromos. Look up: 16 of its columns are still standing, catching the light as they have for centuries.
items.speech: You are now before the Temple of Zeus Lepsinos, the temple of Zeus at Euromos. Look up: 16 of its columns are still standing, catching the light as they have for centuries.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the stadium and the theatre, then the bouleuterion and the city walls.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the stadium and the theatre, then the bouleuterion and the city walls.

items.text: Did you know? An inscription on the temple records that it was dedicated in the name of Emperor Hadrian. With sixteen columns still standing, the Temple of Zeus Lepsinos is among the best-preserved temples in Anatolia. Look closely and you will see that some columns were never fluted: the temple was left unfinished, and the stone itself tells you so. Inscriptions on the columns even record, by name, which citizen paid for each one.

items.text: Here is Nysa, an ancient city in Aydın province whose story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 6th century AD. It lies near Sultanhisar, and it is known for its tunnel-lined street and its grand library.

items.text: Founded in the Hellenistic period, Nysa became a wealthy cultural centre of the Maeander valley. Its huge library and the tunnel-lined basilica street still show the splendour the city reached in the Roman era.
items.speech: Founded in the Hellenistic period, Nysa became a wealthy cultural centre of the Maeander valley. Its huge library and the tunnel-lined basilica street still show the splendour the city reached in the Roman era.

items.text: You are now at the Tunnel Street. A vaulted stone tunnel was built over the stream that divides the city, and on top of it ran the city's street and square. Think of it: daily life went on above, while the water flowed beneath.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Library and the Theatre, and make your way to the Stadium and the Gymnasium too.

items.text: Did you know? The library at Nysa is the second-largest ancient library in Anatolia after the Library of Celsus at Ephesus. The vaulted tunnel carrying the city over its ravine runs about 100 metres, among the longest bridge vaults of antiquity. The geographer Strabo studied here as a young man and described the city from first-hand observation. And the council house survives almost intact, marble seating and all.

items.text: People have lived here since the 3rd millennium BC. The city was important in Lydian times, and under Rome it grew wealthy from its dye and textile industries. As one of the Seven Churches, Thyatira was the most important Roman city east of Smyrna.

items.text: Did you know? Thyatira was one of the seven churches of Revelation, and the city was famous for dyeing. Its name is linked to the region's famed dyeing industry, and its purple dye is celebrated in ancient sources. Lydia, the 'seller of purple' whom Paul met at Philippi in Acts, came from here. Today the ruins sit on an island of ground in the middle of modern Akhisar, ringed by apartment blocks.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Noel Baba olarak bilinen Aziz Nikolaos, MS 270 civarında bu kentte doğdu. Likya Birliği'nin meclis binası da burada. Temsilciler kentlerinin büyüklüğüne göre oy kullanırdı ve bu sistem, Montesquieu üzerinden ABD anayasa tartışmalarında federalizm örneği olarak anıldı. Bir de fener var: Neron döneminde dikilen deniz feneri, dünyanın ayakta kalabilmiş en eski fenerlerinden biri. Parçaları bulunup yeniden birleştirildi.

items.text: Here at Patara, an ancient city in Antalya province, the story reaches back to the 5th century BC. This was the capital of the Lycian League, and home to what may be the world's first parliament building.
items.speech: Here at Patara, an ancient city in Antalya province, the story reaches back to the 5th century BC. This was the capital of the Lycian League, and home to what may be the world's first parliament building.

items.text: Patara was Lycia's principal port and the seat of an oracle of Apollo. It became the Roman provincial capital, and then, for centuries, it lay preserved beneath sand dunes.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Bouleuterion, the assembly building, and the Triumphal Arch; then visit the theatre, the lighthouse and the colonnaded street.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Bouleuterion, the assembly building, and the Triumphal Arch; then visit the theatre, the lighthouse and the colonnaded street.

items.text: Did you know? Saint Nicholas, better known as Santa Claus, was born here around AD 270. The Lycian League met in the council house here, and its system, with delegates voting in proportion to their city's size, reached the American constitutional debates as a model of federalism, by way of Montesquieu. And the lighthouse, raised under Nero, is among the oldest surviving anywhere; its blocks were found and reassembled.

items.text: Ksanthos'un hikâyesinde ağır bir gurur var. Kent tarih boyunca iki kez, teslim olmaktansa kendini yakmayı seçti. Ve Likçe yazıtların en zengin koleksiyonu, işte bu kentten çıktı.

items.text: Gezerken Harpy Anıtı'nın ve Nereidler Anıtı'nın önünde durun, Likya lahitlerinin arasında yürüyün. Tiyatroya ve Letoon kutsal alanına da mutlaka uğrayın.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Nereidler Anıtı'nın özgün blokları bugün British Museum'da sergileniyor. Kent, tarihinde iki kez düşmana teslim olmaktansa kendini yaktı: önce Perslere karşı, sonra Roma iç savaşında Brutus'a karşı. Herodotos ve Appianos bu iki olayı da anlatır. Nereidler Anıtı ve Harpy Anıtı'nın kabartmaları 1842'de sökülüp British Museum'a götürüldü; bugün yerlerinde müzedeki kopyalarıyla duruyorlar. Ve Likçe yazılı dikilitaş, bilinen en uzun Likçe metin; bu dilin çözülmesindeki anahtar belgelerden biri.

items.text: You are in Xanthos, an ancient city in Antalya province whose story goes back to the 8th century BC. It was Lycia's largest city and the capital of monumental tomb architecture.
items.speech: You are in Xanthos, an ancient city in Antalya province whose story goes back to the 8th century BC. It was Lycia's largest city and the capital of monumental tomb architecture.

items.text: Xanthos has a proud and painful past: twice in its history, the city chose self-immolation over surrender. It also gave us the richest collection of Lycian inscriptions known.
items.speech: Xanthos has a proud and painful past: twice in its history, the city chose self-immolation over surrender. It also gave us the richest collection of Lycian inscriptions known.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Harpy Monument and the Nereid Monument, the Lycian sarcophagi and the theatre, and finally the Letoon sanctuary.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Harpy Monument and the Nereid Monument, the Lycian sarcophagi and the theatre, and finally the Letoon sanctuary.

items.text: Did you know? Twice in its history the city burned itself rather than surrender: first to the Persians, then to Brutus in Rome's civil war. Herodotus and Appian each record one. In 1842 the Nereid and Harpy Monument reliefs were removed to the British Museum, where the original blocks of the Nereid Monument are displayed today; casts stand in their place here. And the inscribed pillar here carries the longest known text in Lycian, a key document in deciphering the language.

items.text: Welcome to Myra, an ancient city in Antalya province from the 5th century BC. This Lycian city is known for two things above all: its cliff of rock tombs and the church of Saint Nicholas.
items.speech: Welcome to Myra, an ancient city in Antalya province from the 5th century BC. This Lycian city is known for two things above all: its cliff of rock tombs and the church of Saint Nicholas.

items.text: Myra was one of the six great cities of the Lycian League. Then, in the 4th century, the tomb of its bishop Nicholas turned it into a pilgrimage centre.
items.speech: Myra was one of the six great cities of the Lycian League. Then, in the 4th century, the tomb of its bishop Nicholas turned it into a pilgrimage centre.

items.text: You are now at the Church of St Nicholas in Myra. The legend of its saint inspired Santa Claus, so a figure known far and wide traces back to this very place.
items.speech: You are now at the Church of St Nicholas in Myra. The legend of its saint inspired Santa Claus, so a figure known far and wide traces back to this very place.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the rock-cut tombs and the Roman theatre, and then the Andriake harbour.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the rock-cut tombs and the Roman theatre, and then the Andriake harbour.

items.text: Did you know? The rock tombs imitate wooden Lycian houses, with beams and doors carved into stone. They are, in effect, a photograph in stone of an architecture that has otherwise vanished. Saint Nicholas served as bishop here; his church stands in modern Demre, and his tomb was in it. And look at the theatre: it was rebuilt after an earthquake, and blocks from the toppled stage building still lie where they fell.

items.text: Here in Antalya province lies Olympos, an ancient city of the 2nd century BC. Its ruins are wrapped in laurel forest, beside the never-dying flames of Chimaera.
items.speech: Here in Antalya province lies Olympos, an ancient city of the 2nd century BC. Its ruins are wrapped in laurel forest, beside the never-dying flames of Chimaera.

items.text: Olympos was once notorious as a pirate base, and it was pacified only when Rome cleared the seas. Around the natural gas flames nearby, the cult of Hephaestus grew — a cult born beside a fire that never goes out.

items.text: You are now at the Chimaera flames, everlasting flames rising from the rock. In myth they are the breath of the Chimera. Pause for a moment and watch them burn.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the harbour baths and the theatre, then the sarcophagi, and finally the bridge piers.

items.text: Did you know? The flames of Chimaera have burned without pause for at least 2,500 years. In the first century BC the pirate chief Zeniketes made the city his base, and Rome had to drive him out. Today the ruins are swallowed by laurel and oleander, with a stream running through the middle of the city to the sea.

items.text: Pine forest, sea and stone: welcome to Phaselis, an ancient city in Antalya province from the 7th century BC. This was a seaside port city with three natural harbours, ringed by pine forest.

items.text: Phaselis was founded by Rhodians, and it prospered on trade in rose oil and timber. It even hosted a famous guest: Alexander the Great spent a winter here.

items.text: Did you know? Phaselis had three harbours within walking distance of each other, so that whichever way the wind blew, one was sheltered. The ancient main street, a colonnaded street, still connects two of those harbours, and you can walk it. Alexander the Great wintered here in 333 BC, and the city greeted him with a golden crown. And its wealth? It grew rich on rose oil and timber.

items.text: Did you know? A water channel ran down the centre of the 250-metre colonnaded street. It was the city's cooling system, ancient air-conditioning for the summer. Apollonius of Perga, who defined the conic sections, came from here: we owe him the words ellipse, parabola and hyperbola. And the city's greatest benefactor was a woman, Plancia Magna, who rebuilt its gate; her statues and inscriptions were found there.

items.text: Imagine a theatre so well kept that music still fills it today. You are in Aspendos, an ancient city in Antalya province whose story reaches back to the 5th century BC. Its theatre is the best-preserved of the ancient world, and it still hosts concerts.
items.speech: Imagine a theatre so well kept that music still fills it today. You are in Aspendos, an ancient city in Antalya province whose story reaches back to the 5th century BC. Its theatre is the best-preserved of the ancient world, and it still hosts concerts.

items.text: Aspendos grew rich on the Eurymedon, trading in salt, oil and horses. Its theatre was built by the architect Zeno in the 2nd century. And why does it still stand? Because the Seljuks reused it as a caravanserai, and so the building never fell out of use.
items.speech: Aspendos grew rich on the Eurymedon, trading in salt, oil and horses. Its theatre was built by the architect Zeno in the 2nd century. And why does it still stand? Because the Seljuks reused it as a caravanserai, and so the building never fell out of use.

items.text: You are now in the Roman Theatre, the most completely preserved theatre of antiquity. Notice how the seating bank and the stage building are bonded into a single block. It reached us intact for one simple reason: the Seljuqs kept it in use as a caravanserai.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Aqueducts and the Basilica, then walk on to the Agora and the Stadium.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Aqueducts and the Basilica, then walk on to the Agora and the Stadium.

items.text: Did you know? The acoustics are so precise that a whisper on stage reaches the 41st row. This is the best-preserved theatre in the Roman world: the stage building stands to its full height, and concerts are still held here. The architect Zeno is named in an inscription, and a legend tells of a king who promised his daughter to whoever built best, with the theatre winning the prize. The city's aqueduct is one of antiquity's rare pressurised systems, working on the inverted-siphon principle.

items.text: Wussten Sie schon? Die Akustik ist so präzise, dass ein Flüstern auf der Bühne bis in die 41. Reihe dringt. Sein Theater ist das am besten erhaltene der römischen Welt – das Bühnengebäude steht in voller Höhe, und es finden noch immer Konzerte darin statt. Der Architekt Zenon wird in einer Inschrift genannt. Der Legende nach versprach der König seine Tochter demjenigen, der am besten baute – und das Theater gewann. Sein Aquädukt ist eines der seltenen Drucksysteme der Antike und arbeitet nach dem Prinzip des umgekehrten Siphons.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Side, Kleopatra ile Marcus Antonius'un buluştuğu kentlerden biri olarak anılır. Adının da bir anlamı var: yerli Anadolu dilinde 'nar' demek. Roma döneminde Akdeniz'in en büyük köle pazarlarından biri buradaydı; korsanlar yağmalarını burada satardı. Ve Apollon Tapınağı'nın denize bakan sütunları, gün batımında kentin simgesi hâline geldi.

items.text: Here the ancient and the modern live side by side. You are in Side, in Antalya province, a city whose story begins in the 7th century BC and whose ruins are woven into a modern town. Its fame rests on the Temple of Apollo, standing out on the point.
items.speech: Here the ancient and the modern live side by side. You are in Side, in Antalya province, a city whose story begins in the 7th century BC and whose ruins are woven into a modern town. Its fame rests on the Temple of Apollo, standing out on the point.

items.text: Side was a port, and a busy one: a major centre of the slave trade, with a language all its own. It grew into one of the largest cities of Pamphylia, and its theatre could seat 15,000 people. Imagine the noise of the harbour and the crowds that filled those seats.

items.text: You are now at the Theatre, the largest in Pamphylia. Most ancient theatres lean against a hillside, but this one is rare: it was built on level ground, its cavea raised on a two-storey vaulted substructure. Its three-storey stage building once faced the colonnaded street of the city.

items.text: Before you is the Monumental Fountain, the city's principal water-dispensing structure. Look for its decoration of gods and mythological figures, and imagine the water flowing past them into the life of the town.

items.text: Here is the city gate, the monumental gateway in the city walls. Gates like this were often built in the form of a triumphal arch, so that arriving here was itself a small ceremony.

items.text: As you wander through Side, don't miss the Temple of Apollo, and make time for the Agora as well.
items.speech: As you wander through Side, don't miss the Temple of Apollo, and make time for the Agora as well.

items.text: Did you know? Side is remembered as one of the places where Cleopatra met Mark Antony. Its very name means 'pomegranate' in the local Anatolian language. In Roman times it held one of the Mediterranean's largest slave markets, where pirates sold what they had taken. And today, at sunset, the seaward columns of the Temple of Apollo have become the emblem of the city.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Tiyatrodan Güllük Dağı'na bakan manzara, antik dünyanın en dramatik sahne arkasıdır. Büyük İskender kenti kuşattı ama alamadan çekildi; Anadolu'da onu geri çeviren ender yerlerden biri. Kent 1000 metrenin üzerinde, kartal yuvası gibi bir yamaçtadır; tiyatronun sahnesinin arkası doğrudan uçuruma ve Güllük Dağı'na bakar. Ve kent hiç sistemli kazılmadı: Devasa lahitler, kaya mezarları ve sarnıçlar, ormanın içinde devrildikleri yerde duruyor.

items.text: Look around you: this is Termessos, an ancient city in Antalya province dating from the 5th century BC. Perched like an eagle's nest at 1,050 m, it is the city Alexander the Great failed to take.
items.speech: Look around you: this is Termessos, an ancient city in Antalya province dating from the 5th century BC. Perched like an eagle's nest at 1,050 metres, it is the city Alexander the Great failed to take.

items.text: The Pisidians founded Termessos, and its natural defences kept invaders out. Yet what armies could not do, an earthquake did: it wrecked the city's water system, the city was abandoned, and the forest slowly swallowed it.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Theatre, the Gymnasium and the Cisterns, then walk on to the Necropolis and the King's Road.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Theatre, the Gymnasium and the Cisterns, then walk on to the Necropolis and the King's Road.

items.text: Did you know? Its theatre looks out over Güllük mountain — arguably antiquity's most dramatic backdrop. Alexander the Great besieged the city and withdrew without taking it, making it one of the few places in Anatolia to turn him back. Termessos sits above 1,000 metres like an eagle's nest; behind the theatre stage there is nothing but the drop and Mount Güllük. The city has never been systematically excavated, so giant sarcophagi, rock tombs and cisterns still lie in the forest where they fell.

items.text: Did you know? Pinara's legendary founder is Pandarus, regarded as the mythical ancestor of the Lycians. The sheer rock face behind the city is honeycombed with hundreds of tombs, and how anyone reached them is still argued over. The reliefs of the 'Royal Tomb' depict four walled Lycian cities: Lycians drawing their own towns. And the theatre stands in the forest, its seating entirely untouched.

items.text: Above the Xanthus valley lies Oenoanda, an ancient city in Muğla province whose story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 3rd century AD. It is famous for one remarkable thing: the colossal inscription of the Epicurean Diogenes.

items.text: Oenoanda was a Lycian city in the north, also known as Termessus Minor. Diogenes of Oenoanda, an Epicurean of the 2nd century AD, had his philosophy inscribed on a vast stone stoa in the city's agora: a lesson in stone for everyone who came to the market.

items.text: You are now looking at the Diogenes Inscription. In this vast stone inscription in the city's agora, the Epicurean philosopher Diogenes of Oenoanda set out his teaching. Imagine stopping on your way through the market to read a philosopher's words cut in stone.

items.text: Did you know? Diogenes' 25,000-word inscription is the longest philosophical text to survive from antiquity. The Epicurean had his philosophy carved onto a wall in the city's market, some 80 metres long: the longest known inscription of antiquity. The city lies at 1,400 metres on a wooded ridge, and blocks of that inscription are still being gathered among the ruins.

items.text: The city was founded as a trading colony in the 2nd century BC and grew with the support of the Cappadocian king Archelaus. Linked to the land by an isthmus, and graced with its theatre, agora and churches, it became one of Cilicia's important ports.

items.text: Did you know? The city's name means 'olive city', and the island's olive trees still bear fruit today. The city began on an islet; when the channel silted up, the island joined the shore and the city spread onto it. King Archelaus of Cappadocia made it his second capital and renamed it Sebaste in honour of Augustus. Today theatre, baths and basilica line up along the shore, with the modern road running straight through them.

items.text: The city was founded by Seleucus I Nicator and grew on the banks of the Göksu, the ancient Calycadnus river. It stood at the crossroads of inland routes, and in Roman and Byzantine times that position made it an important centre of Cilicia.

items.text: Did you know? Founded in the 3rd century BC, the city bears the name of the Seleucid dynasty: 'Seleucia on the Calycadnus'. Its founder, Seleucus I Nicator, was Alexander's general, and this is one of the many cities he named after himself. Here in 1190, on the Third Crusade, Frederick Barbarossa drowned in the Göksu — the ancient Calycadnus — and the crusade fell apart. Today a column of the Temple of Zeus and the Roman bridge still stand amid the traffic of modern Silifke.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Höyükte dokuz farklı kent katmanı üst üste duruyor; Homeros'un Troya'sı büyük olasılıkla Troya VI/VII. Schliemann 1871'de kazarken Homeros'un Troya'sını arıyordu. Hızla derine indi, aradığı katı geçti ve 'Priamos'un Hazinesi'ni bin yıl daha eski bir katta buldu. Tahta attan ise hiçbir iz bulunmadı. Buna karşılık Hitit tabletlerinde, Troya'nın yeriyle uyuşan 'Wilusa' adlı bir kentle yapılan antlaşmalar geçiyor. Son olarak: Kentin surlarındaki eğimli taş duvarın, İlyada'da Patroklos'un üç kez tırmanıp üç kez geri atıldığı duvar olduğu sanılıyor.

items.text: Here legend meets the earth. You are at Troy, a mound in Çanakkale province, whose story reaches back to 3000 BC. Beneath your feet lie nine cities, one on top of another — the legendary mound behind Homer's Iliad.
items.speech: Here legend meets the earth. You are at Troy, a mound in Çanakkale province, whose story reaches back to 3000 BC. Beneath your feet lie nine cities, one on top of another, the legendary mound behind Homer's Iliad.

items.text: People lived here for 5,000 years. In the 1870s Heinrich Schliemann excavated the mound. He proved the legend was real — but in doing so, he damaged its layers.

items.text: And here stands the Trojan horse replica, a copy of the famous wooden horse from Homer's Iliad. Look up at it and imagine the story that made it immortal.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the city walls, the ramped gateway, the Odeon and the Temple of Athena.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the city walls, the ramped gateway, the Odeon and the Temple of Athena.

items.text: Did you know? Nine cities stand stacked in this mound, and Homer's Troy is most likely level VI/VII. Digging in 1871, Schliemann drove straight past the layer he was looking for and found his 'Treasure of Priam' in one a thousand years too old. No trace of the wooden horse has ever been found. Hittite tablets, however, record treaties with a city called Wilusa, in the right place to be Troy. And the battered stone wall of the citadel is taken for the one that Patroclus climbs three times in the Iliad — and is thrown back from three times.

items.text: Wussten Sie schon? Der Hügel birgt neun Stadtschichten; Homers Troja ist höchstwahrscheinlich Schicht VI/VII. Im Hügel liegen neun Städte übereinander. Als Schliemann 1871 grub, stieß er geradewegs an der gesuchten Schicht vorbei und fand seinen „Schatz des Priamos“ in einer, die tausend Jahre zu alt war. Vom hölzernen Pferd wurde keine Spur gefunden. Hethitische Tontafeln verzeichnen jedoch Verträge mit einer Stadt namens Wilusa, die genau dort lag, wo Troja sein müsste. Die geböschte Steinmauer der Zitadelle gilt als jene, die Patroklos in der Ilias dreimal erklimmt und von der er dreimal zurückgeworfen wird.

items.text: А вы знали? Холм хранит девять городских слоёв; Троя Гомера — скорее всего, слой VI/VII. В холме друг над другом лежат девять городов. Копая в 1871 году, Шлиман прошёл прямо сквозь искомый слой и нашёл свой «клад Приама» в слое на тысячу лет древнее. Никаких следов деревянного коня не найдено. Однако хеттские таблички упоминают договоры с городом под названием Вилуса, который находился как раз там, где должна быть Троя. Покатую каменную стену цитадели принимают за ту, на которую в «Илиаде» трижды взбирается Патрокл и с которой его трижды отбрасывают.

items.text: High above the Aegean, in Çanakkale province, lies Assos, an ancient city whose story begins in the 7th century BC. Here a temple of Athena crowns the city where Aristotle taught.

items.text: Aristotle lived and taught here for three years. The city itself was known for its andesite walls and its busy harbour.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Temple of Athena and the ancient harbour, then follow the city walls to the necropolis, and end at the agora.

items.text: Did you know? Assos sarcophagi were believed to consume flesh — hence the word 'sarcophagus'. Aristotle spent three years here, founded a school, and married the ruler's niece, and he began his biological work in the gulf below. The Temple of Athena is the only archaic Doric temple in Anatolia. And Saint Paul walked here from Troas on his third journey and took ship from this harbour; Acts records it by name.

Zamanla oluşan kum seti onu anakaraya bağladı ve kent bugün Kapıdağ Yarımadası'nın boynundadır. Ve paraları: Kyzikos elektron staterleri yüzyıllarca Ege ve Karadeniz ticaretinin ortak parası gibi kullanıldı.

items.text: You are standing at Cyzicus, an ancient city in Balıkesir province, whose story begins in the 7th century BC. This was a great Marmara city on the Kapıdağ peninsula, and it is remembered above all for its Hadrian temple.
items.speech: You are standing at Cyzicus, an ancient city in Balıkesir province, whose story begins in the 7th century BC. This was a great Marmara city on the Kapıdağ peninsula, and it is remembered above all for its Hadrian temple.

items.text: Cyzicus was founded as a colony of Miletus. Its electrum coins became a standard of Aegean and Black Sea trade, and in antiquity its Temple of Hadrian was called the eighth wonder.
items.speech: Cyzicus was founded as a colony of Miletus. Its electrum coins became a standard of Aegean and Black Sea trade, and in antiquity its Temple of Hadrian was called the eighth wonder.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Temple of Hadrian, the Amphitheatre, the Aqueducts and the Harbour remains.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Temple of Hadrian, the Amphitheatre, the Aqueducts and the Harbour remains.

items.text: Did you know? The city was once an island. A sandbar tied it to the mainland, and today it sits on the neck of the Kapıdağ peninsula. Its amphitheatre is one of only a handful of true amphitheatres in Anatolia. The Temple of Hadrian was called the eighth wonder of the world, and travellers in the fifteenth century still counted thirty columns standing. And Cyzicene electrum staters served for centuries as a common currency across Aegean and Black Sea trade.

İznik Gölü'nün suları altında MS 4. yüzyıla ait bir bazilika bulunuyor. 325'te İznik Konsili burada toplandı ve bugün hâlâ okunan İznik İnancı burada yazıldı. 787'de kent ikinci kez bir konsile ev sahipliği yaptı; ikon kırıcılığı burada sona erdirildi. Ve 1204'te Haçlılar İstanbul'u alınca Bizans'ın sürgündeki başkenti İznik oldu. İmparatorluk da buradan geri kazanıldı.

items.text: Beside a lake in Bursa province lies Nicaea, an ancient city whose story begins in the 4th century BC. Its 5 km of walls still stand, and this is the city that hosted the church councils.
items.speech: Beside a lake in Bursa province lies Nicaea, an ancient city whose story begins in the 4th century BC. Its 5 kilometres of walls still stand, and this is the city that hosted the church councils.

items.text: The city was founded by Antigonus, one of Alexander's generals. In AD 325 it hosted the Council of Nicaea, and later it served as a Byzantine capital.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Roman walls and the Istanbul Gate. Visit the theatre and the Hagia Sophia (Orhan Mosque), and look for the lake basilica.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Roman walls and the Istanbul Gate. Visit the theatre and the Hagia Sophia (Orhan Mosque), and look for the lake basilica.

items.text: Did you know? A 4th-century basilica lies submerged beneath the waters of Lake İznik. The Council of Nicaea met here in 325 and wrote the creed still recited today. In 787 the city hosted a second council, which brought iconoclasm to an end. And when the crusaders took Constantinople in 1204, Nicaea became the Byzantine capital in exile; it was from here that the empire was won back.

items.text: You are standing in Alexandria Troas, an ancient city in Çanakkale province, whose life stretches from 310 BC to the 6th century AD. It was founded by Antigonus, one of Alexander's generals, and it grew into one of the largest ancient cities of Anatolia.
items.speech: You are standing in Alexandria Troas, an ancient city in Çanakkale province, whose life stretches from 310 BC to the 6th century AD. It was founded by Antigonus, one of Alexander's generals, and it grew into one of the largest ancient cities of Anatolia.

items.text: Antigonus Monophthalmus founded the city in 310 BC in the Troad, and it quickly became one of Rome's most important harbour cities. Emperors came here: Augustus and Hadrian both visited. So did St Paul, passing through on his journeys west. And the scale! Covering some 400 hectares, it was even larger than Ephesus, one of the largest urban fabrics of the Roman world.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Roman Bath and the Odeon, then the Theatre and the Gymnasium, and finally the City Walls.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Roman Bath and the Odeon, then the Theatre and the Gymnasium, and finally the City Walls.

items.text: Did you know? The city covered roughly 400 hectares, even more than Ephesus, making it one of the largest Roman cities in Anatolia. It was also one of Anatolia's largest ports under Rome, and by ancient report Constantine seriously considered founding his capital here. It was here that Saint Paul dreamed of the man calling 'Come over to Macedonia' — Christianity's crossing into Europe began at this harbour. Today the ruins lie scattered through oak woodland, and the locals call the bath building the 'Honey Palace'.

items.text: You have arrived at Parium, an ancient city in Çanakkale province, with a story spanning the 7th century BC to the 13th century AD. It was a Greek harbour city on the Troad coast of the Sea of Marmara, and it was famed for two things: its odeon and its coinage.

items.text: Parium was founded in the 7th century BC by colonists from Paros, Thasos and Erythrae. It prospered thanks to its strategic harbour at the southern entrance to the straits. Under Rome and Byzantium it was an important bishopric, until it was abandoned in the 13th century.

items.text: Did you know? Parium won the status of a Roman colony and struck its own coins, marked with a Gorgon's head. Its hemidrachms bearing the Gorgon are among the best-known coins of the ancient world. Thousands of graves have been excavated in its necropolis, making it one of Anatolia's richest records of Roman burial custom.

items.text: Did you know? The Persian reliefs of Dascylium are among the most important examples of Achaemenid art found in Anatolia. This was the seat of the Persian satrapy of western Anatolia, the best-documented site of Persian rule in the region. Hundreds of clay sealings survive: all that is left of an archive that burned, preserved because the fire baked them. And the mound overlooks Lake Manyas; ancient sources describe the satrap's garden here as a hunting park.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Lampsakos, antik dünyanın en zengin darphanelerinden birine sahipti; kentin koruyucusu ise bahçe tanrısı Priapos'tu. Pers Kralı Artakserkses, Atinalı komutan Themistokles'e sürgününde bu kenti 'şarap parası' olarak bağışladı. Filozof Anaksagoras burada öldü ve kent, onun anısına her yıl çocuklara okulun tatil olduğu bir gün ilan etti. Bir filozofu okul tatiliyle anmak... Ve bereket tanrısı Priapos'un kültünün merkezi burası olduğu için, kentin adı antik edebiyatta sık sık geçer.

items.text: On the eastern shore of the Dardanelles, in Çanakkale province, lie the remains of Lampsacus, an ancient city of the 7th century BC – 4th century AD. It was famous for two things: its mint and the cult of Priapus.
items.speech: On the eastern shore of the Dardanelles, in Çanakkale province, lie the remains of Lampsacus, an ancient city of the 7th century BC, 4th century AD. It was famous for two things: its mint and the cult of Priapus.

items.text: Phocaean colonists founded the city in the 7th century BC. Its strategic position by the straits brought trade, and trade brought wealth. Under Persia and Rome, Lampsacus remained a cultural centre — and its name lives on today in the modern town of Lapseki.

items.text: Did you know? Lampsacus had one of the richest mints in the ancient world, and its patron god, Priapus, was the deity of gardens. The Persian king Artaxerxes granted the city to the exiled Athenian Themistocles to cover his wine. The philosopher Anaxagoras died here, and the city honoured his memory with an annual school holiday for its children. And as the centre of the cult of Priapus, its name recurs again and again in ancient literature.

items.speech: Above Altınoluk, on Kaletaşı hill in Balıkesir province, lies Antandros, an ancient city of the Troad whose story runs from the 8th century BC to the 4th century AD. It is known for its mosaic villas and its tomb necropolis.

items.text: People have lived here since the 8th century BC. The city was famed for its timber, which was used to build Persian warships. Under Rome it was adorned with luxurious villas, and since excavations began in 2001 they have been coming back to light.

items.text: Did you know? The 'Abduction of Europa' mosaic in the Roman villa at Antandros, found in 2005, counts among Turkey's most important mosaic discoveries. In Virgil's Aeneid, it was right here that Aeneas built the ships he fled Troy in, from the timber of Mount Ida. And the mosaics and wall paintings of an excavated Roman villa record a life of coastal luxury at the foot of the Kaz mountains.

items.text: Did you know? The Midas tumulus contains the oldest standing wooden chamber in the world. The Gordian Knot was here too, in the city's temple, with its prophecy that whoever untied it would rule Asia — and Alexander cut it with his sword. And residues in the cauldrons of the burial chamber have been analysed: the funeral feast was washed down with a drink of honey, grape and barley.

Ölüler evin tabanının altına, ailenin uyuduğu platformların altına gömülürdü. Ve bir duvar resmi var ki arkasında patlayan bir volkanla birlikte kuşbakışı bir yerleşim planı gösterir. Bu resim, dünyanın bilinen en eski haritası ve en eski volkan tasviri sayılıyor; dünyanın en eski haritası olabileceği öne sürülüyor.

items.text: Picture a town without streets. You are at Çatalhöyük, a mound in Konya province dating to 7400 BC, and one of the world's earliest urban settlements.
items.speech: Picture a town without streets. You are at Çatalhöyük, a mound in Konya province dating to 7400 BC, and one of the world's earliest urban settlements.

items.text: Some 8,000 people once lived here, and they entered their houses through the roof. Their wall paintings and mother-goddess figurines are landmarks of prehistoric art.
items.speech: Some 8,000 people once lived here, and they entered their houses through the roof. Their wall paintings and mother-goddess figurines are landmarks of prehistoric art.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the North excavation shelter and the Experimental house. Look for the wall paintings, and then head on to the South mound.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the North excavation shelter and the Experimental house. Look for the wall paintings, and then head on to the South mound.

items.text: Did you know? This 9,000-year-old settlement has no streets. Houses were built wall to wall and entered by ladder through the roof, so the rooftops were the street. The dead were buried beneath the floors of the houses, under the platforms where the family slept. And one wall painting shows a settlement plan from above, with an erupting volcano behind it. It is considered by some the world's oldest known map, and the oldest known depiction of a volcano.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Tabletlerin arasında dünyanın bilinen en eski evlilik sözleşmelerinden biri de var. Anadolu yazıyla burada tanıştı: Asurlu tüccarların bıraktığı 23.000'den fazla çivi yazılı tablet, Anadolu'nun ilk yazılı belgeleridir. Ama bunlar destan değil, muhasebe. Borç senetleri, ortaklık sözleşmeleri, mahkeme kayıtları, eve yazılmış mektuplar. Birinde bir tüccarın karısı, ona daha iyi kumaş göndermesini yazıyor. Höyüğün eteğindeki karum ise tüccarların yaşadığı ayrı bir mahalleydi; bilinen en eski uluslararası ticaret kolonilerinden biri.

items.text: This is where Anatolia learned to write. You are at Kültepe, ancient Kanesh, a mound in Kayseri province whose story reaches back to the 3rd millennium BC. Here an Assyrian trading colony left behind Anatolia's first written documents.
items.speech: This is where Anatolia learned to write. You are at Kültepe, ancient Kanesh, a mound in Kayseri province whose story reaches back to the 3rd millennium BC. Here an Assyrian trading colony left behind Anatolia's first written documents.

items.text: Assyrian merchants came here and founded a karum, a trading colony. They left behind over 23,000 cuneiform tablets, found on this very site, and with them begins the written history of Anatolia.
items.speech: Assyrian merchants came here and founded a karum, a trading colony. They left behind over 23,000 cuneiform tablets, found on this very site, and with them begins the written history of Anatolia.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Karum quarter and the Palace remains, then the Tablet archives and the Mound itself.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Karum quarter and the Palace remains, then the Tablet archives and the Mound itself.

items.text: Did you know? Among the tablets is one of the world's earliest known marriage contracts. Anatolia met writing here: the 23,000-plus cuneiform tablets left by Assyrian merchants are the earliest written documents from Anatolia. Yet they are not epic but bookkeeping — promissory notes, partnership contracts, court records, letters home. One merchant's wife writes telling him to send better cloth. And the karum at the foot of the mound was a separate merchants' quarter, one of the earliest known international trading colonies.

items.text: You stand at the gate of Cappadocia. This is Tyana, an ancient city in Niğde province whose story reaches back to the 2nd millennium BC. A Roman city, with aqueducts and a sacred pool.

items.text: Tyana was built over the late Hittite town of Tuwanuwa, and under Rome it became Cappadocia's second city. It is also the birthplace of the philosopher Apollonius.
items.speech: Tyana was built over the late Hittite town of Tuwanuwa, and under Rome it became Cappadocia's second city. It is also the birthplace of the philosopher Apollonius.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Roman aqueduct and the Spring pool, then the Mosaics and the Mound.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Roman aqueduct and the Spring pool, then the Mosaics and the Mound.

items.text: Did you know? The spring that fed the aqueduct still fills the city's pool today. The philosopher Apollonius of Tyana came from here; his contemporaries credited him with miracles, and Rome long set him up as a rival figure to Christ. In the Hittite period the city was Tuwanuwa, and the nearby İvriz relief records the region's Neo-Hittite phase.

items.text: Here, in Eskişehir province, lies Pessinus, an ancient city whose story runs from the 8th century BC to the 4th century AD. This was the cult centre of the Mother Goddess Cybele, and the holiest city of the Phrygians.
items.speech: Here, in Eskişehir province, lies Pessinus, an ancient city whose story runs from the 8th century BC to the 4th century AD. This was the cult centre of the Mother Goddess Cybele, and the holiest city of the Phrygians.

items.text: Pessinus was the homeland of the Cybele cult and the holiest city of Phrygia, and its fame reached all the way to Rome. In 205 BC the Romans resolved to carry off the city's sacred black stone to secure victory over Hannibal; in 204 BC the stone arrived in Rome. Yet Pessinus did not fade: it remained important under Galatian and Roman rule.

items.text: Did you know? When the Romans carried Cybele's sacred black stone from here to Rome, it marked the first transfer of an Anatolian cult to the capital. Pessinus was the sanctuary of Cybele, and in 204 BC, following a prophecy meant to defeat Hannibal, Rome took the goddess's sacred black stone away to the capital. The marble steps in front of the sanctuary served both as a ceremonial stair and as theatre seating. And the stream that divides the city was channelled in antiquity between marble-faced banks.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Amorium, Bizans'ın Anadolu'daki en büyük askerî üslerinden biriydi ve imparator hanedanının memleketiydi. 838'de Halife Mutasım kenti kuşatıp yıktı. Bu Amorion kuşatmasında yakalanan komutanlar İslam'a geçmeyi reddetti ve idam edildi. Onlar, 'Amorium'un 42 Şehidi' olarak Bizans azizler takvimine girdi; '42 Şehit', Hristiyanlık tarihinin ünlü efsanelerinden biri oldu.

items.text: You are standing in Amorium, an ancient city in Afyonkarahisar province whose story runs from the 2nd millennium BC to the 11th century AD. It was a major Byzantine military city, and it is remembered above all for the Arab sack of 838.
items.speech: You are standing in Amorium, an ancient city in Afyonkarahisar province whose story runs from the 2nd millennium BC to the 11th century AD. It was a major Byzantine military city, and it is remembered above all for the Arab sack of 838.

items.text: People lived here from Phrygian times. The city lay on the military road from Constantinople to Cilicia, and it was the birthplace of Emperor Theophilos. Then came 838. The Abbasids sacked Amorium, and it never fully recovered.

items.text: Did you know? Amorium was one of Byzantium's largest military bases in Anatolia, and the home town of a ruling dynasty. In 838 the caliph al-Mu'tasim besieged and destroyed it. Officers captured during that siege refused to convert, and they were executed. Their story became one of the most famous tales of Christian history: the '42 Martyrs of Amorium', who entered the Byzantine calendar as the Forty-Two Martyrs of Amorium.

items.text: You are standing on Alişar Höyük, a mound near Yozgat, in Yozgat province. Its story stretches from the 4th millennium BC to the 1st millennium BC, and in the Iron Age it is thought to have belonged to the land of Tabal.
items.speech: You are standing on Alişar Höyük, a mound near Yozgat, in Yozgat province. Its story stretches from the 4th millennium BC to the 1st millennium BC, and in the Iron Age it is thought to have belonged to the land of Tabal.

items.text: Beneath your feet lie layers of unbroken life. The mound has been occupied continuously since the 4th millennium BC, and it was an important centre in Hittite and Phrygian times. Its modern story begins with Erich Schmidt, whose excavations of 1927–32 rank among the pioneering campaigns of Anatolian archaeology.

items.text: Did you know? The distinctive pottery known as 'Alişar ware' gives its name to the 'Alişar IV' period in archaeology. Excavated between 1927 and 1932, this mound is where the chronology of Anatolian archaeology was first built, and for a long time other digs dated themselves against it. Hattian, Assyrian trading-colony and Hittite layers sit one atop another here: three worlds in a single hill.

items.text: You have come to Comana, an ancient city in Adana province, whose story runs from the 2nd millennium BC to the 6th century AD. This was a temple city of the Mother Goddess Ma, linked to the Hittite city of Kummanni.
items.speech: You have come to Comana, an ancient city in Adana province, whose story runs from the 2nd millennium BC to the 6th century AD. This was a temple city of the Mother Goddess Ma, linked to the Hittite city of Kummanni.

items.text: Comana is identified with the Kummanni of Hittite records. In classical times it ruled a great temple-state of the Mother Goddess Ma. Under Rome it was called a 'holy city', and according to Strabo it was home to more than six thousand sacred attendants. Imagine the bustle of so many serving one goddess.

Kadeş Antlaşması'nın Hititçe kopyası burada bulundu. Bilinen en eski yazılı barış antlaşması olan bu metnin bir kopyası ise New York'taki Birleşmiş Milletler binasının duvarında sergileniyor. Ve Yazılıkaya açık hava tapınağına gittiğinizde kaya duvarlara bakın: altmıştan fazla tanrı, bir geçit töreni halinde yürür.

items.text: Did you know? A copy of the Treaty of Kadesh hangs on a wall at the United Nations. Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite Empire, ringed by six kilometres of wall, and the 70-metre stone tunnel under Yerkapı can still be walked through today. The Hittite copy of the Treaty of Kadesh was found here — the oldest known written peace treaty, with a replica on display at the UN in New York. And on the rock walls of the Yazılıkaya open-air sanctuary, more than sixty gods walk in procession.

items.text: Did you know? The sun disc found here served for decades as the emblem of Ankara. The bronze 'sun discs' from its royal tombs became the most reproduced archaeological emblem in modern Türkiye. The reliefs flanking the Sphinx Gate show a Hittite religious ceremony step by step. And excavation began in 1935 on Atatürk's instruction, among the first major digs the young Republic ran with its own resources.

Its colonnaded street and mosaic villa floors show how far Roman luxury reached, even into provincial towns.

items.text: Did you know? Queen Amastris founded the city and gave it her own name, making it one of the few ancient cities named for a woman. The Kuşkayası rock relief works as a maintenance record of the Roman road network. Pliny wrote to Trajan asking leave to cover the open sewer running through the city — and the emperor's reply survives too. And the Roman 'Bird Gate' still stands within the street fabric of modern Amasra.

items.text: Here, on the Yeşilırmak, lies Amaseia, an ancient city in Amasya province whose story stretches from the 3rd millennium BC to today. It was the capital of Pontus, it guards royal rock tombs, and it was home to the geographer Strabo. Let us begin.
items.speech: Here, on the Yeşilırmak, lies Amaseia, an ancient city in Amasya province whose story stretches from the 3rd millennium BC to today. It was the capital of Pontus, it guards royal rock tombs, and it was home to the geographer Strabo. Let us begin.

items.text: As capital of the Kingdom of Pontus, Amaseia rose under Mithridates VI to become one of the mightiest cities of Anatolia. Its importance did not fade with the kings. Through Roman, Byzantine and Seljuk times it remained a city that mattered, and today its history lies in layers before you: in the rock tombs, in the castle and in the Ottoman mansions.
