items.text: Look up at the cliffs. These are the Pontic Royal Tombs, carved into the rock overlooking the Yeşilırmak valley at Amasya. Here the kings of Pontus chose to rest, high above their capital.

items.text: Did you know? The geographer Strabo was born here in Amaseia. The man who wrote the first comprehensive geography of the known world also described his own town, calling it 'a fortress built by nature'. The rock tombs of the Pontic kings are cut into the cliff above the town, and at night they are lit up. And under the Ottomans, princes learned to govern here as provincial governors, which is why the town is called the 'city of princes'.

items.text: Here, in Sinop province, lies Sinope, an ancient city whose story runs from the 7th century BC to today. It was the oldest Greek colony on the Black Sea, the birthplace of Diogenes, and the city that lent its name to the pigment sinopia.
items.speech: Here, in Sinop province, lies Sinope, an ancient city whose story runs from the 7th century BC to today. It was the oldest Greek colony on the Black Sea, the birthplace of Diogenes, and the city that lent its name to the pigment sinopia.

items.text: Sinope was founded by Milesian settlers in the 7th century BC, and it soon became a key port of Black Sea trade. Xenophon mentions it in his Anabasis. From Roman to Seljuk times the city never lost its calling: it remained, through every change of rule, a maritime centre.

items.text: Did you know? The Cynic philosopher Diogenes was born here, and the city lent its name to the reddish pigment sinopia. Diogenes lived in a jar, and when Alexander asked him what he wanted, he simply replied, 'stand out of my light'. Sinope also has the only naturally sheltered harbour on the Black Sea, which made it first a Milesian colony and later the Pontic naval base. And Mithridates VI, the king who held out longest against Rome, was born here too.

items.text: Here on the coast lies Heraclea Pontica, an ancient city in Zonguldak province with a history running from 560 BC to the 4th century AD. It was a Bithynian coastal city founded by Megarians, and it is the setting of the legend of Heracles.

items.text: Around 560 BC, colonists from Megara founded the city, and it grew into a powerful city-state in the rich Black Sea trade. But Heraclea was famous for more than trade. The Greeks believed that Heracles descended to the underworld through the Cehennemağzı caves here.

items.text: Did you know? Clearchus, one of antiquity's philosopher-tyrants, seized power here, and the city was known for its philosophical school. Antiquity held that the caves here, Cehennemağzı, the Mouth of Hell, were where Heracles dragged Cerberus up from the underworld. And as a Megarian colony, the city is singled out in ancient sources for reducing the native Mariandynians to serfdom.

items.text: Long before Samsun there was Amisus, an ancient city in Samsun province, from the 7th century BC to the 4th century AD. It was a Black Sea port city, and it left behind tumuli and underground tombs.

items.text: Milesians founded the city in the 7th century BC. It grew into a major port of Pontus, and under Rome it gained free-city status. Then, in 1995, came a remarkable find: royal tombs on Amisos Hill.

items.text: Did you know? Gold jewellery from the royal tombs found at Amisos in 1995 is displayed in the Samsun Museum. This Hellenistic gold jewellery from the tumuli is the most striking evidence of wealth on this coast. The city was also one of Mithridates' principal ports, and it was burned during the resistance to Rome.

items.text: Did you know? Tieion is one of the rare Anatolian cities that carried its ancient name to the present day. This city at Filyos is among the least excavated on the Black Sea coast, and its theatre has only recently been uncovered. Ancient sources say it took its name from a priest, Tios, and that it was the smallest independent city in the region.

items.text: Pause for a moment: you are standing at Göbekli Tepe, a sanctuary in Şanlıurfa province dating to 9600 BC. This is the world's oldest known temple complex, and its T-shaped pillars rewrote history.

items.text: Who built it? Not farmers, but hunter-gatherers, millennia before agriculture. Its discovery reversed an old assumption: that settlement came first, and monumental religion only afterwards.

items.text: You are now looking at Enclosures A–D, one of the oldest monumental structures known and the earliest dated of the circles. Look at the two pillars at its centre: they have arms, hands and a belt. These stones are human in form, and they face one another.

items.text: Did you know? Göbekli Tepe predates Stonehenge by about 6,000 years and the pyramids of Giza by 7,000. Its builders were hunter-gatherers, not farmers, which reversed the assumption that people settle down first and build temples afterwards. The T-shaped pillars carry carved foxes, snakes, scorpions and cranes, and the heaviest weighs about sixteen tonnes.

items.text: On the Euphrates, in Gaziantep province, lies Zeugma, an ancient city dating from 300 BC. This is the city of villa mosaics, and the home of the famous 'Gypsy Girl'.
items.speech: On the Euphrates, in Gaziantep province, lies Zeugma, an ancient city dating from 300 BC. This is the city of villa mosaics, and the home of the famous 'Gypsy Girl'.

items.text: Seleucus I founded the city at a crossing of the Euphrates, and it later became a Roman legionary base. Its extraordinary mosaics were rescued before the Birecik dam flooded the site.

items.text: Did you know? The 'Gypsy Girl' mosaic is displayed in the world's largest mosaic museum. The city's name is Greek for 'crossing': this was the easiest ford on the Euphrates, and the lock on the eastern trade. Among the mosaics saved in the rescue dig before the Birecik dam flooded the site is the 'Gypsy Girl', now one of the best-known ancient images in Türkiye. And Rome's Legio IV Scythica was stationed here; the city's wealth came directly from the frontier garrison.

items.text: High on Mount Nemrut, in Adıyaman province, stands a monument from the 1st century BC. Colossal statues of gods and a royal burial tumulus wait for you here, at 2,150 metres. Take a breath of this mountain air, and let us begin.
items.speech: High on Mount Nemrut, in Adıyaman province, stands a monument from the 1st century BC. Colossal statues of gods and a royal burial tumulus wait for you here, at 2,150 metres. Take a breath of this mountain air, and let us begin.

items.text: This is the hierotheion of King Antiochus I of Commagene, the sacred place he built here. His statues fused eastern and western gods. But time was not kind: earthquakes struck, and the statues lost their heads.
items.speech: This is the hierotheion of King Antiochus I of Commagene, the sacred place he built here. His statues fused eastern and western gods. But time was not kind: earthquakes struck, and the statues lost their heads.

items.text: You are now on the East terrace, the tomb-sanctuary King Antiochus I of Commagene built at 2,150 metres. At the foot of a gravel tumulus, gods eight to nine metres tall sit enthroned: the king himself, Commagene, Zeus, Apollo and Herakles. At either end stand an eagle and a lion, and a stepped altar faces them. In the model, the heads are back on their shoulders, just as they once were.

items.text: And here are the colossal heads, lined up on Nemrut's east and west terraces. Look into their faces. They have gazed out from this summit for centuries.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the West terrace, the Tumulus and the Lion horoscope.

items.text: Did you know? The lion relief on the west terrace is one of the oldest known star charts. King Antiochus I of Commagene raised a burial mound for himself at 2,150 metres and ringed it with colossal gods. Earthquakes brought every head to the ground, and today they sit apart from their bodies. The pantheon is deliberately hybrid, Zeus-Oromasdes, Apollo-Mithras, because the king fused Greek and Persian gods into a single dynastic religion.

items.text: Восточная терраса. Гробница-святилище, которую царь Коммагены Антиох I возвёл на высоте 2150 метров: у подножия щебневого кургана восседают на тронах боги высотой восемь-девять метров — царь, Коммагена, Зевс, Аполлон и Геракл, — по краям орёл и лев, а напротив них ступенчатый алтарь. Модель возвращает головы на их плечи.

items.text: А вы знали? Рельеф со львом на западной террасе — одна из древнейших известных звёздных карт. Царь Коммагены Антиох I насыпал для себя погребальный курган на высоте 2150 метров и окружил его колоссальными богами. Землетрясения сбросили на землю все головы, и теперь они стоят отдельно от своих тел. Пантеон намеренно смешанный — Зевс-Оромазд, Аполлон-Митра. Царь слил греческих и персидских богов в единую династическую религию.

items.text: This is Harran, an ancient city in Şanlıurfa province with roots in the 3rd millennium BC. It is a city of beehive houses, and home to the first university of the Islamic world.
items.speech: This is Harran, an ancient city in Şanlıurfa province with roots in the 3rd millennium BC. It is a city of beehive houses, and home to the first university of the Islamic world.

items.text: Harran was a centre of the moon-god Sin and a crossroads for caravans. Later it became something new: a hub of medieval astronomy and medicine.

items.text: Now you are looking at Harran's iconic beehive houses. Their conical mud-brick roofs keep the interiors cool. Step closer and imagine the relief of stepping inside on a hot day.
items.speech: Now you are looking at Harran's iconic beehive houses. Their conical mud-brick roofs keep the interiors cool. Step closer and imagine the relief of stepping inside on a hot day.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Great Mosque and its minaret, Harran Castle and the City gates.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Great Mosque and its minaret, Harran Castle and the City gates.

items.text: Did you know? The beehive houses are built of mudbrick and stay about 10°C cooler inside. Their conical shape is an architecture for staying cool without electricity, and it has not changed in millennia. Harran is one of the longest continuously inhabited places on earth; in the Book of Genesis, Abraham stayed here with his family. It was the cult centre of the moon god Sin and one of the last places to give up its pagan tradition, and under Islam its school became famous for astronomy and mathematics.

Devasa sarnıç ise kuşaklar boyunca 'zindan' sanıldı; oysa aslında kentin su deposuydu. Kayaya oyulmuş bu dev sarnıçlar, kuşatmada kentin ne kadar dayanabileceğini belirleyen asıl silahtı. Ve nekropoldeki kayaya oyulmuş çok katlı mezar odaları, bölgedeki en etkileyici Geç Antik yapılardan.

items.text: You have arrived at Dara, an ancient city in Mardin province, dating from AD 505. This was a Byzantine frontier garrison, and it still keeps its rock-cut cisterns and a monumental necropolis.
items.speech: You have arrived at Dara, an ancient city in Mardin province, dating from AD 505. This was a Byzantine frontier garrison, and it still keeps its rock-cut cisterns and a monumental necropolis.

items.text: Emperor Anastasius built Dara as a fortress city on the Sasanian frontier. What impresses most is its engineering: the water system, and the vast underground cistern that locals call the 'dungeon'. Both are engineering marvels.
items.speech: Emperor Anastasius built Dara as a fortress city on the Sasanian frontier. What impresses most is its engineering: the water system, and the vast underground cistern that locals call the 'dungeon'. Both are engineering marvels.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the 'Dungeon', the cisterns, the necropolis, the dam and the agora.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the 'Dungeon', the cisterns, the necropolis, the dam and the agora.

items.text: Did you know? The huge cistern was long mistaken for a dungeon, but it was the city's water reservoir. Dara was Byzantium's forward fortress on the Sasanian frontier, and at the Battle of Dara in 530, Belisarius defeated a numerically superior Persian army here. In a siege, the vast rock-cut cisterns were the real weapon: they decided how long the city could hold. And the multi-storey rock-cut tomb chambers in the necropolis are among the most striking late antique structures in the region.

items.text: You have reached Carchemish, an ancient city in Gaziantep province, its story running from the 3rd millennium BC to the 7th century BC. This was a royal city on the Euphrates, famed for its Hittite and Neo-Hittite reliefs.
items.speech: You have reached Carchemish, an ancient city in Gaziantep province, its story running from the 3rd millennium BC to the 7th century BC. This was a royal city on the Euphrates, famed for its Hittite and Neo-Hittite reliefs.

items.text: It all began at a crossing of the Euphrates. Here the city was founded, and under Mitanni, the Hittites and the Neo-Hittites it served as a regional capital. In 605 BC the Battle of Carchemish brought Assyria to its end. Much later, in 1911–14, Leonard Woolley excavated the site.

items.text: Did you know? Carchemish straddles today's Turkish-Syrian border. Part of the mound lies inside a military zone, and because the site was mined, it could not be dug for years. The city's Neo-Hittite reliefs form the backbone of the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara. And T. E. Lawrence — Lawrence of Arabia — worked here as a young archaeologist on the 1911-14 excavations.

items.text: Höyüğün kökleri İlk Tunç Çağı'na uzanıyor. Geç Hitit döneminde burası Sam'al Krallığı'nın merkezi oldu ve kent Asur yönetimi altında gelişti. Peki toprağın altından neler çıktı? Kent surları, hilani sarayları ve ünlü yazıtlar. Her biri, bu krallığın sesini bugüne taşıyor.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Kral Kilamuwa'nın yazıtı, Anadolu'da bulunan en eski Sami dili yazıtlarından biridir. Kentin planı da sıra dışı: dairesel bir çift surla çevrili bu tasarımın benzerine Yakın Doğu'da az rastlanır. Kral Kilamuwa ve Panamuwa yazıtları, Sami dillerinin tarihinde birinci elden belgelerdir; bu kentte Fenikece, Aramca ve Luvice bir arada kullanıldı. Peki kapıları bekleyen o aslanlar şimdi nerede? Bugün Berlin ve İstanbul müzelerinde sergileniyorlar.

items.text: Pause for a moment at Sam'al, an ancient city in Gaziantep province, whose story runs from the 3rd millennium BC to the 7th century BC. This is Zincirli Höyük, capital of a Neo-Hittite kingdom, famed for the lions of its gateways.

items.text: The story of this mound reaches back to the Early Bronze Age. In the Neo-Hittite period it became the capital of the kingdom of Sam'al, and under Assyrian rule it flourished. Excavations here uncovered city walls, hilani palaces and celebrated inscriptions.

items.text: You are now at the Hilani Palace. The hilani is a palace type of Neo-Hittite architecture, known for its pillared reception hall. Imagine visitors being received between those pillars.

items.text: Now look at the Double Gate Reliefs, the carvings that adorned the paired gateway of Sam'al. Pause and picture the gateway they once framed.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Gateway Lions, and take time to follow the line of the City Walls.

items.text: Did you know? King Kilamuwa's inscription is one of the earliest Semitic-language texts found in Anatolia. The city's circular double walls make a plan with few parallels in the Near East. The inscriptions of kings Kilamuwa and Panamuwa are primary documents in the history of the Semitic languages, and here Phoenician, Aramaic and Luwian were all in use. And the famous gate lions? Today they are displayed in the museums of Berlin and Istanbul.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Buradaki Mitridates kabartması, Anadolu'nun en büyük kabartmalarından biridir. Arsameia, Kommagene'nin yazlık başkentiydi; Nemrut'taki mezarın sahibi Antiokhos, babası Mithridates için burayı kutsal alan yaptı. Herakles ile Kral Mithridates'in el sıkıştığı kabartma, en iyi korunmuş Kommagene eseridir; bir tanrıyla bir kral, aynı boyda. Ve kayaya oyulmuş 158 metrelik dik tünel, hâlâ tam olarak ne işe yaradığı bilinmeyen bir yapıdır.

items.text: You are at Arsameia, an ancient city at Eski Kahta in Adıyaman province, whose story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. This was the royal cult centre of the Kingdom of Commagene, and it is famous for one image above all: the colossal Mithridates relief.
items.speech: You are at Arsameia, an ancient city at Eski Kahta in Adıyaman province, whose story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. This was the royal cult centre of the Kingdom of Commagene, and it is famous for one image above all: the colossal Mithridates relief.

items.text: Arsameia was the sacred seat of King Mithridates I Kallinikos, and his son Antiochus I expanded it. With its tunnel, its palace ruins and its six-metre relief, it is the second most important site of Commagene.

items.text: You are now in front of the Mithridates Relief. This six-metre relief depicts King Mithridates I standing with Herakles. Look closely at the two figures, a king and a god face to face.

items.text: Now look at the Rock Inscriptions. Royal and sacred texts were carved straight into the rock here, so that the words would last as long as the mountain.

items.text: Did you know? The relief of Mithridates here is one of the largest relief carvings in Anatolia. Arsameia was the summer capital of Commagene: Antiochus, whose tomb crowns Nemrut, made it a sanctuary for his father Mithridates. The relief of Heracles shaking hands with King Mithridates is the best-preserved Commagene work, and god and king are shown the same height. And the 158-metre shaft cut straight into the rock remains a structure whose purpose is still not fully understood.

items.text: Here, on the Tigris, lies Hasankeyf, an ancient city in Batman province. The river splits this historic town in two, and its story stretches from the 1st millennium BC to the 20th century AD, while its cave settlements reach back many thousands of years further still.
items.speech: Here, on the Tigris, lies Hasankeyf, an ancient city in Batman province. The river splits this historic town in two, and its story stretches from the 1st millennium BC to the 20th century AD, while its cave settlements reach back many thousands of years further still.

items.text: People have lived in the caves beside the Tigris since the Neolithic era. Later, Hasankeyf rose to become a capital under the Artuqids and the Akkoyunlu. Then, in 2020, the waters of the Ilısu Dam covered part of the old town. But look up: the citadel still stands.

items.text: You are now looking at Hasankeyf Citadel, the high citadel above the Tigris, with its cave settlements. Imagine the generations who made their homes in this rock.

items.text: Here is the Tigris Bridge, the historic bridge of Hasankeyf. Its piers survive today, still standing in the river and recalling the crossing they once carried.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Great Palace and the Great Mosque, and save time for the Rock-cut Tombs.

items.text: Did you know? Caves along the Tigris at Hasankeyf show evidence of settlement some 12,000 years old. That 12,000-year-old settlement was largely submerged by the Ilısu dam in 2020. One monument made a journey of its own: the tomb of Zeynel Bey was lifted whole and moved to new ground. The Artuqid bridge was reckoned the widest-spanning in the Middle East of its day, and its piers still break the water. And thousands of cave dwellings were cut into the cliff; some were still lived in during the twentieth century.

items.text: In the Tektek Mountains of Şanlıurfa province lies Soğmatar, a sanctuary of the 2nd century AD – 7th century AD. Here, a sacred hill and rock tombs were dedicated to the moon god Sin.

items.text: In the 2nd century AD, under the Abgar dynasty, this was a cult centre where the people of Harran worshipped the moon and the planetary gods. As you explore, you will find the Pognon Cave, a Sacred Hill with reliefs of deities, and six mausolea.

items.text: Did you know? Local tradition holds that the Prophet Moses lived here, and his well is still visited today. Soğmatar was an open-air sanctuary of the planets and of the moon god Sin, and Syriac inscriptions were cut into its rock in the second and third centuries AD. Around the central sacred hill, seven separate structures are thought to be scattered, one for each planet.

items.text: Ani grew on the Silk Road, and its population is estimated to have approached 100,000. So why is it empty today? Earthquakes struck, trade routes shifted, and in the end the city was abandoned.

items.text: Did you know? The Menüçehr Mosque is regarded as the oldest known Seljuk mosque in Anatolia. Ani was known as the city of a thousand and one churches, and at its height it approached a hundred thousand people, spoken of alongside Constantinople and Baghdad. Trdat, the cathedral's architect, was the very man who repaired the earthquake-collapsed dome of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. When the Silk Road shifted, and after the earthquake of 1319, the city emptied. Today it stands on the border, alone in the steppe.

items.text: Wussten Sie schon? Die Menüçehr-Moschee gilt als die älteste bekannte seldschukische Moschee Anatoliens. Bekannt als die Stadt der tausendundein Kirchen, näherte sie sich auf ihrem Höhepunkt hunderttausend Einwohnern und wurde in einem Atemzug mit Konstantinopel und Bagdad genannt. Trdat, der Architekt der Kathedrale, war derjenige, der die bei einem Erdbeben eingestürzte Kuppel der Hagia Sophia in Konstantinopel reparierte. Als sich die Seidenstraße verlagerte, und nach dem Erdbeben von 1319, leerte sich die Stadt. Heute steht sie an der Grenze, allein in der Steppe.

items.text: А вы знали? Мечеть Менучехра считается древнейшей известной сельджукской мечетью в Анатолии. Известный как город тысячи и одной церкви, в период расцвета он приближался к ста тысячам жителей и упоминался наравне с Константинополем и Багдадом. Трдат, архитектор собора, — тот самый человек, который восстановил обрушившийся при землетрясении купол Айя-Софии в Константинополе. Когда Шёлковый путь сместился, и после землетрясения 1319 года город опустел. Сегодня он стоит на границе, одинокий посреди степи.

items.text: Gezerken kral mezarlarını ve çivi yazılı yazıtları mutlaka görün. Eski Van şehrinin izlerini de unutmayın.
items.speech: Gezerken kral mezarlarını ve çivi yazılı yazıtları mutlaka görün. Eski Van şehrinin izlerini de unutmayın.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Tuşpa, Urartu'nun başkentiydi. Kayaya oyulmuş kral mezarlarına ve I. Argişti'nin yıllıklarına, kalenin dik yüzünden bakılabiliyor. Kalede bir de Pers kralı Kserkses'in kayaya oyulmuş üç dilli çivi yazılı yazıtı var: kayalığın erişilmesi güç bir yerinde duruyor ve hâlâ okunabiliyor. Kalenin eteğindeki düzlük ise 1915 öncesi Eski Van şehrinin yeri. O şehir bugün yok; geriye yalnızca iki cami ayakta kaldı.

items.text: Look up at the rock ridge rising over Lake Van. This is Tushpa, also known as Van Fortress, in Van province, and its story begins in the 9th century BC. Here stood the Urartian capital.
items.speech: Look up at the rock ridge rising over Lake Van. This is Tushpa, also known as Van Fortress, in Van province, and its story begins in the 9th century BC. Here stood the Urartian capital.

items.text: Tushpa was founded by King Sarduri, and it became the administrative heart of Urartu. Its royal tombs, cut into the rock, survive to this day, together with its cuneiform inscriptions.

items.text: You are now at the Sardur Bastion, a defensive bastion built by the Urartian king Sarduri. Pause for a moment and imagine the guards who once kept watch from here.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the royal tombs and the cuneiform inscriptions, and look down too, towards old Van city.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the royal tombs and the cuneiform inscriptions, and look down too, towards old Van city.

items.text: Did you know? A trilingual inscription of the Persian king Xerxes is carved into the cliff here. This was the capital of Urartu, and the rock-cut royal tombs and the annals of Argishti I look out from the sheer face of the citadel. Xerxes' trilingual cuneiform inscription is cut into an all but unreachable spot on the cliff, yet it can still be read. And the flat ground below the citadel is where the old city of Van stood before 1915; nothing of it remains now but two mosques.

items.text: This brings our journey through Tushpa, Van Fortress, to an end. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. This rock has guarded its kings' words for centuries; let it keep them for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.

items.text: Bu kaleyi Kral II. Sarduri yaptırdı. Ama Çavuştepe'nin en şaşırtıcı mirası taşta değil, suda. Kentin altındaki Şamran Kanalı, 2700 yıldır tarlaları sulamaya devam ediyor. Bir düşünün: o su bugün de akıyor.

Sarduri'nin kalesidir; Anadolu'da bilinen en eski tuvaletlerden biri de burada. Haldi Tapınağı'nın cilalı bazalt blokları o kadar düzgün işlenmiştir ki aralarına bıçak bile girmez.

items.text: You are at Çavuştepe, an ancient city in Van province from the 8th century BC. This was an Urartian fortress, with a royal palace and a temple, and an irrigation canal that is still in use.

items.text: Çavuştepe was built by King Sarduri II. And look below the site: the Şamran canal has watered the fields here for 2,700 years.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Upper fortress and the Temple of Haldi, then the Palace kitchen, and finally the Şamran canal.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Upper fortress and the Temple of Haldi, then the Palace kitchen, and finally the Şamran canal.

items.text: Did you know? This was the fortress of the Urartian king Sarduri II, and the site of one of the oldest known lavatories in Anatolia. Look closely at the temple of Haldi: its polished basalt blocks fit without mortar, smooth as glass, and they are dressed so finely that a knife will not pass between them.

Ve Arslantepe, 2021'de UNESCO Dünya Mirası Listesi'ne alındı.

items.text: This is Arslantepe, a mound in Malatya province whose story begins in the 6th millennium BC. Within it lies one of the earliest known palaces in the world.
items.speech: This is Arslantepe, a mound in Malatya province whose story begins in the 6th millennium BC. Within it lies one of the earliest known palaces in the world.

items.text: Arslantepe's layers record something momentous: the birth of the state and of centralised power. And the swords found here are among the oldest metal swords known.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the 4th-millennium palace, the Lion gate, the Wall paintings and the Protective shelter.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the 4th-millennium palace, the Lion gate, the Wall paintings and the Protective shelter.

items.text: Did you know? Seal impressions found here show how bureaucracy worked before writing was invented. The building of around 3300 BC is among the earliest known palaces in the world: the first architecture of the thing we call a state. The arsenical copper swords found here are counted among the oldest known swords in the world. And in 2021 Arslantepe was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

items.text: High above Elazığ, a whole history waits. This is Harput, an ancient city in Elazığ province, lived in from the 2nd millennium BC until today. It is a historic mound and castle town whose story spans Urartu to Ottoman times. Shall we climb in?
items.speech: High above Elazığ, a whole history waits. This is Harput, an ancient city in Elazığ province, lived in from the 2nd millennium BC until today. It is a historic mound and castle town whose story spans Urartu to Ottoman times. Shall we climb in?

items.text: People have lived here since the 2nd millennium BC. Harput was an important centre under Urartu, Rome, Byzantium, the Seljuks and the Ottomans. Think of it as a book of many pages: a city of 4,000 years lies layered beneath Harput Castle.

items.text: You are now before Harput Castle, the fortress on the rock above Elazığ. Its story spans Urartu to Ottoman times. Look up, and imagine every age that kept watch from these walls.

items.text: Here is the Sara Hatun Complex. This Harput complex was built in the name of Uzun Hasan's mother, Sara Hatun, a son's tribute set in stone.

items.text: And here is the Harput Museum, displaying archaeological finds from the Harput region. Inside, the layers of this city come to light.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Great Mosque.

items.text: Did you know? The dome of Harput's Great Mosque is among the oldest mosque domes in Anatolia. The fortress was used without a break from Urartu to the Ottomans. Its name, 'Milk Castle', comes from a legend that milk was mixed into the mortar instead of water. And one more story: the city of Elazığ was founded when Harput came down to the plain in the nineteenth century. The modern town is the old one, relocated.

items.text: Palu, Urartu Krallığı'nın sınırındaydı ve Roma ile Bizans dönemlerinde de kale kenti olarak kullanıldı. Kalenin girişindeki Urartu yazıtı ise bugün de okunabiliyor. Taşa kazınmış o satırlar, yüzyıllardır yerinde.

items.text: Şimdi Palu Kalesi'ne bakıyorsunuz. Fırat'ın doğusundaki bu tarihi kale, bir Urartu yazıtı taşıyor.

items.text: Burası Cimşit Bey Hamamı, Osmanlı döneminden kalma Palu hamamı. Suyun sesinin ve sohbetlerin bu duvarlar arasında yankılandığını bir an hayal edin.

items.text: Şimdi Eski Köprü'ye bakıyorsunuz. Burada, tarihi bir köprünün kalıntıları duruyor. Bir zamanlar üzerinden geçen yolcuları düşünün.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Palu Kalesi, Urartu Kralı Menua'ya ait olduğu düşünülen bir yazıt barındırır. Kaledeki bu çivi yazılı kaya yazıtı Urartu Kralı I. Menua'ya aittir ve bölgedeki Urartu varlığının en batıdaki kanıtlarından biridir. Bir de hüzünlü bir not: Eski Palu, depremlerden sonra 20. yüzyılda terk edildi. Cami, kilise ve evleriyle bugün bir hayalet yerleşim olarak duruyor.

Bir de hüzünlü bir not: Eski Palu, depremlerden sonra 20. yüzyılda terk edildi. Cami, kilise ve evleriyle bugün bir hayalet yerleşim olarak duruyor.

items.text: Palu turumuz burada sona eriyor. Kalıntılara dokunmayın, işaretli yollarda kalın ve yanınızda su bulundurun. Bu eski taşlar, sizden sonra gelenlere de hikâyelerini anlatsın. İyi gezmeler.

items.text: You have reached Palu, an ancient city in Elazığ province, lived in from the 9th century BC to today. This historic town lies east of the Euphrates, and above it stands a castle bearing Urartian inscriptions.
items.speech: You have reached Palu, an ancient city in Elazığ province, lived in from the 9th century BC to today. This historic town lies east of the Euphrates, and above it stands a castle bearing Urartian inscriptions.

items.text: Palu once guarded the western frontier of Urartu. Empires changed, but its role did not: under Rome and Byzantium it remained a fortified town. And the Urartian inscription at the castle gate? You can still read it today.

items.text: You are now at Palu Castle, the historic fortress east of the Euphrates. Look for the Urartian inscription it bears.

items.text: Here is the Cimşit Bey Bath, an Ottoman-era bathhouse at Palu. Imagine the warmth and the voices once filling its rooms.

items.text: Now to the Old Bridge. These are the remains of the historic bridge over the Murat, a branch of the Euphrates.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Urartian Inscription and the Great Mosque.

items.text: Did you know? Palu Castle holds a cuneiform rock inscription in the citadel thought to belong to the Urartian king Menua, and it is among the westernmost proofs of Urartian reach. Old Palu was abandoned after earthquakes in the twentieth century, and today it stands as a ghost settlement of mosque, church and houses.

items.text: Van'ın güneyindesiniz, Hoşap Kalesi'nin eteğinde. Bu kayalığın hikâyesi MÖ 9. yüzyıldan MS 17. yüzyıla uzanıyor. Başınızı kaldırın: karşınızdaki, 17. yüzyılda Mahmudi Beyliği'nin yükselttiği görkemli kale. Hazırsanız, kapıdan içeri adım atalım.

Kayalık bir tepeyi baştan aşağı saran görüntüsüyle Anadolu'nun en teatral kalelerinden biridir. Ve bir anlatıya göre bey, benzerinin bir daha yapılmaması için mimarın elini kestirmiştir.

items.text: Look up at Hoşap Castle, south of Van, in Van province. Its story runs from the 9th century BC to the 17th century AD, and what you see is the magnificent castle of the 17th-century Mahmudi principality.

items.text: This rock was already occupied in Urartian times. Centuries later, in the 17th century, Sarı Süleyman Bey of the Mahmudi tribe rebuilt it. The result is among the finest surviving examples of Ottoman-Van architecture.

items.text: Now the Inner Courtyard: the innermost court, where a fortress's defences were strongest. This was the heart that every wall around you was built to protect.

items.text: Did you know? The Persian inscription on the castle gate reads 'there is nothing like it in the world'. The castle was built in 1643 by Sarı Süleyman, bey of the Mahmudi, and as it wraps a whole rock outcrop it is one of the most theatrical castles in Anatolia. And a darker tale: the story goes that the bey had the architect's hand cut off, so that its like could never be built again.

items.text: On Akdamar Island, out in Lake Van in Van province, stands a monument whose story runs from the 10th century AD to today: the Church of the Holy Cross, famous for its carved reliefs.
items.speech: On Akdamar Island, out in Lake Van in Van province, stands a monument whose story runs from the 10th century AD to today: the Church of the Holy Cross, famous for its carved reliefs.

items.text: The church was built in 915–921 for King Gagik I by the architect-monk Manuel, and it served as the royal church of the Kingdom of Vaspurakan. Look at its exterior walls: the biblical reliefs carved there are unique in the world.

items.text: You are now standing before the Church of the Holy Cross, the relief-carved church on Akdamar Island, built for King Gagik I in 915–921. Let your eyes travel slowly across its walls and read the stories carved in stone.

items.text: Did you know? On 19 September 2010 a service was held in the church for the first time in some 95 years, and one has been held every year since. The exterior of the Church of the Holy Cross, built for King Gagik I between 915 and 921, is covered wall to wall in relief: Jonah, David and Goliath, vine scrolls and animals. And in 2007 the church was restored and opened as a museum.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Bölge halkı bu alana 'Keçilitepe' der. 2023'te burada bulunan 2,3 metrelik oturan erkek heykeli, bilinen en eski gerçekçi insan heykellerinden biri sayılıyor. Karahan Tepe, Göbekli Tepe'nin çağdaşı. Ana odada, ana kayadan yontularak bırakılmış on bir sütun yükseliyor ve duvardan bir insan başı çıkıyor. Burası, bölgedeki benzer alanları kapsayan 'Taş Tepeler' araştırma programının merkezlerinden biri. Üstelik kazılan alan henüz çok küçük; yani bu hikâye daha yeni başlıyor.

items.text: You have come to Karahan Tepe, a mound in Şanlıurfa province, and to one of the oldest chapters of the human story: the 10th millennium BC. This is a pre-pottery Neolithic sanctuary, built before people had even learned to fire clay. Its T-shaped pillars and sculptures have earned it a fitting nickname — Göbekli Tepe's 'sister site'.
items.speech: You have come to Karahan Tepe, a mound in Şanlıurfa province, and to one of the oldest chapters of the human story: the 10th millennium BC. This is a pre-pottery Neolithic sanctuary, built before people had even learned to fire clay. Its T-shaped pillars and sculptures have earned it a fitting nickname, Göbekli Tepe's 'sister site'.

items.text: The site was first identified in 1997 by Bahattin Çelik, and since 2019 it has been excavated under the Taş Tepeler, or Stone Hills, Project. Pause for a moment and consider what you are looking at. These monumental structures date to the 10th–9th millennium BC, and they were raised by hunter-gatherers. They show that such communities could organise complex building work and shared ritual long before the first farming villages.

items.text: Here are the circular enclosures. These round-planned cult enclosures house T-shaped pillars, the great hallmark of the Taş Tepeler period. Imagine the people who gathered inside these rings, surrounded by standing stones.

items.text: Now look at the rock-cut basins. They were carved straight into the bedrock, and they are thought to have served ritual purposes. What was poured into them, and why, we can only wonder.

items.text: And now, the anthropomorphic statues: human-shaped figures of stone. They are among the earliest monumental examples of the Neolithic era — some of the first times people carved themselves on this scale.

items.text: This is the structure with a stone bench. Stone benches run inside the building, and it was used as a gathering place. Picture people seated side by side here, talking, listening, deciding together.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the T-shaped pillars, rising here as they did when they were first set up.

items.text: Did you know? Locals call the site 'Keçilitepe'. The 2.3 m seated male statue found in 2023 is among the earliest realistic human sculptures known. Karahan Tepe is a contemporary of Göbekli Tepe. In the main chamber, eleven pillars were left standing out of the bedrock itself, and a human head emerges from the wall. The site is one of the hubs of the 'Taş Tepeler' research programme, which covers similar sites across the region — and only a small part of it has been dug so far.

items.text: This brings our tour of Karahan Tepe to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have kept their secrets for a very long time; let them keep them for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.

Fırat kıyısındaki bu Çanak Çömleksiz Neolitik yerleşim bugün Atatürk Barajı'nın suları altında kaldı. Ama adını unutturmayan iki şey var: kült yapısı ve taştan yontulmuş baş heykelleri. items.text: Pause for a moment at Nevali Çori, a mound in Şanlıurfa province from the 9th millennium BC. This pre-pottery Neolithic settlement once stood on the Euphrates; today it is flooded by the Atatürk Dam reservoir. It is famous for its cult building and its stone head sculptures.
items.speech: Pause for a moment at Nevali Çori, a mound in Şanlıurfa province from the 9th millennium BC. This pre-pottery Neolithic settlement once stood on the Euphrates; today it is flooded by the Atatürk Dam reservoir. It is famous for its cult building and its stone head sculptures.

items.text: The site was rescued between 1983 and 1991 by a University of Heidelberg team led by Harald Hauptmann. The settlement, dated c. 8400–8100 BC, gave up two remarkable discoveries: a 'cult building' with T-shaped pillars like those of Göbekli Tepe, and the world's oldest domesticated einkorn wheat.

items.text: Did you know? The salvaged stone heads and the stele known as the 'Nevali Çori Stela' are displayed today in the Şanlıurfa Museum. The site itself lies beneath the Atatürk dam. Its T-shaped pillars were the first sign that such a world existed, years before Göbekli Tepe was dug. And its limestone figures of humans and birds are among the oldest monumental sculpture known.

items.text: You are standing on Aşıklı Höyük, a mound in Aksaray province whose story belongs to the 9th–8th millennium BC. This is a pre-pottery Neolithic mound near Aksaray, and from its soil have come the world's earliest domesticated sheep and buildings of moulded mudbrick. Shall we go back to the very beginnings of village life?
items.speech: You are standing on Aşıklı Höyük, a mound in Aksaray province whose story belongs to the 9th–8th millennium BC. This is a pre-pottery Neolithic mound near Aksaray, and from its soil have come the world's earliest domesticated sheep and buildings of moulded mudbrick. Shall we go back to the very beginnings of village life?

items.text: For about a millennium, between c. 8200 and 7500 BC, people lived here almost without a break. Since 1989 the mound has been excavated by Istanbul University, and what has come to light is remarkable: houses of moulded mudbrick, planned streets and the domestication of sheep. Together they make Aşıklı one of the earliest examples of settled life in Anatolia.

items.text: Look at the moulded mudbrick houses. They were built from mudbrick blocks shaped in moulds, a building method that sets this mound apart. Imagine the builders turning out block after block, all of the same shape.

items.text: Here are the ovens and hearths. This is where daily life happened: food was cooked over them, and they kept the houses warm. Pause for a moment and imagine the glow of the fire at the heart of each home.

items.text: Now notice the regular street layout. This settlement was planned, with streets running parallel to one another. It is not a random cluster of huts, but a village laid out with intention.

items.text: Next come the trash pits and burials. Burials and household pits may sound modest, but for archaeologists they are a treasure: they yield rich evidence of how people here lived their daily lives.

items.text: Now picture the village-planned settlement as a whole. Its layout is arranged around communal spaces, just as is typical of early settlements. Here, life was organised around places that everyone used.

items.text: Did you know? The earliest domesticated sheep bones found at Aşıklı are among the strongest pieces of evidence that sheep were domesticated in present-day Turkey. This is also the oldest known village in central Anatolia, from about 8400 BC, and it offers a step-by-step record of how farming arrived here. Perhaps the most moving find of all is a woman's skeleton bearing the trace of skull surgery, among the oldest evidence of brain surgery anywhere. She survived it, and lived on for some time afterwards.

Acemhöyük, Asur ticaret kolonileri çağının büyük merkezlerindendi ve saray depolarından fildişi eserler ve obsidiyen kaplar çıktı. Yani bu höyük yalnızca eşyaları değil, insanların adlarını da saklamış.

items.text: You are standing at Acemhöyük, a mound in Aksaray province whose story spans the 3rd–2nd millennium BC. Close to Aksaray, it was one of the richest centres of the Assyrian Trade Colonies period, and it is renowned above all for two things: its palaces and its ivory artefacts. Shall we begin?

items.text: This mound was most likely ancient Purušhanda, or Purušḫanda. People lived here from the early 3rd millennium BC, but its golden age came in the Assyrian Trade Colonies period (c. 1950–1750 BC). Monumental buildings rose here, among them the 'Saray' and the 'Hatipler Sarayı', and the town became a centre of trade and administration, a contemporary of Kültepe.

items.text: Did you know? An ivory box found at the mound, inlaid with lapis lazuli, bronze and iron, is among the finest examples of early luxury craftsmanship in Anatolia. Acemhöyük was one of the great centres of the Assyrian trading-colony period, and its palace stores yielded ivories and obsidian vessels. And the seal impressions from the palace record, name by name, the people with whom the trade with Mesopotamia and Syria was carried out.

items.text: Deep in Çorum province, at Ortaköy, lies Sapinuwa, an ancient city of the 14th century BC. This was a Hittite religious and administrative city, and from its ground have come thousands of cuneiform tablets. Let us step into the world that wrote them.
items.speech: Deep in Çorum province, at Ortaköy, lies Sapinuwa, an ancient city of the 14th century BC. This was a Hittite religious and administrative city, and from its ground have come thousands of cuneiform tablets. Let us step into the world that wrote them.

items.text: Excavations here have run since 1990, led by Aygül and Mustafa Süel. What they uncovered was a royal residence: in the 14th century BC, during the reign of Tudhaliya II, the city served the king. It covered about 9 km², making it one of the largest cities of the ancient Near East. And its thousands of tablets? They survived because a fire baked them hard.

items.text: Sapinuwa was a city on two tiers: the upper city, the elevated citadel, and the lower city, the settlement spread below it. As you look around, try to picture how the two halves fitted together into one city.

items.text: Did you know? Building A alone has yielded over 3,000 tablets and fragments, written in Hittite, Hurrian, Akkadian and other languages, among them many Hurrian purification rituals. Because Hittite kings resided here, some scholars count Sapinuwa a second capital. In all, counting those found outside Building A, the excavations have produced more than four thousand cuneiform tablets and fragments. And here is the twist: the fire that destroyed the palace baked the clay tablets hard, so instead of destroying the archive, it carried it down to us.

This is the Midas Monument, also called Yazılıkaya: a Phrygian open-air sanctuary and rock-cut city of the 8th–6th century BC, famous above all for the 17 m-high Midas Monument itself. Let us begin.
items.speech: Out in Han district, in Eskişehir province, a face of rock has been carved into the front of a temple. This is the Midas Monument, also called Yazılıkaya: a Phrygian open-air sanctuary and rock-cut city of the 8th–6th century BC, famous above all for the 17 metres-high Midas Monument itself. Let us begin.

items.text: The monument was carved into the rock in the 6th century BC for the Phrygian Mother Goddess, Matar, also known as Cybele. In 1800 it was rediscovered by William Martin Leake. But why 'Midas'? Its Phrygian inscription contains the word 'Midai', and that word gave the monument its name. The plateau around it is still called 'Midas City'.

items.text: Did you know? The word 'Midas' in the inscription does not refer to the legendary king, but is an epithet of the Phrygian Mother Goddess Matar. Nor was the monument a tomb: it was an open-air temple for her statue. The rock monument rises seventeen metres high, and an old Phrygian inscription on it names Midas. It looks like a temple façade, yet there is no chamber behind it. Everything, even the door, is relief: the idea of a temple, drawn on rock.

items.text: In the 9th–7th century BC, the Urartians built this fortress on a 60 m volcanic hill overlooking the Euphrates. Between 1959 and 1968, Tahsin Özgüç brought it back to light. Its apadana palace, great hall, storehouses and multi-roomed rock-cut tombs are key examples of Urartian architecture.

items.text: Did you know? The fragments of Urartian wall painting found at Altıntepe are among the most important known examples of palace wall painting in the Urartian kingdom. The columned hall of this Urartian fortress is regarded as a forerunner of the Persian apadana. Together, its wall paintings and the bronzes from its royal tombs are among the best-preserved works of Urartian art.

items.text: On the eastern shore of Lake Van, in Van province, rises Ayanis Fortress, an ancient city of the 7th century BC. This Urartian fortress was built by King Rusa II, and today it is famous for its exceptionally well-preserved Temple of Haldi. Let us step into its story.
items.speech: On the eastern shore of Lake Van, in Van province, rises Ayanis Fortress, an ancient city of the 7th century BC. This Urartian fortress was built by King Rusa II, and today it is famous for its exceptionally well-preserved Temple of Haldi. Let us step into its story.

items.text: Its story begins around 673/2 BC, when Rusa II founded it as 'Rusahinili opposite Mount Eiduru'. Yet it did not last long. In the mid-7th century BC an earthquake and fire struck, and the fortress was abandoned. Here lies the paradox of Ayanis: the very collapse that ended it effectively sealed the site, and that is why its temple walls, inscriptions and bronze weapons are so remarkably preserved.

items.text: Did you know? One of the longest Urartian inscriptions survives on the temple façade: the long cuneiform text on the wall of the Temple of Haldi tells the fortress's founding in the king's own words. The lion-headed bronze shield found in 1997 is the first example of its kind ever recovered in excavation. And because Rusa II built the fortress in one campaign in the seventh century BC, and it was destroyed soon after, Ayanis is a single-period time capsule.

items.text: Kaunos, MÖ 10. yüzyılda kuruldu. İki limanı vardı ve önemli bir ticaret kentiydi. Yüzyıllar boyunca el değiştirdi: önce Pers, sonra Rodos, ardından Roma egemenliği altında yaşadı. Peki bu liman kenti nasıl sustu? Dalyan Çayı'nın getirdiği alüvyonlar limanlarını doldurdu ve kent denizle bağlantısını kaybetti. Sonra bir de sıtma geldi; salgın yüzünden Kaunos 15. yüzyılda tamamen terk edildi.

items.text: Opposite Dalyan, on the border between Caria and Lycia, lies a harbour city watched over by tombs cut into the cliffs. You have arrived at the Ancient City of Kaunos, in Muğla province. Its story begins in the 10th century BC, and it is famed for its impressive rock-cut tombs.
items.speech: Opposite Dalyan, on the border between Caria and Lycia, lies a harbour city watched over by tombs cut into the cliffs. You have arrived at the Ancient City of Kaunos, in Muğla province. Its story begins in the 10th century BC, and it is famed for its impressive rock-cut tombs.

items.text: Kaunos was founded in the 10th century BC and grew into an important trading city with two harbours. The Persians, Rhodes and Rome ruled it in turn. But the Dalyan river silted up, filling its harbours and cutting it off from the sea. The final blow was a malaria epidemic, which led to its abandonment in the 15th century AD.

items.text: Did you know? Around 150 rock-cut tombs are carved into the cliff face. The temple-fronted ones date to the 4th century BC and show Lycian influence; cut as temple façades, they face you head-on as the boat passes down the Dalyan river. The harbour itself silted into a lake, leaving a maritime city stranded behind the reed beds. And the malaria left its mark on the people: ancient writers describe the Caunians as sallow, and Strabo remarks on their greenish complexion.

items.text: You are standing in the Ancient City of Stratonikeia, in Muğla province, at Eskihisar near Yatağan. Its story begins in the 3rd century BC. Vast and built of marble, it carries a memorable nickname: the 'City of Gladiators'.
items.speech: You are standing in the Ancient City of Stratonikeia, in Muğla province, at Eskihisar near Yatağan. Its story begins in the 3rd century BC. Vast and built of marble, it carries a memorable nickname: the 'City of Gladiators'.

items.text: Long before its marble streets, the settlement was known as Atriya in Hittite times. After 281 BC it was renamed after Stratonike, wife of the Seleucid king Antiochus I. In the Hellenistic and Roman periods it was a major Carian city, and under Rome it housed a renowned gladiator school. And here life never stopped: the city remained continuously inhabited through the Byzantine, Beylik and Ottoman periods.

items.text: Did you know? The city is nicknamed the 'City of Gladiators' because gladiatorial games were held in its huge theatre. Later, an Ottoman village was built inside the ancient city: the houses, coffee house and fountain of Eskihisar stand among ancient columns, two layers living inside each other. Its north gate is one of the largest ancient city gates in Anatolia. And the name? It comes from the Seleucid queen Stratonice, the woman at the centre of a famous story about her marriages within the royal house.

items.text: The earliest finds here date to around 600 BC. Then, in the 4th century BC, came the Hecatomnid rulers: Mausolus and his brother Idrieus. They transformed Labraunda into a splendid cult centre, raising the Temple of Zeus, banqueting halls called androns, stoas and monumental gateways, the propylaia. The sanctuary remained in use in Roman times, and the cult endured until a Byzantine church was built on the site.

items.text: Did you know? Zeus Labraundos was shown holding a double-headed axe, the labrys, and the word 'labyrinth' shares the same root. The sanctuary owes its splendour to the Carian satrap Mausolus and his brother Idrieus: this was the mountain temple of the very dynasty that raised the Mausoleum. A fourteen-kilometre Sacred Way linked it to Mylasa, and we know the procession climbed it on foot. And its andrones, the royal banqueting halls, are the best-preserved examples known anywhere in the Greek world.

items.text: In Aydın province lie the remains of an Ionian city whose great temple became a landmark of ancient architectural design. This is the Ancient City of Magnesia ad Maeandrum, whose story begins in the 5th century BC, and which is famed for the Temple of Artemis Leukophryene.

items.text: The city was founded by Magnetes from Thessaly, and around 400 BC it was moved to a new site on the Lethaios river. Its golden age came under the Seleucids and the Kingdom of Pergamon, and in the Roman period it was an independent city. Carl Humann excavated here in 1891, and the work goes on: the site is still being excavated today.

items.text: Did you know? Hermogenes' pseudodipteral Temple of Artemis established a plan type that the Roman architect Vitruvius cited as a model. The silt of the Maeander buried the city again and again; its stadium lay underground for centuries until excavation brought it back. And the temple's Amazonomachy frieze? Today it is split between museums in Paris and Berlin.

items.text: Teos was founded in the 11th–10th century BC and became one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League. In the 6th century BC it fell to Persia, and some of its citizens fled to found Abdera in 543 BC. In the Hellenistic period the city came under Pergamon, and in the late 3rd century BC it hosted the Guild of Dionysiac Artists. Even in Roman times, Teos kept its importance.

Its story runs in two layers: settlement at Liman Tepe goes back to the 4th millennium BC, while the city itself dates from the 8th century BC. items.text: Settlement at Liman Tepe reaches back to the 4th millennium BC. Then, in the 5th century BC, fear changed everything: dreading the Persians, the inhabitants abandoned the mainland city and moved across to Karantina Island. Yet Klazomenai was never only a place of retreat. It struck some of the earliest silver coins in the 6th century BC and ran advanced olive oil workshops. Later, Alexander the Great bound the island to the mainland with a causeway.

items.text: Did you know? The olive oil workshop here dates to the 6th century BC, and with its 15 rock-cut pits it is among the earliest evidence of industrial-scale olive oil production, one of the oldest known anywhere. It has even been rebuilt and run experimentally, so the ancient process can be tried again. Anaxagoras came from here too: the philosopher who was put on trial in Athens for saying the sun was a red-hot stone. And finally, the painted terracotta 'Clazomenian sarcophagi' are rare witnesses to archaic painting.

items.text: You have arrived at Klaros, the Sanctuary of Apollo, in İzmir province. Its story is said to reach back to the 13th century BC. This was the renowned oracular sanctuary of Apollo, belonging to Kolophon — a place whose fame rivalled Delphi and Didyma. Come, let us listen to what the god once had to say.

items.text: Tradition places the founding of the sanctuary in the 13th century BC. The Doric oracular temple of Apollo was begun in the 3rd century BC and only completed under Hadrian, and the oracle kept speaking until the 4th century AD. A sacred road 2 km long linked the sanctuary to Notion. Then alluvium slowly covered it and kept it buried for centuries — and that is exactly why it survives so exceptionally well preserved today.

items.text: Did you know? In the temple cella, fragments of the cult statues of Apollo, Artemis and Leto still lie in place. The seated Apollo is thought to have stood nearly eight metres high, and even the surviving feet and hands show how colossal these figures were. The sanctuary also holds the 'hekatomb' block, used to tether a hundred sacrificial animals. And this was, above all, an oracle of Apollo: in a chamber beneath the temple the prophet drank from the sacred spring and gave the answer in verse. Those vaulted oracular chambers and the water channel beneath the temple survive, and you can still see the stair the prophet went down.

items.text: Aizanoi's story reaches back to the Early Bronze Age. In the Hellenistic period it grew into an important centre of the Phrygian region. Then came Rome, and with it, especially in the 2nd century AD, a golden age: this is when the Temple of Zeus and the theatre-stadium complex were built. The city also housed the earliest known ancient stock exchange building, the macellum.

Look up: most of its columns are still standing.

items.text: Did you know? The macellum at Aizanoi is considered the world's first stock exchange building, and it bears an inscribed inflation price list. In fact, Diocletian's Price Edict, carved on the wall of the macellum, turns what is called the first known exchange building into a document. The Temple of Zeus is the best-preserved temple of Zeus in Anatolia, and beneath it lies a vaulted undercroft belonging to Cybele: two religions, two storeys. And one more: theatre and stadium were built back to back as a single structure, a combination extremely rare in the ancient world.

items.text: You have arrived at Letoon Sanctuary, in Muğla province, a sacred place whose story runs from the 6th century BC to the 4th century AD. This Lycian sanctuary was dedicated to Leto and her twins, Apollo and Artemis, and together with Xanthos it is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
items.speech: You have arrived at Letoon Sanctuary, in Muğla province, a sacred place whose story runs from the 6th century BC to the 4th century AD. This Lycian sanctuary was dedicated to Leto and her twins, Apollo and Artemis, and together with Xanthos it is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

items.text: Letoon was more than a place of worship. It was the federal sanctuary of Lycia, where the religious and political decisions of the Lycian League were proclaimed. In the 4th century BC temples rose here to Leto, Artemis and Apollo. And it was here that the famous trilingual inscription of 337 BC was found, written in Lycian, Greek and Aramaic. In the Early Christian period the sanctuary was gradually abandoned.

items.text: Did you know? The trilingual inscription of 337 BC found at Letoon was the key to deciphering the Lycian language. Three temples stand side by side here, to Leto, Apollo and Artemis: a whole sanctuary dedicated to one family. And look closely at the ground — rising groundwater has flooded part of the site, so the temple foundations are now mirrored in the water.

items.text: You have arrived at Limyra Ancient City, in Finike, Antalya province. This Lycian city spans a long story, from the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD, and it is known for three treasures: the tomb monument of Pericles of Limyra, a Roman theatre and the Kaineus relief.
items.speech: You have arrived at Limyra Ancient City, in Finike, Antalya province. This Lycian city spans a long story, from the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD, and it is known for three treasures: the tomb monument of Pericles of Limyra, a Roman theatre and the Kaineus relief.

items.text: In Lycian inscriptions the city appears as 'Zemuri'. In the first half of the 4th century BC, under King Pericles, it became the capital of Lycia. Roman rule brought it new life, until the earthquake of AD 141 dealt it a heavy blow. Yet Limyra endured, and in the Byzantine period it continued to exist as a bishopric.

items.text: Did you know? The Kaineus relief here is the most famous ancient depiction of the hero Kaineus, who was pinned into the ground with spears. Limyra was the capital of the Lycian king Pericles, and more than four hundred tombs are ranged on the cliff above it. And one more story: Gaius Caesar, Augustus' grandson and heir, died here, and the reliefs of the cenotaph raised for him were found in the city.

items.text: Look out from the terraces of Arykanda Ancient City, in Antalya province. This spectacular Lycian city, built on terraces facing the mountains, spans the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD, and it offers a unique panorama over the Finike plain.
items.speech: Look out from the terraces of Arykanda Ancient City, in Antalya province. This spectacular Lycian city, built on terraces facing the mountains, spans the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD, and it offers a unique panorama over the Finike plain.

items.text: Arykanda was a member of the Lycian League, inhabited from the 5th century BC, and its terraced urban layout took shape during the Hellenistic and Roman periods. In the 2nd century AD came a major building boom. Then, in the 6th century, earthquakes struck: the city was severely damaged and was gradually abandoned.

items.text: Did you know? Arykanda is one of the rare ancient cities built on five large rock-cut terraces ascending a mountainside. Theatre, stadium and baths are stacked one above another up the steep slope, and its view is singled out among ancient cities. Even its name tells a story: the '-anda' ending is native Anatolian, showing the city existed long before Greek colonisation. And a final detail: ancient sources remark on the Arykandans' appetite for pleasure, and on their debts.

items.text: Tlos was one of the six founding cities of the Lycian League, and people have lived here without a break for more than 4,000 years. Under Roman rule it grew into a major metropolis of the region and a leading member of the League. Even then its story was not over: the fortress on the acropolis stayed in use through the Byzantine and Ottoman periods.

items.text: Did you know? In mythology Tlos is regarded as the city of the hero Bellerophon, who killed the Chimera with his winged horse Pegasus. Tlos is one of Lycia's oldest cities, inhabited without a break for four thousand years, and a nineteenth-century Ottoman lord's castle crowns its acropolis.

items.text: Welcome to Kibyra, known as the 'City of Gladiators', an ancient city in Burdur province. Its story runs from the 2nd century BC to the 6th century AD. Two things made it famous: the world-renowned Medusa mosaic in its odeon, and its gladiator school.
items.speech: Welcome to Kibyra, known as the 'City of Gladiators', an ancient city in Burdur province. Its story runs from the 2nd century BC to the 6th century AD. Two things made it famous: the world-renowned Medusa mosaic in its odeon, and its gladiator school.

items.text: According to Strabo, Kibyra was founded by Lydians who migrated to the Kabalis region, and with its neighbours it formed the 'Tetrapolis', a league of four cities. Then, in AD 23, an earthquake destroyed it. The city was rebuilt with the aid of Emperor Tiberius and, in gratitude, took a new name: 'Caesarea Kibyra'. Under Rome it became a centre of justice and trade, famous for its gladiator school.

items.text: You have arrived at Antiochia ad Pisidiam, Antioch of Pisidia, an ancient city in Isparta province whose story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 6th century AD. This was a Roman colony where Paul the Apostle preached, and its proudest monument is the Temple of Augustus, the Augusteum. Let us walk through it together.
items.speech: You have arrived at Antiochia ad Pisidiam, Antioch of Pisidia, an ancient city in Isparta province whose story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 6th century AD. This was a Roman colony where Paul the Apostle preached, and its proudest monument is the Temple of Augustus, the Augusteum. Let us walk through it together.

items.text: The city was born as a frontier post. Around 275 BC the Seleucid dynasty founded it to control Galatian raids. Then, in 25 BC, Augustus made it a Roman colony called 'Colonia Caesarea'. Soon a new voice was heard here: Paul the Apostle preached with Barnabas in the local synagogue. That visit was never forgotten, and the city remained an important Christian pilgrimage centre into the Byzantine period.

items.text: Did you know? In Roman times the city's main street, the 'Cardo Maximus', led straight up to the Temple of Augustus to promote the imperial cult, and the community here was known as the 'People of Augustus'. It was here that Saint Paul preached his first major sermon; this is the city whose synagogue Acts names. One of the most important Latin copies of Augustus' Res Gestae, his own account of his deeds, was also found here. And one more detail: the city was founded as a colony settled with retired legionaries, which is why its street plan follows the logic of a military camp.

items.text: Here on the Mediterranean, in Mersin province, lies Anemurium. Its story runs from the 4th century BC to the 7th century AD. This well-preserved Roman and late Roman coastal city stands out for its baths, its aqueduct and its vast necropolis. Shall we explore?
items.speech: Here on the Mediterranean, in Mersin province, lies Anemurium. Its story runs from the 4th century BC to the 7th century AD. This well-preserved Roman and late Roman coastal city stands out for its baths, its aqueduct and its vast necropolis. Shall we explore?

items.text: Anemurium was founded beside Cape Anamur, and in the Roman and Byzantine periods it was an important port on the Eastern Mediterranean trade route. Then came the Arab raids of the 7th century, and the city was largely abandoned. Yet it was not entirely forgotten: in the 12th century, under the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, it was partly reoccupied.

items.text: Did you know? Anemurium lies right beside Cape Anamur, the southernmost point of Asia Minor and of Anatolia, only 64 km from Cyprus; on a clear day, the coast of Cyprus is visible 64 kilometres away. With over three hundred monumental tombs, most of them two-storeyed and vaulted, it has one of the largest necropolises of the ancient world. And with two bath complexes, two theatres and mosaic-floored churches, the city lies just as it was left, sloping down to the sea.

This was the sacred centre of the priest-kings of Olba, and today it is famous for the standing columns of the Temple of Zeus Olbios.

items.text: Uzuncaburç began life as a sanctuary, the sacred heart of the Hellenistic kingdom of Olba. Then came the Romans. Under Emperor Vespasian it was turned into a separate Roman city with a new name: Diocaesarea. The colonnaded street, the theatre and the temples you will see all survive from this period.

items.text: Here is the Temple of Tyche, a small temple dedicated to Tyche, goddess of fortune. Modest in size, perhaps, but who would not have wanted fortune on their side?

items.text: Did you know? The city's name means 'tall tower', after the high Hellenistic tower on the city's northern edge, a tower depicted on the city's ancient coins. The Temple of Zeus Olbios is among the earliest Corinthian temples in Anatolia, raised not long after the order itself was devised. The city was ruled by the Teucrids, a dynasty of priest-kings: a rare arrangement in which priesthood and rule sat in the same person. And that twenty-two-metre Hellenistic tower, which gives the village its name, still stands today.

items.text: You have arrived at Karatepe-Aslantaş Open-Air Museum in Osmaniye province, a Late Hittite fortress of the 8th century BC. Why is it kept as an open-air museum? Because of a single bilingual inscription — the text that unlocked the decipherment of Luwian hieroglyphs. Let us step inside.
items.speech: You have arrived at Karatepe-Aslantaş Open-Air Museum in Osmaniye province, a Late Hittite fortress of the 8th century BC. Why is it kept as an open-air museum? Because of a single bilingual inscription, the text that unlocked the decipherment of Luwian hieroglyphs. Let us step inside.

items.text: Its builders called it Azatiwataya. In the 8th century BC it was raised as the frontier fortress of the Adanawa city-state, yet the castle was abandoned shortly after its foundation. For centuries it lay silent. Then came the excavations of 1946, and with them a new life: Karatepe became Turkey's first open-air museum.

items.text: Did you know? The Karatepe bilingual inscription carries the same text in Phoenician and in Hieroglyphic Luwian. Phoenician alphabet beside Luwian hieroglyphs: like a 'Rosetta Stone', it was pivotal in deciphering Anatolian hieroglyphs, the key that unlocked Luwian hieroglyphic — Anatolia's Rosetta Stone. And there is more. The reliefs in King Azatiwataş's fortress were never removed, so you see them exactly where the king set them. That is thanks to Halet Çambel, who led the excavation: she had the surroundings declared a national park, choosing to protect the works in place rather than move them to a museum.

items.text: Rome brought the city under its control in the 1st century BC, and under Septimius Severus it gained the proud title of metropolis. The centuries that followed saw Byzantine, Arab, Armenian and Mamluk periods, and people kept on living here through all of them. So how did it end? After the Mamluks took the city in 1375, it was abandoned.

items.text: Did you know? Anavarza is known as the birthplace of the famous physician Dioscorides, author of De Materia Medica — for centuries Europe's standard pharmacology text. Excavations since 2013 have revealed the world's first known double-lane colonnaded road. The city sits at the foot of a vast sheer rock, with the castle on top and the city on the plain. Its colonnaded street and triumphal arch survive, and the mosaics from its villas are among the finest in the region.

This was a Bronze Age city of the Amuq plain, and it is famous above all for one treasure: the cuneiform archive of King Niqmepa. Shall we step back in time?

items.text: In the 2nd millennium BC, Alalakh was the capital of the kingdom of Mukiš, and with its palaces and temples it was one of the most important centres of the region. Its secrets came back to light when Leonard Woolley excavated the mound between 1937 and 1949. The mound lies just southeast of Tell Tayinat.

items.text: Did you know? The inscription on the statue of King Idrimi is one of the most important documents of the ancient Near East: an autobiography written in cuneiform, in the first person. King Idrimi had his life story carved onto his own statue in 104 lines — how he lost his throne, fled, and returned. The statue is now in the British Museum. On the palace walls, frescoes were found painted in the technique of the Minoan palaces of Crete, some of the most concrete evidence of the link between the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean. And the cuneiform archive of King Niqmepa records how a small Bronze Age kingdom kept its footing between great powers.

items.text: Her şey bir dertle başladı. Seleukeia Pieria, Antakya'nın limanıydı; ama arkasındaki dağdan inen sel suları limanı sürekli alüvyonla dolduruyordu. Vespasianus döneminde cesur bir çözüme girişildi: suyu limanın yanından geçirip denize atmak için dağı boydan boya delmek. Patlayıcı yoktu. Yalnızca çekiç ve keski vardı. Yazıtlar, bu işi Roma askerlerinin ve mahkûmların yaptığını kaydediyor. Taşa inen her darbeyi bir an düşünün.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Tünelin tamamlanması yaklaşık yüz yıl sürdü; girişteki yazıtta işi başlatan Vespasianus ile bitiren Titus'un adları birlikte geçer. Tünel 1380 metre uzunluğunda, yer yer 7 metre yüksekliğinde ve baştan sona elle, çekiç ve keskiyle oyulmuş. Antik dünyanın bilinen en büyük su tahliye tüneli bu. Üstelik iki uçtan aynı anda kazılmaya başlandı ve ekipler dağın ortasında buluştu; birleşme noktasındaki hafif kaymayı bugün tünelin içinde çıplak gözle görebilirsiniz. Ve tünelin çıkışında başka bir dünya bekliyor: Beşikli Mağara, kayaya oyulmuş on iki mezar odasından oluşan bir Roma nekropolü.

items.text: Imagine cutting a path for water straight through a mountain, by hand. You are at the Vespasian–Titus Tunnel, a monument in Hatay province from the 1st century AD. This 1.4-kilometre Roman diversion tunnel was cut through solid rock to keep floodwater out of the harbour of Seleucia Pieria.
items.speech: Imagine cutting a path for water straight through a mountain, by hand. You are at the Vespasian–Titus Tunnel, a monument in Hatay province from the 1st century AD. This 1.4-kilometre Roman diversion tunnel was cut through solid rock to keep floodwater out of the harbour of Seleucia Pieria.

items.text: To understand this tunnel, start with the harbour. Seleucia Pieria was the port of Antioch, and floodwater pouring off the mountain behind it kept silting that harbour up. The answer, begun under Vespasian, was bold: cut clean through the mountain and throw the water into the sea beside the port. There were no explosives. The tunnel was carved with hammer and chisel, and inscriptions record who did the work: Roman soldiers and convicts.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the tunnel mouth, then follow the channel and watercourse. Look out for the Beşikli Cave tombs, and be sure to find the Vespasian–Titus inscription.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the tunnel mouth, then follow the channel and watercourse. Look out for the Beşikli Cave tombs, and be sure to find the Vespasian–Titus inscription.

items.text: Did you know? The tunnel took roughly a century to finish, and the inscription at its mouth names both Vespasian, who began it, and Titus, who completed it. It runs 1,380 metres and stands up to seven metres high in places, all of it cut by hand with hammer and chisel — the largest known diversion tunnel of the ancient world. Digging began from both ends at once, and the teams met inside the mountain; look closely and you can still see, with the naked eye, the slight misalignment where they joined. Finally, the Beşikli Cave at the tunnel's outflow is a Roman necropolis of twelve rock-cut burial chambers.

Bu büyük karst mağarası, Anadolu'nun bilinen en eski insan yerleşimlerinden biri; Paleolitik'ten Klasik döneme kadar hiç kesintisiz kullanılmış. Karain Mağarası sesli rehberine hoş geldiniz. Bir an durun: insanlar bu kayaların altına ne zamandan beri sığınıyor?

items.text: You are at Karain Cave, in Antalya province, and the story here begins about 500,000 years ago. This great karst cave is one of the oldest known human dwellings in Anatolia, used without a break from the Palaeolithic to the classical age.
items.speech: You are at Karain Cave, in Antalya province, and the story here begins about 500,000 years ago. This great karst cave is one of the oldest known human dwellings in Anatolia, used without a break from the Palaeolithic to the classical age.

items.text: The cave lies at the foot of Mount Katran, and for roughly half a million years it was in use without a break. Its layers have yielded Neanderthal as well as Homo sapiens remains, hearths, and tools of stone and bone. In the classical period its mouth became a sanctuary, with votive niches and inscriptions cut into the rock. Pause and imagine the generations who sheltered here.

items.text: Did you know? Karain was the first Palaeolithic cave excavated in Türkiye, and the first evidence of Neanderthals in Anatolia came out of it. Its deposits are eleven metres deep and hold an unbroken sequence of half a million years of occupation; there is nothing else like it in Türkiye. The first Neanderthal remains found in Anatolia came from here, and traces of Homo sapiens occur in the same layers.

items.text: Before you, cut into the rock above a spring, is the İvriz Rock Relief, a monument in Konya province from the 8th century BC. This Neo-Hittite relief shows King Warpalawas standing before Tarhunzas, the storm god, with ears of grain and a bunch of grapes.
items.speech: Before you, cut into the rock above a spring, is the İvriz Rock Relief, a monument in Konya province from the 8th century BC. This Neo-Hittite relief shows King Warpalawas standing before Tarhunzas, the storm god, with ears of grain and a bunch of grapes.

items.text: In the eighth century BC, Warpalawas, king of Tuwana, had himself and Tarhunzas, the god of plenty, carved into the rock above this spring. The result is among the largest works of Neo-Hittite art. Look closely: the god, shown nearly twice the king's height, holds a sheaf of grain and a bunch of grapes.

items.text: Did you know? The grain and grapes in the god's hands are among the earliest known images of a deity holding the produce of farming — a god's bounty made visible — and the same iconography reappears in the region's art centuries later. The god is shown nearly twice the king's height, because in Neo-Hittite art scale is the standard way of stating rank.

items.text: In the last century of the Hittite Empire, a monumental pool was built over a spring in dressed stone. Now look at its north face. İşte bu yüzden Göreme vadisi 10. yüzyıldan itibaren manastırlara dönüştü. Kiliseler, yemekhaneler, hücreler… hepsi tek tek kayaya kazıldı. Kilise adını tek bir küçük pencereden alır. İçeri az ışık girdiği için freskleri, Kapadokya'nın en canlı renkli resimleridir. Bir de şuna dikkat edin: kaya kiliselerinin çoğunda hiçbir yük taşımayan sütunlar ve kemerler yontulmuştur. Kayanın içinde gereksiz olan bu ögeler, yalnızca gerçek bir kilise gibi görünsün diye yapıldı. Ve son olarak, Tokalı Kilise'nin o mavisi lapis lazuli taşından elde edilmişti; o dönemde altından bile pahalı bir taştan.

items.text: You are standing in Göreme Open Air Museum, a rock settlement in Nevşehir province whose story belongs to the 10th–12th century AD. All around you, monasteries and churches have been cut straight into the tuff. And somewhere among them waits the Dark Church, whose frescoes are among the best-preserved Byzantine paintings anywhere. Shall we step into this world of rock?
items.speech: You are standing in Göreme Open Air Museum, a rock settlement in Nevşehir province whose story belongs to the 10th–12th century AD. All around you, monasteries and churches have been cut straight into the tuff. And somewhere among them waits the Dark Church, whose frescoes are among the best-preserved Byzantine paintings anywhere. Shall we step into this world of rock?

items.text: Why here? The answer lies in the stone itself. Volcanic tuff is soft enough to dig with a pick, yet it hardens once cut. That is why, from the tenth century on, the Göreme valley became a landscape of monasteries, as churches, refectories and cells were hollowed out one by one. Some were painted on plaster, others straight onto the rock. And the Dark Church? It kept its colours because only a single small window lets the light in.
