items.text: On the Turabdin plateau in Mardin province stands Mor Gabriel Monastery, a monastery and church founded in 397. It is the oldest continuously inhabited Syriac Orthodox monastery in the world, and its domed church was given mosaics by Byzantine emperors.
items.speech: On the Turabdin plateau in Mardin province stands Mor Gabriel Monastery, a monastery and church founded in 397. It is the oldest continuously inhabited Syriac Orthodox monastery in the world, and its domed church was given mosaics by Byzantine emperors.

items.text: Founded in 397, this is the oldest surviving Syriac Orthodox monastery in continuous use. It is named after Gabriel, the bishop who lived here in the seventh century. Look for the mosaics of the main church's dome: they were paid for by Byzantine emperors. And life here goes on, for on the Turabdin plateau the monastery still houses a bishop and a monastic community.

items.text: You have come to Mor Hananyo Monastery, a monastery and church in Mardin province, founded in 493. For centuries it was the seat of the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate. And beneath it lies something even older: a vaulted room that survives from a sun temple that stood here before the monastery.

items.text: The monastery was founded in 493, and from the twelfth century until 1932 it was the seat of the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate. Its name carries a lovely story: saffron, it is said, was mixed into its mortar. Beneath the buildings lies a vaulted room whose blocks were laid without mortar. It is far older than the monastery and belongs to the sun temple that stood here.

Vadi, Göreme Milli Parkı ile birlikte Dünya Mirası kapsamındadır.

items.text: Listen to the quiet. You are in Soğanlı Valley, a rock settlement in Kayseri province from the 9th to the 13th century. This is the quiet valley of Cappadocia: dozens of churches are cut into its slopes, and their frescoes, unlike Göreme's, mostly stand without a crowd in front of them.
items.speech: Listen to the quiet. You are in Soğanlı Valley, a rock settlement in Kayseri province from the 9th to the 13th century. This is the quiet valley of Cappadocia: dozens of churches are cut into its slopes, and their frescoes, unlike Göreme's, mostly stand without a crowd in front of them.

items.text: This valley in southern Cappadocia was a monastic district, settled by Byzantine monks between the ninth and thirteenth centuries. The dozens of churches cut into its slopes repeat, in domed and cross-plan form, what Göreme offers. The difference? Here their frescoes usually stand without anyone in front of them. The valley falls within the World Heritage inscription made with the Göreme National Park.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Domed Church and the Church of the Snake, step into the Karabaş Church and the Church of the Deer, and look up at the Dovecotes.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Domed Church and the Church of the Snake, step into the Karabaş Church and the Church of the Deer, and look up at the Dovecotes.

items.text: Did you know? The dovecotes cut into the valley's rock were not decorative. For centuries, pigeon droppings were the main fertiliser of its vineyards and gardens. And although the valley falls within the same World Heritage inscription as the Göreme National Park, it sees only a fraction of its visitors.

items.text: Ankara'dasınız, Anadolu Medeniyetleri Müzesi'nde. 1921'de kurulan bu müze bir Osmanlı bedesteninin içinde yaşıyor. Burada Anadolu'nun hikâyesini, Paleolitik'ten Roma'ya kadar tek bir güzergâhta yürüyerek dinleyeceksiniz. Ve yolunuz, dünyanın en kapsamlı Hitit ve Geç Hitit koleksiyonundan geçecek.

items.text: Müzenin binası da başlı başına bir hikâye. 15. yüzyıldan kalma Mahmut Paşa Bedesteni ile Kurşunlu Han restore edildi ve birleştirildi. Çalışma, Atatürk'ün bir 'Eti Müzesi' kurma isteğiyle başladı; zamanla Anadolu'nun bütün dönemlerini kapsayan bir koleksiyona dönüştü. Sergileme kronolojik ilerliyor: Paleolitik'ten başlıyor, Çatalhöyük, Hitit, Frig ve Urartu salonlarından geçerek Roma'ya ulaşıyorsunuz.

items.text: You are about to walk through the whole of Anatolia's past in a single building: the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, in Ankara province, founded in 1921. Housed in an Ottoman bedesten, it tells Anatolia's story from the Palaeolithic to Rome along a single route, and it holds the world's fullest Hittite and Neo-Hittite collection.
items.speech: You are about to walk through the whole of Anatolia's past in a single building: the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, in Ankara province, founded in 1921. Housed in an Ottoman bedesten, it tells Anatolia's story from the Palaeolithic to Rome along a single route, and it holds the world's fullest Hittite and Neo-Hittite collection.

items.text: The museum was created by restoring and joining two old buildings: the fifteenth-century Mahmut Pasha bedesten and the Kurşunlu Han. It began with Atatürk's wish for a 'Hittite Museum', and grew into a collection covering every period of Anatolia. The display is chronological: you start in the Palaeolithic and walk on through the Çatalhöyük, Hittite, Phrygian and Urartian halls, all the way to Rome.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Çatalhöyük hall and the Hittite hall, then the Neo-Hittite orthostats, and further on the Phrygian hall and the Urartian hall.

items.text: Did you know? In 1997 it was named European Museum of the Year — the first museum in Türkiye to win the award. The museum was made by restoring and joining a fifteenth-century bedesten and a han, so the building itself is part of the collection. And it holds the world's fullest Hittite and Neo-Hittite collection: the orthostats of Karatepe, Carchemish and Arslantepe line up together in one hall.

items.text: İstanbul'dasınız, Türkiye'nin ilk müzesinin kapısında. İstanbul Arkeoloji Müzeleri'ni 1891'de Osman Hamdi Bey kurdu. Ve aynı bahçede, birkaç adım içinde, İskender Lahdi'ni, Kadeş Antlaşması tabletini ve Çinili Köşk'ü bulacaksınız. Hoş geldiniz.

items.text: Bu müzenin doğuşu bir kararla bağlantılı. Osmanlı'da eski eserlerin yurt dışına çıkarılmasını yasaklayan düzenlemeler geldiğinde bir soru ortaya çıktı: kazılardan çıkanlar ülkede kalacaksa nerede duracaktı? Cevabı Osman Hamdi Bey verdi ve müzeyi 1891'de açtı. Bugün müze üç bölümden oluşuyor: Arkeoloji Müzesi, Eski Şark Eserleri Müzesi ve Çinili Köşk. Koleksiyonun çekirdeğini ise Sidon kral nekropolünden çıkarılan lahitler oluşturuyor.

Bu müze Türkiye'nin ilk müzesi ve eski eserlerin yurt dışına çıkarılmasını yasaklayan düzenlemelerle birlikte doğdu: kazıdan çıkanın ülkede kalması için bir yer gerekiyordu. Bir de şu var: Kadeş Antlaşması'nın çivi yazılı tableti burada. Bilinen en eski yazılı barış antlaşmasının bir kopyası ise New York'taki BM binasında asılı duruyor.

items.text: You are entering Istanbul Archaeological Museums, in İstanbul province: Türkiye's first museum, founded in 1891 by Osman Hamdi Bey. Here the Alexander Sarcophagus, the Kadesh treaty tablet and the Tiled Kiosk share a single garden. Where shall we start?
items.speech: You are entering Istanbul Archaeological Museums, in İstanbul province: Türkiye's first museum, founded in 1891 by Osman Hamdi Bey. Here the Alexander Sarcophagus, the Kadesh treaty tablet and the Tiled Kiosk share a single garden. Where shall we start?

items.text: Osman Hamdi Bey opened the museum in 1891, and its birth was tied to a turning point: the regulations that stopped antiquities leaving the Ottoman Empire. What came out of the ground needed somewhere to stay, and this became that place. Today it has three parts: the Archaeological Museum, the Museum of the Ancient Orient and the Tiled Kiosk. At the heart of the collection lie the sarcophagi from the royal necropolis of Sidon.
items.speech: Osman Hamdi Bey opened the museum in 1891, and its birth was tied to a turning point: the regulations that stopped antiquities leaving the Ottoman Empire. At the heart of the collection lie the sarcophagi from the royal necropolis of Sidon.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Alexander Sarcophagus and the Sarcophagus of the Mourning Women. Look for the Kadesh treaty tablet and the Ishtar Gate panels, and then step across to the Tiled Kiosk.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Alexander Sarcophagus and the Sarcophagus of the Mourning Women. Look for the Kadesh treaty tablet and the Ishtar Gate panels, and then step across to the Tiled Kiosk.

items.text: Did you know? The Alexander Sarcophagus is misnamed. It was made not for Alexander but for Abdalonymus, king of Sidon in his time; Alexander appears only in the carving. This was also Türkiye's first museum, born alongside the rules that stopped antiquities leaving the country, because what came out of the ground needed somewhere to stay. And one more treasure: the cuneiform tablet of the Treaty of Kadesh is here, while a copy of this oldest known written peace treaty hangs at the UN in New York.

items.speech: You are about to enter the Zeugma Mosaic Museum in Gaziantep province, opened in 2011. It is the largest mosaic museum in the world, and every floor here has a story: these mosaics were rescued from Zeugma before the Birecik dam flooded the city.

items.text: In 2000 the Birecik dam began to fill, and the water was set to drown most of Zeugma. An international rescue excavation lifted the floor mosaics out of the villas. Here, the museum lays them out following the plan of the rooms they came from — so you do not walk across the mosaics, you walk through the houses.

items.text: Did you know? This is the largest mosaic museum in the world, and its floors were lifted out in a rescue dig before the Birecik dam filled. items.text: Welcome to the Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum, in Şanlıurfa province, opened in 2015. This is the home of the finds from Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe, and of the Balıklıgöl statue — the oldest known life-size sculpture of a human being.
items.speech: Welcome to the Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum, in Şanlıurfa province, opened in 2015. This is the home of the finds from Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe, and of the Balıklıgöl statue, the oldest known life-size sculpture of a human being.

items.text: Opened in 2015, the museum has the largest indoor exhibition area in Türkiye. Inside it, one of the enclosures of Göbekli Tepe has been rebuilt at excavation scale. The Neolithic hall keeps growing with finds from the region's 'Taş Tepeler' digs, and the Balıklıgöl statue stands on the same floor as the T-shaped pillars of Nevali Çori.

items.text: Antakya, Roma İmparatorluğu'nun en büyük üçüncü kentiydi. Çevresindeki villalarda taban mozaikleri olağanüstü bir yaygınlıkla kullanılıyordu. 1930'lardaki kazılarda bu mozaikler birer birer gün yüzüne çıktı ve onlar için 1948'de bir müze kuruldu. Koleksiyon 2014'te yeni binasına taşındı. Mozaiklere yakından bakın: yalnızca mitolojik sahneler yok; gündelik hayat, yemek sofraları, hatta nazarlıklar da var.

items.text: Mosaics are waiting for you at the Hatay Archaeology Museum, in Hatay province, founded in 1948. It holds one of the richest mosaic collections in the world, lifted from the Roman villas of Antioch and Samandağ.
items.speech: Mosaics are waiting for you at the Hatay Archaeology Museum, in Hatay province, founded in 1948. It holds one of the richest mosaic collections in the world, lifted from the Roman villas of Antioch and Samandağ.

items.text: Antioch was the third city of the Roman Empire, and in the villas around it floor mosaics were laid on an extraordinary scale. A museum was founded in 1948 for what the excavations of the 1930s had brought to light, and in 2014 the collection moved to a new building. Look closely as you go: these mosaics show not only mythological scenes but daily life, dining tables and charms against the evil eye.

items.text: Did you know? The museum's 'Evil Eye' mosaic paints the curse as an eye and sets crows, a scorpion and a snake upon it: a charm against bad luck from the second century AD. And remember the city behind it all. Antioch was the third city of the Roman Empire, and the floors of the villas around it make up one of the richest collections of Roman mosaic in the world.

items.speech: You are now inside the Ephesus Museum, a museum in İzmir province, opened in 1964. This is the museum of the Ephesus excavations. Here you will meet the two statues of Artemis, along with the frescoes and sculpture from the Terrace Houses.

items.text: The museum at Selçuk holds what came out of the Ephesus excavations but could not be shown on site. Frescoes and sculpture from the Terrace Houses, finds from the city's daily life and objects from the cult of Artemis each have their own hall. If you have just walked through Ephesus, this is where you see the inside of the city — the display was arranged for exactly that.

items.text: Did you know? What the egg-shaped protrusions covering the Artemis statues represent is still argued over: breasts, bulls' testicles, dates and votive pouches have all been proposed. Take a look and decide for yourself. The frescoes and mosaics of the Terrace Houses are here too, among the fullest surviving evidence of what the inside of a wealthy Roman home looked like.

items.text: You are about to step into Antalya Museum, in Antalya province, founded in 1922. It is one of Anatolia's largest museums, home to the imperial and divine sculpture of Perge, Lycian sarcophagi and the Elmalı coin hoard.
items.speech: You are about to step into Antalya Museum, in Antalya province, founded in 1922. It is one of Anatolia's largest museums, home to the imperial and divine sculpture of Perge, Lycian sarcophagi and the Elmalı coin hoard.

items.text: The museum was founded in 1922, and it began with one person: a schoolteacher whose personal effort aimed to stop the city's antiquities leaving the country. Today the backbone of the collection is Perge. The imperial and divine statues from its theatre and baths form one of the best-preserved groups of Roman sculpture anywhere.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Gallery of Gods and the Gallery of Emperors, then look for the Sarcophagus of Heracles, the Elmalı coin hoard and the Lycian sarcophagi.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Gallery of Gods and the Gallery of Emperors, then look for the Sarcophagus of Heracles, the Elmalı coin hoard and the Lycian sarcophagi.

items.text: Did you know? The upper half of the museum's Weary Heracles was smuggled out in the 1960s and sold in Boston, while the lower half stayed in Antalya. The two halves were finally reunited in 2011. And the museum itself owes its existence to a schoolteacher: it was founded in 1922 through the personal effort of someone trying to keep the city's antiquities from leaving the country.

Koleksiyon, Türkiye kıyılarında kazılan batıklardan oluşur. Bunların en ünlüsü Uluburun batığı. MÖ 14. yüzyıla tarihlenen bu gemi, bakır külçelerden fildişine, Mısır mücevherinden Baltık kehribarına kadar on bir farklı kültürün malını taşıyordu. Tek bir gemide, koca bir dünya.

items.text: You are inside a crusader castle in Muğla province, and within its walls lies the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, founded in 1962. It holds one of the world's foremost collections of shipwreck finds, among them the Bronze Age Uluburun wreck.
items.speech: You are inside a crusader castle in Muğla province, and within its walls lies the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, founded in 1962. It holds one of the world's foremost collections of shipwreck finds, among them the Bronze Age Uluburun wreck.

items.text: The walls around you are a story in themselves. Bodrum Castle was built by the Knights of Rhodes in the fifteenth century, partly from the stones of the Mausoleum. The collection comes from wrecks excavated off the Turkish coast. Its star is the Uluburun ship, of the fourteenth century BC, which was carrying goods from eleven different cultures: copper ingots, ivory, Egyptian jewellery and Baltic amber.

items.text: Close to the mound of Troy, in Çanakkale province, stands the Troy Museum, opened in 2018. Notice its shape: a cube half-sunk into the ground. Inside, it lays out Troy's nine layers and traces what was carried away from the city.
items.speech: Close to the mound of Troy, in Çanakkale province, stands the Troy Museum, opened in 2018. Notice its shape: a cube half-sunk into the ground. Inside, it lays out Troy's nine layers and traces what was carried away from the city.

items.text: The museum opened in 2018, about a kilometre from the mound. It was designed as a rusted steel cube sunk into the ground, so that the building, like the excavation, is read from the bottom up. The display works through Troy's nine layers in order, and it states plainly where the objects taken from the city — the Treasure of Priam among them — are held today.

items.text: Did you know? The 'Treasure of Priam' that Schliemann removed went first to Germany, vanished in the Second World War, and surfaced in Moscow in 1993. It is still in Russia today. And the museum itself was designed as a rusted steel cube sunk into the ground, so you walk it from the bottom up, just like the excavation.

items.text: You are now at the Mevlâna Museum, a museum in Konya province from the 13th century. Here lies the tomb of Mevlâna Celâleddin Rumi, with the Mevlevi lodge around it. Look up at the green-tiled dome: it is the emblem of Konya.
items.speech: You are now at the Mevlâna Museum, a museum in Konya province from the 13th century. Here lies the tomb of Mevlâna Celâleddin Rumi, with the Mevlevi lodge around it. Look up at the green-tiled dome: it is the emblem of Konya.

items.text: This building stands on ground that was once the rose garden of the Seljuk palace, given to Mevlâna's father. When Mevlâna died in 1273, a tomb was raised over him. Over the following centuries a semahane, dervish cells, kitchens and a fountain grew up around it, and together they became a Mevlevi lodge. In 1926 it opened as a museum.

items.text: Did you know? The night Mevlâna died is called Şeb-i Arûs, 'the wedding night', for the union it was held to be, and Konya marks it every 17 December. The green-tiled dome dates from the thirteenth century and is the emblem of Konya. And the ground beneath it was once the rose garden of the Seljuk palace.

items.text: In the late 1930s, excavations behind Sultanahmet uncovered a vast mosaic floor that once paved the colonnaded court of the Byzantine Great Palace. Rather than lifting it and carrying it away, they roofed it where it lay and opened it as a museum. It dates to the early Byzantine period, and surprisingly it shows not the life of the court but the countryside.
items.speech: In the late 1930s, excavations behind Sultanahmet uncovered a vast mosaic floor that once paved the colonnaded court of the Byzantine Great Palace. It dates to the early Byzantine period, and surprisingly it shows not the life of the court but the countryside.

items.text: As you wander, take in the Mosaic floor as a whole, then look closer at the Hunting scenes. Walk along the Peristyle gallery, and don't miss the Elephant and lion panel.
items.speech: As you wander, take in the Mosaic floor as a whole, then look closer at the Hunting scenes. Walk along the Peristyle gallery, and don't miss the Elephant and lion panel.

items.text: Did you know? More than a hundred human and animal figures have been counted across its scenes, and not one of them is religious or dynastic. The mosaic was never lifted: it is kept exactly where it was found, as the courtyard floor of the Byzantine palace. Instead of emperors or saints, hunters, herdsmen and animals describe life in the countryside.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Hierapolis nekropolü, Anadolu'nun en büyük antik mezarlıklarından biridir: iki kilometre boyunca binden fazla mezar sıralanır ve müzedeki lahitlerin çoğu oradan gelir. items.text: Did you know? The necropolis of Hierapolis is among the largest ancient cemeteries in Anatolia, with over a thousand tombs along two kilometres, and most of the sarcophagi in the museum came out of it. Because the museum sits in the vaulted halls of the city's Roman baths, the building is part of the collection too. And the reliefs taken from the theatre's stage building are among the fullest Roman sequences describing the cult of Apollo and Artemis.

items.text: You are in the Uşak Archaeology Museum, in Uşak province, opened in 1978. This is the home of the Lydian Hoard from the tumuli of the region, and its emblem is a winged sea-horse brooch that was stolen and recovered years later.
items.speech: You are in the Uşak Archaeology Museum, in Uşak province, opened in 1978. This is the home of the Lydian Hoard from the tumuli of the region, and its emblem is a winged sea-horse brooch that was stolen and recovered years later.

items.text: The story of this museum is bound up with looting. In the 1960s the Lydian tumuli around Uşak were plundered, and pieces were taken out of the country. They came back in 1993, after a suit brought against the Metropolitan Museum in New York. Ever since, the collection known as the Lydian Hoard has been shown here.

items.text: In 2017 the museum moved into the restored halls of the Milli Mensucat textile mill, built at the start of the twentieth century, and became one of the largest museum buildings in Türkiye. Alongside finds that run from the mounds of the Çukurova to its Roman cities, it also displays something unexpected: the mill's own looms.

items.text: Welcome to Van Museum, a museum in Van province, founded in 1972. It is one of the few museums anywhere with an Urartian collection of this depth: the bronze belts, helmets and cuneiform tablets from Çavuştepe, Ayanis and Toprakkale.

items.text: Founded in 1972, the museum gathers the finds from excavations at the Urartian centres around Lake Van: Çavuştepe, Ayanis and Toprakkale. Its bronze belts, helmets, horse harness and cuneiform tablets make one of the fullest collections of Urartian metalwork anywhere. The group of stelae found at Hakkâri is displayed here too.

items.text: You are now inside Amasya Museum, a museum in Amasya province, founded in 1925. Its halls carry Amasya's finds from the Chalcolithic to the Ottomans. And alongside them rests something rare: six mummies surviving from the Ilkhanid period.

items.text: The museum was founded in 1925 and later moved to its present building. It follows Amasya's finds from the Chalcolithic to the Ottomans. Its best known holding, though, is the group of Ilkhanid-period mummies found in the tomb chamber of the Seljuk-era Burmalı Minare Mosque.

items.text: You are about to enter Trabzon Museum, in Trabzon province, opened in 2001. The building is the Kostaki mansion: its painted ceilings and joinery have been left in place, and on the floor below wait the region's Roman and Byzantine finds.
items.speech: You are about to enter Trabzon Museum, in Trabzon province, opened in 2001. The building is the Kostaki mansion: its painted ceilings and joinery have been left in place, and on the floor below wait the region's Roman and Byzantine finds.

items.text: The house was built between the end of the nineteenth century and the start of the twentieth for the banker Kostaki Theophylaktos. It later passed to the Nemlizade family, and in 1924 it served as Atatürk's residence in the city. Once restored, it opened as a museum in 2001, with its painted ceilings and joinery left in place and the region's Roman and Byzantine finds on the floor below.

items.speech: Welcome to Çorum Museum, in Çorum province, founded in 1968. This is the central museum for the Hattusa, Alacahöyük and Şapinuwa excavations, and it holds what they produced: Hittite cuneiform tablets, seals and bull figurines.

items.text: The museum was founded in 1968 and later moved into the old Çorum hospital. Today it is the central collection for the Hattusa, Alacahöyük, Şapinuwa and Ortaköy excavations, gathering the cuneiform tablets, seals and cult objects of the Hittite world. After them, in the same sequence, come the region's Phrygian, Roman and Byzantine layers.

items.text: Look up, and you will see a night sky made of tiles. You are in the Karatay Museum of Tiles, in Konya province, a Seljuk madrasa built in 1251. Its dome is tiled in blue and black like the night, and beneath it are displayed the figured tiles taken from the Kubadabad palace.
items.speech: Look up, and you will see a night sky made of tiles. You are in the Karatay Museum of Tiles, in Konya province, a Seljuk madrasa built in 1251. Its dome is tiled in blue and black like the night, and beneath it are displayed the figured tiles taken from the Kubadabad palace.

items.text: The madrasa was built in 1251 for the Seljuk emir Celâleddin Karatay, and since the middle of the twentieth century it has served as a museum of tiles. The blue, black and turquoise of its dome compose a night sky, reflected in the pool below. The heart of the collection, though, is the figured tilework taken from the Kubadabad palace on the shore of Lake Beyşehir.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Milet, ızgara planlı kent tasarımının kâşifi Hippodamos'un memleketidir. Müzenin anlattığı bu kent planı, bugün dünyanın çoğu şehrinde hâlâ kullanılıyor. Fikrin kendi kentinde de bir karşılığı oldu: Miletli Hippodamos'un kenti, Perslerce yıkıldıktan sonra onun planına göre yeniden kuruldu. Müze, Milet'in yanı sıra Didyma ve Priene buluntularını da barındırır; üç kentin de limanı Menderes'in alüvyonuyla doldu.

items.text: You are at the Miletus Museum, in Aydın province, opened in 1973. It gathers the finds of Miletus, Didyma and Priene, and in a single hall it lays out what a city managed to leave behind, even after all four of its harbours silted up.
items.speech: You are at the Miletus Museum, in Aydın province, opened in 1973. It gathers the finds of Miletus, Didyma and Priene, and in a single hall it lays out what a city managed to leave behind, even after all four of its harbours silted up.

items.text: The museum stands at the entrance to the Miletus site, beside the excavation house. Its collection covers Didyma and Priene as well as Miletus. And here is the twist: the harbours of all three silted up under the Meander, so finds from these port cities are now displayed kilometres inland.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Archaic sculpture, the Roman portraits, the finds from Didyma and the Byzantine-period works.

items.text: Did you know? Miletus was the home of Hippodamus, who devised the grid city plan. The layout the museum explains is still the one most of the world's cities use, and after the Persians destroyed Miletus, the city was rebuilt to his design. The museum also holds the finds of Didyma and Priene alongside those of Miletus — and the harbours of all three were filled by silt from the Meander.

items.text: By 1979 the excavations had produced more sculpture than the town could hold, so the museum was built at the edge of the site. The marble quarry was two kilometres away, and the city's school of sculptors supplied the empire. Here, their work stays where it was made.

items.text: You are in the Kütahya Tile Museum, a museum in Kütahya province, opened in 1999. It is housed in the imaret of Yakup Bey II, and it follows four centuries of the Kütahya workshops, which carried Ottoman tilemaking on after İznik declined.
items.speech: You are in the Kütahya Tile Museum, a museum in Kütahya province, opened in 1999. It is housed in the imaret of Yakup Bey II, and it follows four centuries of the Kütahya workshops, which carried Ottoman tilemaking on after İznik declined.

items.text: The museum occupies the imaret built by Yakup Bey II in the fifteenth century. When the İznik workshops closed in the seventeenth, Kütahya became the centre of Ottoman tilemaking. The craft carried on into the twentieth century, in workshops where Armenian and Turkish masters worked side by side.

items.text: Did you know? Kütahya ware parts ways with İznik's blue and white: its yellows, light greens and freer drawing leave the maker's hand visible. After the İznik workshops closed, Ottoman tilemaking carried on here at Kütahya, in continuous production into the twentieth century.

items.text: You are in Alanya Museum, in Antalya province, opened in 1967. Here the town's Roman and Seljuk layers are shown side by side. Its best known pieces are the sarcophagi in its garden and a small bronze statuette of Herakles.

items.text: Some of the oldest written words of Anatolia are waiting for you here. This is the Kayseri Archaeology Museum in Kayseri province, opened in 1969. It holds the finds of the Kültepe-Kanesh excavation, including the cuneiform tablets and clay envelopes of the Assyrian merchants.
items.speech: Some of the oldest written words of Anatolia are waiting for you here. This is the Kayseri Archaeology Museum in Kayseri province, opened in 1969. It holds the finds of the Kültepe-Kanesh excavation, including the cuneiform tablets and clay envelopes of the Assyrian merchants.

items.text: The heart of the museum is the Kültepe-Kanesh excavation, twenty kilometres north-east of the city. There, in the second millennium BC, Assyrian merchants founded a karum, and it produced Anatolia's earliest written documents. What did they write about? Business: trade contracts and promissory notes.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Kültepe tablets and their clay envelopes and seals, then move on to the Hittite works and the Roman sculpture.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Kültepe tablets and their clay envelopes and seals, then move on to the Hittite works and the Roman sculpture.

items.text: Did you know? The Kültepe tablets came out of the ground inside clay envelopes. A summary of the contract was written on the envelope, which was sealed and broken open only if there was a dispute. The Kültepe-Kanesh tablets are Anatolia's earliest written documents, and every one of them is a trade record, a contract or a note of debt.

items.text: Did you know? A woman's skeleton from Aşıklı Höyük carries the earliest known trace of brain surgery. The bone around the opening in her skull had begun to heal, so she lived on afterwards. Think of that. And the collection as a whole spans ten thousand years, from Neolithic Aşıklı Höyük to the Seljuk caravan road.

items.speech: Step inside Erzurum Museum, a museum in Erzurum province, opened in 1967. Here the Early Bronze Age and Urartian finds of eastern Anatolia are gathered together, with the black burnished pottery of the Karaz culture at their heart.

items.text: Opened in 1967, the museum gathers the Early Bronze Age cultures of eastern Anatolia. At its core is the black burnished pottery tradition named after the Karaz mound near Erzurum — a tradition that spread across a wide belt from the Caucasus to Iran.
items.speech: Opened in 1967, the museum gathers the Early Bronze Age cultures of eastern Anatolia. At its core is the black burnished pottery tradition named after the Karaz mound near Erzurum, a tradition that spread across a wide belt from the Caucasus to Iran.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Karaz culture pottery, the Urartian works, the Seljuk section and the ethnography hall.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the Karaz culture pottery, the Urartian works, the Seljuk section and the ethnography hall.

items.text: Did you know? Karaz pottery was built by hand rather than thrown, then burnished with a pebble after firing. That is why it still shines like a mirror thousands of years on. The same pottery appears across a belt from the Caucasus to Iran, pointing to a wide network of movement in the Early Bronze Age.

items.text: You are in Kars Museum, a museum in Kars province founded in 1959. It holds the finds from the Ani excavations, and in its garden, Russian-era steam engines and church bells tell the story of the city's last two centuries.
items.speech: You are in Kars Museum, a museum in Kars province founded in 1959. It holds the finds from the Ani excavations, and in its garden, Russian-era steam engines and church bells tell the story of the city's last two centuries.

items.text: Founded in 1959, the museum became the central collection for the excavations at Ani. But the city itself is also its subject. Kars was under Russian rule between 1878 and 1918, so its last two centuries are part of the story here, and railway engines and machinery from those years stand in the garden.

items.text: Founded in 1934, the museum brings together the excavations of the upper Tigris basin. The Çayönü mound, in this region, is among the best documented places for humanity's passage to farming and settled life — and here the museum shows you that passage layer by layer.

items.text: When it opened in 1982, the museum became the central collection for the kingdom of Commagene. In the 1980s, rescue excavations were run at settlements about to disappear under the Atatürk dam, and their finds were brought here too. That is how the mosaics of Samosata survive.

items.text: Welcome to Yarımburgaz Cave, a cave in İstanbul province whose story begins in the Lower Palaeolithic. It is one of Thrace's longest caves, and it holds two very different chapters: in its Lower Palaeolithic layers, the oldest human traces around the Sea of Marmara; in its upper ones, a Byzantine church.
items.speech: Welcome to Yarımburgaz Cave, a cave in İstanbul province whose story begins in the Lower Palaeolithic. It is one of Thrace's longest caves, and it holds two very different chapters: in its Lower Palaeolithic layers, the oldest human traces around the Sea of Marmara; in its upper ones, a Byzantine church.

items.text: The cave overlooks Lake Küçükçekmece. It has two storeys, runs for more than a kilometre and is among the largest in Thrace. In its Lower Palaeolithic layers, stone tools and cave-bear bones record the oldest human presence around the Sea of Marmara. Much later, in Byzantine times, a church was cut into its upper levels.

items.text: As you explore, don't miss the Lower Palaeolithic layers, the remains of the cave bear, the Byzantine church and the two-storey gallery system.
items.speech: As you explore, don't miss the Lower Palaeolithic layers, the remains of the cave bear, the Byzantine church and the two-storey gallery system.

items.text: Did you know? For years the cave was used as a quarry and as a mushroom farm, and part of its archaeological sequence was destroyed before it could be excavated. Its Lower Palaeolithic layers record the oldest human presence around the Sea of Marmara. And in its upper levels a Byzantine church was cut: the same cave, used twice, hundreds of thousands of years apart.

items.text: You are at Öküzini Cave, in Antalya province, in the Upper Palaeolithic. Its neighbour is Karain. What makes this cave special is its layers: it is one of the few places where the passage from the end of the ice age to the Neolithic is recorded in an unbroken sequence.
items.speech: You are at Öküzini Cave, in Antalya province, in the Upper Palaeolithic. Its neighbour is Karain. What makes this cave special is its layers: it is one of the few places where the passage from the end of the ice age to the Neolithic is recorded in an unbroken sequence.

items.text: The cave lies a kilometre south of Karain. Its layers, between 16,000 and 10,000 BC, document the end of the ice age in Anatolia better than anywhere else. Turkish and French excavations traced, step by step, how hunter-gatherer groups changed their diet and their tools as the climate warmed.

items.text: İstanbul'da, Alibey Deresi'nin vadisinde, Mimar Sinan'ın imzasını taşıyan bir su kemerinin önündesiniz: Mağlova Kemeri. Tarih 1554-1563. Kırkçeşme su yolları için kurulan bu iki katlı kemer, su mühendisliğini ve anıt mimarisini tek bir yapıda birleştiriyor.
items.speech: İstanbul'da, Alibey Deresi'nin vadisinde, Mimar Sinan'ın imzasını taşıyan bir su kemerinin önündesiniz: Mağlova Kemeri. Tarih 1554 ile 1563. Kırkçeşme su yolları için kurulan bu iki katlı kemer, su mühendisliğini ve anıt mimarisini tek bir yapıda birleştiriyor.

items.text: Kanuni Sultan Süleyman, İstanbul'a su getirme işini Mimar Sinan'a verdi. Kırkçeşme sisteminin en zor noktası, Alibey Deresi'nin geçtiği bu vadiydi; Sinan bu düğümü burada çözdü. Ama 1563'teki büyük sel, iki katlı kemere zarar verdi. Sinan da onu yeniden yaptı. Bugün Alibey Barajı'nın suları, kemerin ayaklarına kadar geliyor.

items.text: Before you stands the Mağlova Aqueduct, in İstanbul province, built in 1554–1563. Sinan threw this two-tier aqueduct across the Alibey stream for the Kırkçeşme water system, joining hydraulic engineering to monumental architecture in one structure.
items.speech: Before you stands the Mağlova Aqueduct, in İstanbul province, built in 1554 to 1563. Sinan threw this two-tier aqueduct across the Alibey stream for the Kırkçeşme water system, joining hydraulic engineering to monumental architecture in one structure.

items.text: Süleyman charged Sinan with bringing water to İstanbul. The hardest point of the Kırkçeşme system lay here, where the Alibey stream cuts its valley, and this is where Sinan solved it. In the great flood of 1563 the two-tier aqueduct was damaged, and he rebuilt it. Today the Alibey reservoir reaches its piers.

items.text: Did you know? Sinan gave the piers a pointed section that splits the current, and it is this detail that has carried the structure through four and a half centuries of floods. The aqueduct was damaged in the great flood of 1563, and Sinan rebuilt it himself.

items.text: Bu sarnıç 4. yüzyılda, konsül Philoxenos'un sarayının altına yapıldı. Yerebatan'dan sonra kentin ikinci büyük kapalı sarnıcıdır. Osmanlı döneminde suyu çekilince bambaşka bir işe yaradı ve iplik atölyesi oldu. Peki adı nereden geliyor? İçindeki sütunların çokluğundan. Ama sayarsanız gerçekte 224 tane bulursunuz.

items.text: Gezerken önce 224 sütunun arasında biraz durun. Sonra iki parçalı sütun gövdelerine yakından bakın, ek yerlerindeki taş bilezikleri bulun ve son olarak başınızı kaldırıp tuğla tonozlara bakın.

items.text: Biliyor muydunuz? Sütunlar tek parça yetmediği için ikişer parça hâlinde üst üste konmuş. Ek yerlerindeki taş bilezikler bu birleşimi gizlemiyor; tam tersine, açıkça gösteriyor. Adı 'bin bir direk' demek, ama gerçekte burada 224 sütun var. Bir kez daha bakın ve saymayı deneyin.

items.text: Step down into Binbirdirek Cistern, in İstanbul province, from the 4th century AD. It is the city's second largest covered cistern. Look at its 224 columns: each is two shafts set one on the other, and you can still see the stone collars at the joins.
items.speech: Step down into Binbirdirek Cistern, in İstanbul province, from the 4th century AD. It is the city's second largest covered cistern. Look at its 224 columns: each is two shafts set one on the other, and you can still see the stone collars at the joins.

items.text: The cistern was built in the fourth century beneath the palace of the consul Philoxenos, and it is the city's second largest covered cistern after the Basilica Cistern. Under the Ottomans it was drained and served as a spinning workshop. Its name means 'a thousand and one columns' — there are in fact 224.

items.text: As you wander among the 224 columns, don't miss the two-part column shafts and the stone collars that join them — and look up at the brick vaults.
items.speech: As you wander among the 224 columns, don't miss the two-part column shafts and the stone collars that join them, and look up at the brick vaults.

items.text: Did you know? Single shafts were not tall enough, so the columns are built in two pieces, and the stone collars at the joins declare the join rather than hide it. And the name 'a thousand and one columns' is a generous one: there are in fact 224.

These columns have stood for centuries; let them keep standing for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.

items.text: Go down into the Theodosius Cistern, a cistern in İstanbul province from AD 428–443. It was built under Theodosius II to store the water brought in by the Valens aqueduct. Its hall of thirty-two marble columns was repaired and, in 2018, opened to visitors.
items.speech: Go down into the Theodosius Cistern, a cistern in İstanbul province from AD 428 to 443. It was built under Theodosius II to store the water brought in by the Valens aqueduct. Its hall of thirty-two marble columns was repaired and, in 2018, opened to visitors.

items.text: Theodosius II had this cistern built to hold the water the Valens aqueduct carried in. Then, for centuries, houses and shops were raised on top of it. It came to light again only during a demolition in 2010, and after eight years of repair it opened to visitors in 2018.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the thirty-two marble columns, their Corinthian capitals, the brick vaults and the inlet channel.

items.text: Did you know? When the buildings above came down, the hall that emerged was a reminder of how many blanks still remain on the map of İstanbul's water system. For centuries houses and shops had stood over the cistern; it came to light again only during a demolition in 2010. After eight years of repair, it opened to visitors in 2018.

Şimdi on iki yüzlü gövdeye yakından bakın. Geometrik ve bitkisel bezeme, her yüzde farklı bir düzenle işlenmiş. Yüzyıllardır bu yamaçta, gölü seyrederek bekliyor.

items.text: Look up at the Halime Hatun Tomb, a tomb in Van province, built in 1358. This twelve-sided tomb tower rises above Lake Van at Gevaş. It is the best preserved piece of Kara Koyunlu stonework and, for its geometric carving, the emblem of the district.
items.speech: Look up at the Halime Hatun Tomb, a tomb in Van province, built in 1358. This twelve-sided tomb tower rises above Lake Van at Gevaş. It is the best preserved piece of Kara Koyunlu stonework and, for its geometric carving, the emblem of the district.

items.text: The tomb was built in 1358 for Halime Hatun, daughter of the Kara Koyunlu lord Melik İzzeddin. It stands on a slope above Lake Van at Gevaş, in the middle of a cemetery of the same period. Walk slowly around it: the geometric and vegetal carving on its twelve faces follows a different arrangement on each one.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the twelve-sided shaft, the conical cap, the geometric carving and the cemetery that surrounds it.
items.speech: As you wander, don't miss the twelve-sided shaft, the conical cap, the geometric carving and the cemetery that surrounds it.

items.text: Did you know? The cemetery around the tomb holds hundreds of gravestones carved as rams and sheep — a form particular to eastern Anatolia, carried over from nomadic practice. And on the tomb itself, each of the twelve faces carries a different arrangement of carving; not one is repeated.

items.text: Milas'taki bu iki katlı anıt mezar MS 2. yüzyılda yapıldı. Alt katta mezar odası var; üstte ise piramit çatıyı taşıyan sütunlu bir bölüm. Yapının, yüz kilometre uzaktaki Halikarnassos Mausoleionu'nun küçültülmüş bir yorumu olduğu kabul ediliyor. Peki bu neden bu kadar önemli? Çünkü o büyük yapı bugün temeline kadar sökülmüş durumda. items.text: The han was built in two campaigns: first the covered hall in 1231, then the courtyard and portal in 1239. items.text: You are standing at the Bridge of Justinian, in Sakarya province, built in AD 559–562. Justinian threw this 430-metre bridge over the Sakarya. But look around you: the river later shifted its bed, and the bridge now stands largely on dry ground.

items.text: Justinian built the bridge between 559 and 562 to lift the road linking the capital to the eastern provinces above the floods of the Sakarya. items.text: Look at how it stretches on and on. This is Uzunköprü Bridge in Edirne province, from 1443. At 1,238 metres over the Ergene, it is the longest stone arch bridge in the world, and the keystones of its 174 arches carry lions, elephants, tulips and other figures.
items.speech: Look at how it stretches on and on. This is Uzunköprü Bridge in Edirne province, from 1443. At 1,238 metres over the Ergene, it is the longest stone arch bridge in the world, and the keystones of its 174 arches carry lions, elephants, tulips and other figures.

items.text: The bridge was completed for Murad II in 1443. It crosses the marshy plain of the Ergene, and it linked Edirne to western Thrace. At 1,238 metres it is the longest stone arch bridge in the world. The town founded at its head took its name from it, and today it is the district centre.

items.text: Köprüyü 1442'de Bursalı tüccar Hoca Muslihiddin yaptırdı. Üzerinde otuz iki dükkânın sıralandığı bir çarşıydı bu. Özgün biçimi 2004'te yeniden inşa edildi ve dükkânlar zanaatkârlara verildi.

items.text: A bridge you can shop on. You are at Irgandı Bridge in Bursa province, built in 1442. It carries a market along its length, one of four bridges of this type still standing anywhere in the world, and craftspeople still work here today.
items.speech: A bridge you can shop on. You are at Irgandı Bridge in Bursa province, built in 1442. It carries a market along its length, one of four bridges of this type still standing anywhere in the world, and craftspeople still work here today.

items.text: In 1442 the Bursa merchant Hoca Muslihiddin built this bridge, and on it a market of thirty-two shops. Then came hard times. Badly damaged by the earthquake of 1855 and by a fire, it was demolished in 1949 and replaced by a flat concrete crossing. But the story did not end there: its original form was rebuilt in 2004, and the shops were handed back to craftspeople.

items.text: On the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, in İstanbul province, stands Beylerbeyi Palace, built in 1861–1865. This was the summer palace of Sultan Abdülaziz, and it was used to house visiting heads of state. It also saw a quieter ending: Abdülhamid II died here under house arrest.
items.speech: On the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, in İstanbul province, stands Beylerbeyi Palace, built in 1861 to 1865. This was the summer palace of Sultan Abdülaziz, and it was used to house visiting heads of state. It also saw a quieter ending: Abdülhamid II died here under house arrest.

items.text: Sultan Abdülaziz had Sarkis Balyan build this summer palace between 1861 and 1865, in place of a wooden kiosk. It was used to receive visiting heads of state, and the Empress Eugénie of France and the Shah of Persia both stayed here. Then the story turns. After his deposition, Abdülhamid II spent his last six years in this palace, under house arrest.

items.text: On the shore of Lake Beyşehir, a sultan once built a town for himself. You are at Kubadabad Palace, in Konya province, raised by Alâeddin Keykubad I in 1226–1237. The figured tiles that once lined its walls now hang in the Karatay Museum in Konya.
items.speech: On the shore of Lake Beyşehir, a sultan once built a town for himself. You are at Kubadabad Palace, in Konya province, raised by Alâeddin Keykubad I in 1226 to 1237. The figured tiles that once lined its walls now hang in the Karatay Museum in Konya.

items.text: Alâeddin Keykubad I had a palace town built for himself on the western shore of Lake Beyşehir. Picture it: a great palace and a lesser one, a boatyard, hunting lodges, and a pavilion on an island in the lake. The figured tiles uncovered in excavations from 1949 onwards are the richest source we have for how a Seljuk palace was decorated.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the Great Palace and the Lesser Palace. Look for the remains of the boatyard, and then turn your eyes to the island pavilion.

items.text: Did you know? The tiles show the sultan himself, along with hunting birds, sirens and double-headed eagles. They are evidence that the prohibition on figures did not hold inside a Seljuk palace. The figured tiles that lined the palace walls are displayed today in the Karatay Museum in Konya.

items.text: In 1394, while preparing to besiege Constantinople, Bayezid I raised this fortress at the narrowest point of the Bosphorus, at the mouth of the Göksu. Sixty years later, Mehmed II built Rumeli Hisarı on the opposite shore. From then on, every ship passing the strait was caught between the guns of the two castles.

items.text: Did you know? There are still houses inside the fortress: the quarter that grew between its walls stayed on after the castle's military life ended. The fortress went up in 1394; sixty years later Rumeli Hisarı rose opposite, and every ship in the strait was caught between the two.

Bu yüzden duvarlarda sütun tamburları, mezar stelleri ve yazıtlı bloklar yan yana duruyor. Kale, Selçuklu ve Osmanlı dönemlerinde de onarıldı ve kullanılmaya devam etti.

items.text: Above you rises Ankara Castle, a castle and walls in Ankara province from the 7th century AD. This citadel wraps the hill the city grew on. Look closely at its walls: they were built course by course from column drums and inscribed blocks stripped out of Roman buildings.
items.speech: Above you rises Ankara Castle, a castle and walls in Ankara province from the 7th century AD. This citadel wraps the hill the city grew on. Look closely at its walls: they were built course by course from column drums and inscribed blocks stripped out of Roman buildings.

items.text: The present walls went up in the seventh century, when Byzantium was building a defensive line against Arab raids. The builders took what lay at hand. Most of the material was stripped from the city's Roman buildings, so column drums, funerary stelae and inscribed blocks now stand side by side in the masonry. Under the Seljuks and Ottomans the castle was repaired and kept in use.

items.text: You are at Mamure Castle, at Anamur in Mersin province, built over the 12th–15th century. It sits right on the shore. Count its towers if you can — there are thirty-nine — and add its moat, and you have the largest and best preserved castle on the Mediterranean coast.
items.speech: You are at Mamure Castle, at Anamur in Mersin province, built over the 12th–15th century. It sits right on the shore. Count its towers if you can, there are thirty-nine, and add its moat, and you have the largest and best preserved castle on the Mediterranean coast.

items.text: The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia rebuilt the castle over a Roman fort, and later the Karamanids and the Ottomans enlarged it. With thirty-nine towers, a moat and three separate courtyards, it is the largest castle on the Mediterranean coast. And the sea comes right up to the foot of its walls.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the thirty-nine towers and the moat, then the inner court with its mosque, and the lighthouse tower.

items.text: Did you know? The moat still fills with water, and turtles live in it. It is one of the few castle moats in Anatolia that still does what it was dug to do. With thirty-nine towers and its moat, Mamure is the largest and best preserved castle on the Mediterranean coast.

items.text: You are standing before Yedikule Fortress, a castle and walls in İstanbul province, dating from 1458. Mehmed II grafted this seven-towered fortress onto the Golden Gate of the Theodosian walls. It served as treasury, as arsenal, and as the state prison where envoys were held.
items.speech: You are standing before Yedikule Fortress, a castle and walls in İstanbul province, dating from 1458. Mehmed II grafted this seven-towered fortress onto the Golden Gate of the Theodosian walls. It served as treasury, as arsenal, and as the state prison where envoys were held.

items.text: In 1458 Mehmed II added three towers to the Golden Gate section of the Theodosian walls. Together with the four already there, they made a fortress of seven towers. It served first as treasury and arsenal, and then became the state prison. When a state went to war with the Ottomans, its ambassadors were held here. And in 1622, Osman II was killed within these walls.

items.text: Did you know? The scratchings prisoners left on the cell walls can still be read: names and dates in Latin, Greek, French and Russian. Imagine the long days behind every line. And the fortress itself was made in 1458 by adding three towers to the Golden Gate of the Theodosian walls; with the four already there, the count reached seven.

items.text: A thousand metres up in the Taurus, on a terrace, stands Alahan Monastery, a monastery and church in Mersin province from the 5th century AD. Its east church holds a treasure: a stone drum, the best preserved of the dome experiments that came before Hagia Sophia.
items.speech: A thousand metres up in the Taurus, on a terrace, stands Alahan Monastery, a monastery and church in Mersin province from the 5th century AD. Its east church holds a treasure: a stone drum, the best preserved of the dome experiments that came before Hagia Sophia.

items.text: The monastery was founded in the fifth century on a terrace a thousand metres up in the Taurus, above the Göksu valley. Picture the community that lived here: a west church, an east church, a baptistery and rock-cut monks' cells, all joined by a colonnaded walk. And the stone drum of the east church is the best preserved of the dome solutions tried before Hagia Sophia.

Maçka vadisinin dik yamacına yaslanan bu yapı topluluğu, Trabzon Rum İmparatorluğu döneminde bölgenin tapu ve vergi kayıtlarını tuttu. Bu kayıtlar bugün Karadeniz'in ortaçağ toplumsal tarihi için en önemli kaynaklardan biri. Manastır ise 1923'te terk edildi ve sessizliğe gömüldü.

items.text: Leaning into the steep side of the Maçka valley, in Trabzon province, stands Vazelon Monastery, a monastery and church founded in 270. It is older than Sümela, and under the Empire of Trebizond it kept the land registers of the region.
items.speech: Leaning into the steep side of the Maçka valley, in Trabzon province, stands Vazelon Monastery, a monastery and church founded in 270. It is older than Sümela, and under the Empire of Trebizond it kept the land registers of the region.

items.text: The monastery was founded in 270, about a century before Sümela. Set into the steep side of the Maçka valley, it kept the land and tax registers of the region under the Empire of Trebizond. Those records are among the most important sources for the medieval social history of the Black Sea. In 1923 the monastery was abandoned.

items.text: On Bülbüldağı, in İzmir province, stands a stone house held to be where Mary spent her last years. This is the House of the Virgin Mary, a monastery and church whose foundations date to the 1st century AD. Popes have visited it, and it is a place of pilgrimage for Christians and Muslims alike.

items.text: The stone house on the slope of Bülbüldağı was sought out on the strength of the visions of a German nun, Anne Catherine Emmerich, and it was found in 1891. Its foundations date to the first century AD, and part of its walls to the Byzantine period. Popes Paul VI, John Paul II and Benedict XVI have all come here.

items.text: Before you rise the bow-fronted, whitewashed houses of Beypazarı, a historic town in Ankara province from the 18th–19th century. It lay on the Ankara branch of the Silk Road, and it is one of the few Anatolian towns restored and kept whole rather than house by house.
items.speech: Before you rise the bow-fronted, whitewashed houses of Beypazarı, a historic town in Ankara province from the 18th–19th century. It lay on the Ankara branch of the Silk Road, and it is one of the few Anatolian towns restored and kept whole rather than house by house.

items.text: The town was a stop and a market on the branch of the Silk Road that ran through Ankara. Its houses, timber-framed, filled with mud-brick and whitewashed, were built in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Then, from the 1990s, a restoration programme preserved the streets as a whole. It is one of the few cases in Anatolia where the fabric of a town, rather than individual buildings, was saved.

items.text: On the slope above Ephesus, in İzmir province, lies Şirince, a historic town of the 19th century. It was once a Greek village; the 1923 exchange of populations emptied its stone houses, yet they were preserved rather than replaced. Step in, and let the village tell you its story.
items.speech: On the slope above Ephesus, in İzmir province, lies Şirince, a historic town of the 19th century. It was once a Greek village; the 1923 exchange of populations emptied its stone houses, yet they were preserved rather than replaced. Step in, and let the village tell you its story.

items.text: Şirince began as a Greek settlement on the slope above Ephesus, and its people lived by winemaking. Then came the population exchange of 1923. The village emptied, and Turks from Salonica settled in its place. Yet the two-storey whitewashed houses on their stone footings and the two churches stayed where they were, and from the 1980s the village was listed as a fabric to be protected.

items.text: Kaleiçi is the present name of the walled city that grew around the harbour of Roman Attaleia. The three-arched gate raised for the emperor Hadrian's visit in AD 130 is still one of its main entrances. Through the Seljuk and Ottoman centuries the city stayed within these walls, and the bow-fronted timber mansions lining its lanes date from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

items.text: You are now at the Alâeddin Mosque in Konya, a mosque and complex in Konya province, built over 1155–1221. This was the congregational mosque of the Anatolian Seljuk capital: a flat-roofed hall on forty-two reused columns, with the tombs of eight sultans beside it.
items.speech: You are now at the Alâeddin Mosque in Konya, a mosque and complex in Konya province, built over 1155 to 1221. This was the congregational mosque of the Anatolian Seljuk capital: a flat-roofed hall on forty-two reused columns, with the tombs of eight sultans beside it.

items.text: The mosque stands on the mound at the centre of Konya, beside what was once the Seljuk palace. Building began in 1155 and finished only in 1221, under Alâeddin Keykubad I — which is why its parts follow different plans. Look up: forty-two reused columns carry a flat wooden ceiling. And in its courtyard, two tombs hold eight Seljuk sultans.

items.text: In Edirne province stands a building that changed Ottoman architecture: the Üç Şerefeli Mosque and its complex, built in 1437–1447. Here came the first attempt at a central dome on this scale. And look at its four minarets, each one built to a different design.
items.speech: In Edirne province stands a building that changed Ottoman architecture: the Üç Şerefeli Mosque and its complex, built in 1437 to 1447. Here came the first attempt at a central dome on this scale. And look at its four minarets, each one built to a different design.

items.text: Murad II built this mosque at Edirne between 1437 and 1447, and it marks the turning point of Ottoman architecture. For the first time, a central dome twenty-four metres across was set over the prayer hall, on a six-support system. Now look at the minarets. Each of the four is a different height, with different shaft decoration, and the mosque takes its name from the three balconies on the tallest.

items.text: This mosque in the village of Kasaba near Kastamonu was built in 1366 for Mahmut Bey of the Candarid dynasty. Its posts, beams and ceiling are all joined by interlocking joinery, without a single nail. The painted decoration on the ceiling and capitals is original; in six hundred and fifty years it has never been renewed. In 2023 it entered the World Heritage List.

items.text: In İstanbul province, above the Eminönü market, rises Rüstem Pasha Mosque, a mosque and complex built in 1561–1563. This is Sinan's mosque, sheathed inside and out in İznik tiles at a density no other Ottoman building attempts.
items.speech: In İstanbul province, above the Eminönü market, rises Rüstem Pasha Mosque, a mosque and complex built in 1561 to 1563. This is Sinan's mosque, sheathed inside and out in İznik tiles at a density no other Ottoman building attempts.

items.text: Sinan built this mosque for Rüstem Pasha, Süleyman's grand vizier and son-in-law. It sits above the Eminönü market on a platform formed by the shops beneath it, an arrangement that both funded the mosque and lifted it above the crowd. Step inside and you will see why it is celebrated: its İznik tiling, inside and out, is denser than in any other Ottoman mosque.

items.text: Did you know? items.text: Look out to the Maiden's Tower, a monument in İstanbul province, on an islet off Üsküdar. Its first structure goes back to the 5th century BC. Over time it has been many things: first a customs post, later a quarantine station, a lighthouse and a watchtower. The building standing today dates from the eighteenth century.

items.text: The first structure on this islet off Üsküdar was raised in the fifth century BC by the Athenian commander Alcibiades — to tax the ships passing the strait. Under Byzantium the islet anchored a chain drawn to the opposite shore. Under the Ottomans it served as a quarantine station, a lighthouse and a watchtower. The building standing today dates from the eighteenth century.

items.text: Imagine a workshop where the sculptors simply put down their tools and never came back. You are at Yesemek Quarry and Sculpture Workshop in Gaziantep province, worked from the 14th to the 8th century BC. It is the largest known open-air sculpture workshop of the Near East: more than three hundred half-finished lions, sphinxes and mountain gods lie across the slope, exactly where they were left.
items.speech: Imagine a workshop where the sculptors simply put down their tools and never came back. You are at Yesemek Quarry and Sculpture Workshop in Gaziantep province, worked from the 14th to the 8th century BC. It is the largest known open-air sculpture workshop of the Near East: more than three hundred half-finished lions, sphinxes and mountain gods lie across the slope, exactly where they were left.

items.text: The workshop opened in the fourteenth century BC under the Hittite empire, and carried on into the eighth under the Neo-Hittite states. On the slope where the basalt was quarried, more than three hundred roughed-out sculptures still lie where they were left: gate lions, sphinxes and mountain gods. Why so many unfinished? Because the workshop was abandoned suddenly under Assyrian attack, and the whole production process froze in place.

items.text: Did you know? Every sculpture here is unfinished. More than three hundred half-finished lions, sphinxes and mountain gods lie on the slope where they were left. The workshop was abandoned suddenly under Assyrian attack, so the process simply froze. That is the gift of Yesemek: every stage, from rough blocking to final carving, can be seen side by side on this one slope.

items.text: Look up at this granite needle. You are standing before the Obelisk of Theodosius, a monument in İstanbul province whose stone dates from the 15th century BC. Thutmose III raised it at Karnak; in AD 390 it was moved to the Hippodrome. Then look down: the reliefs on its base show, step by step, how it was set upright.
items.speech: Look up at this granite needle. You are standing before the Obelisk of Theodosius, a monument in İstanbul province whose stone dates from the 15th century BC. items.text: The obelisk's story begins at Karnak, where Pharaoh Thutmose III raised it in the fifteenth century BC. In the fourth century AD Constantius had it brought to Alexandria. Then, in 390, Theodosius I moved it to Constantinople and set it up on the spine of the Hippodrome. But the journey took its toll: it broke in transit, so only about a third of its original height stands today.

Bugün dört katı ziyarete açık. Onu Kapadokya'nın diğer yeraltı şehirlerinden ayıran şey, kat aralarına açılmış dar borular. Saldırganlar sürgü taşını kırmaya uğraşırken, bu borulardan üzerlerine kaynar sıvı dökülebiliyordu.

items.text: How was this place found? In 1972 a farmer watering his field north of Avanos noticed the water disappearing into the ground. Below lay this underground city. Four of its levels are open today. What sets it apart from Cappadocia's other underground cities are the narrow pipes cut between the storeys: while attackers struggled at the rolling stone door, hot liquid could be poured down on them.

items.text: You have come to Açıksaray, a rock settlement near Gülşehir in Nevşehir province, from the 9th–11th century. Here you will find dwellings and stables rather than churches. It is the clearest picture in Cappadocia of how a provincial Byzantine landowner lived.
items.speech: You have come to Açıksaray, a rock settlement near Gülşehir in Nevşehir province, from the 9th–11th century. Here you will find dwellings and stables rather than churches. It is the clearest picture in Cappadocia of how a provincial Byzantine landowner lived.

items.text: Unlike Cappadocia's other sites, this rock settlement near Gülşehir is civil rather than religious. Its six separate complexes, dated to the ninth to eleventh centuries, hold dwellings, stables, kitchens and courtyards, each group arranged as the unit of a household or farm. Churches? There are few, and they are small.

items.text: These rock clefts, a kilometre and a half north-east of Hattusa, formed the largest open-air sanctuary of the Hittite empire. On the walls of Chamber A, two processions of gods walk towards each other and meet in the middle, at the chief god and goddess. Chamber B is dedicated to king Tudhaliya IV. The reliefs were carved in the thirteenth century BC: the Hittite roll of gods, set into stone.

items.text: The temple of Apollo Smintheus was built in the second century BC at Chryse in the Troad. Its cult appears in the opening pages of the Iliad: it is from here that Apollo, answering the prayer of his priest Chryses, sends plague arrows into the Greek camp. The temple's frieze is carved with scenes from the Iliad, a rare case of an epic depicted at its own cult centre.

items.text: You are standing at Domuztepe, a mound in Kahramanmaraş province, around 6000 BC. This was the largest known settlement of the Halaf culture. It also holds a mass burial called the Death Pit — one of the most argued-over finds in prehistoric Anatolia.

items.text: This mound on the Kahramanmaraş plain is the largest known settlement of the Halaf culture, dating to the sixth millennium BC. Excavations from the 1990s uncovered the mass burial known as the Death Pit. Inside it, the disarticulated bones of at least thirty-five people were found mixed with animal bone. What happened here? What the deposit means is still argued over.

items.text: Did you know? Five explanations have been proposed for the Death Pit: warfare, epidemic, ritual feasting, ancestor rites and cannibalism. Yet none of them accounts for everything found in it. The mound is the largest known settlement of the Halaf culture and dates to the sixth millennium BC. In the Death Pit, the disarticulated bones of at least thirty-five people lay mixed with animal bone, and what it means is still argued over today.

items.text: Picture a flat-topped hill with sheer sides rising above the plain. On it stood one of the four great cities of Pamphylia. In 333 BC Alexander besieged it and withdrew without taking it — one of the few places in Anatolia to end that way. Its Hellenistic tower and gate system largely survive. The hill itself proved less lasting: in 1969 a landslip carried away part of it, and the theatre and stadium with it.

items.text: Founded in 1933, the museum is the central collection for Phrygia. Nearby lie the quarries of Docimium, which supplied the Roman world's most sought-after white and purple-veined marble. Most of the sarcophagi and sculpture here carry their workmanship.

items.text: The museum opened in 1971 as the central collection for the Arslantepe excavation. On the mound stood a palace dated to the fourth millennium BC, and swords were found inside it. items.text: The museum was founded in 1943 in a building put up in the Republic's first years. Its collection comes from the rock tombs of Paphlagonia and from the Pompeiopolis excavation. But the building has its own story too: in 1925, Atatürk announced the hat reform in this hall.

items.text: Did you know? The Paphlagonian rock tombs, with temple fronts cut into the cliff, resemble those of Lycia — yet no connection between the two regions is known. And it was in the hall of this very building that Atatürk announced the hat reform in 1925.

items.text: Welcome to Metropolis, an ancient city in İzmir province, from the 3rd century BC. It sits on a slope above the Torbalı plain, and it is known for its council house, its theatre and a bath-gymnasium built to serve two thousand people.

items.text: In Uşak province, on a promontory ringed on three sides by deep gorges, stands Blaundus. Its story begins in the 3rd century BC, and its walls, temple and rock tombs are still largely standing. Here, the landscape itself was the first line of defence.

items.text: The city was built on a promontory ringed on three sides by deep gorges, a position that made it defend itself. It was founded in the Hellenistic period, grew under Rome and became a bishopric under Byzantium.

items.text: Three lands meet here. You are in Tripolis on the Meander, an ancient city in Denizli province from the 2nd century BC, founded where Lydia, Caria and Phrygia meet. Recent excavation has brought its colonnaded street and great church back into the light.
items.speech: Three lands meet here. You are in Tripolis on the Meander, an ancient city in Denizli province from the 2nd century BC, founded where Lydia, Caria and Phrygia meet. Recent excavation has brought its colonnaded street and great church back into the light.

items.text: The city was founded at the meeting point of Lydia, Caria and Phrygia, on the edge of the Meander plain, and its very name refers to that junction. In recent years the excavators have uncovered its colonnaded street, its theatre and a large early Christian church.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the colonnaded street and the theatre. Then visit the basilica, and walk out to the city walls.

items.text: Did you know? The paved street has been uncovered along its full length, together with the shops that lined it, and that is a rare survival. The city was founded where Lydia, Caria and Phrygia meet, and its name refers to that triple border. Uncovering a colonnaded street whole, shops and all, is a rare thing indeed.

items.text: On the shore of Lake Bafa, among the boulders of the Beşparmak range, lies Heracleia under Latmus, an ancient city in Muğla province from the 4th century BC. Its Hellenistic walls run six kilometres around the slope.
items.speech: On the shore of Lake Bafa, among the boulders of the Beşparmak range, lies Heracleia under Latmus, an ancient city in Muğla province from the 4th century BC. Its Hellenistic walls run six kilometres around the slope.

items.text: The city was built among the granite boulders of the Beşparmak range, on the shore of what was then a sea gulf. Then the Meander did its slow work: its silt closed the gulf, the sea became Lake Bafa, and the harbour town was left inland. Around the slope, its Hellenistic walls run for six kilometres.

items.text: The Carian city grew rich on the marble quarries around it and on its black granite. Under Rome it won the status of a free city. Its temple of Apollo, its bouleuterion and a market building reaching two hundred metres have all been uncovered.

items.text: Welcome to Alinda, an ancient city in Aydın province, from the 4th century BC. This is the city where the Carian queen Ada adopted Alexander, and its three-storey market building is among the best preserved commercial structures of antiquity.
items.speech: Welcome to Alinda, an ancient city in Aydın province, from the 4th century BC. This is the city where the Carian queen Ada adopted Alexander, and its three-storey market building is among the best preserved commercial structures of antiquity.

items.text: Ada, queen of Caria, took refuge here after her brother deposed her. Then, in 334 BC, she made a bold move: she adopted Alexander, and in return she got the rule of Caria back. Look around, too, at the city's three-storey market building, among the best preserved commercial structures of antiquity.

items.text: This harbour town on a peninsula lived by fishing and by the blue-and-white veined marble it quarried, which was sold in Rome as cipollino and used in imperial buildings. Its story is older still: traces of settlement go back to the second millennium BC and the Mycenaean period.

items.text: This is Rhodiapolis, an ancient city in Antalya province from the 3rd century BC. It was the city of Opramoas, Lycia's greatest benefactor, whose tomb carries one of the longest records of public giving to survive from antiquity.
items.speech: This is Rhodiapolis, an ancient city in Antalya province from the 3rd century BC. It was the city of Opramoas, Lycia's greatest benefactor, whose tomb carries one of the longest records of public giving to survive from antiquity.

items.text: This small city in Lycia's mountainous interior was the home of the benefactor Opramoas. In the second century AD, after earthquakes, he sent aid to twenty-eight Lycian cities. The inscription cut into the walls of his tomb lists every one of those gifts: generosity recorded in stone.

items.text: As you wander, don't miss the tomb of Opramoas and the theatre, then the basilica and the baths.

items.text: Did you know? The Opramoas inscription runs to seventy-one documents, and it is the most detailed source we have for how public giving worked in the Roman provinces. In the second century AD, after earthquakes, Opramoas sent aid to twenty-eight Lycian cities.

items.text: Here at Andriake, an ancient city in Antalya province from the 2nd century BC, you stand in the harbour of Myra. Its vast granary, built by Hadrian, records the stop this coast made for the grain fleet running from Egypt to Rome.
items.speech: Here at Andriake, an ancient city in Antalya province from the 2nd century BC, you stand in the harbour of Myra. Its vast granary, built by Hadrian, records the stop this coast made for the grain fleet running from Egypt to Rome.

items.text: Andriake was the harbour of Myra, and the stop this coast made for the fleet carrying Egyptian grain to Rome. The granary built by Hadrian still stands almost entire, with its eight chambers. And one famous traveller passed this way: Paul changed ships here on his way to Rome.

items.text: You have climbed eleven hundred metres above the Köprülü canyon. Welcome to Selge, a Pisidian city in Antalya province from the 5th century BC. Its theatre, built for ten thousand, still stands in the middle of a village.
items.speech: You have climbed eleven hundred metres above the Köprülü canyon. Welcome to Selge, a Pisidian city in Antalya province from the 5th century BC. Its theatre, built for ten thousand, still stands in the middle of a village.

items.text: The Pisidian city was built eleven hundred metres up, above the Köprülü canyon, and that lofty position kept it independent for a long time. Selge struck its own coinage and grew rich on the trade in storax resin. And its theatre still stands today, right in the middle of a village.

items.text: You are entering Lagina, Sanctuary of Hecate, in Muğla province, from the 2nd century BC. It is the only major temple to Hecate known in the ancient world, reached by a sacred way from Stratonikeia along which the yearly procession of the key was carried.

items.text: The temple of Hecate here is the only major sanctuary of that goddess known in the ancient world. A sacred way eleven kilometres long ran to it from Stratonikeia, and each year the procession of the key was carried along it. Look for the frieze too: it is carved with scenes from Carian history.

items.text: Did you know? Hecate was the goddess of crossroads, thresholds and passages, which is why a sanctuary reached by a procession from gate to gate suits her so well. items.text: On the slope above the Meander gorge stands the Sanctuary of Apollo Lairbenos, a sanctuary in Denizli province from the 2nd century BC. Its temple has left us something rare: hundreds of confession inscriptions, the frankest record of popular religion in the Roman countryside.
items.speech: On the slope above the Meander gorge stands the Sanctuary of Apollo Lairbenos, a sanctuary in Denizli province from the 2nd century BC. Its temple has left us something rare: hundreds of confession inscriptions, the frankest record of popular religion in the Roman countryside.

items.text: This temple, on the slope above the Meander gorge, grew up where a local Anatolian god came to be identified with Apollo. Hundreds of inscriptions from here record, plainly and by name, the offences of people whom the god had punished with illness or misfortune. These are the so-called confession inscriptions.

items.text: Twelve cities once gathered on this ground. You are at Panionium, a sanctuary in Aydın province from the 7th century BC. It was the common sanctuary of the twelve Ionian cities and the seat of their league, and Herodotus writes that resistance to Persia was debated here.

items.text: The common sanctuary of the twelve Ionian cities stood at the foot of Mount Mycale, and it was the meeting place of the Ionian League. items.text: You are standing on Hacılar, a mound in Burdur province dating back to 7000 BC. Excavated by James Mellaart in the 1950s, it produced the earliest and richest Neolithic painted pottery in Anatolia.
items.speech: You are standing on Hacılar, a mound in Burdur province dating back to 7000 BC. Excavated by James Mellaart in the 1950s, it produced the earliest and richest Neolithic painted pottery in Anatolia.

items.text: James Mellaart excavated the mound between 1957 and 1960, and the results changed the understanding of the Anatolian Neolithic. Its painted pottery ranks among the earliest and most accomplished in the Near East. But the story has a twist: the fake Hacılar vessels that later appeared on the market became a famous case of forgery in archaeology.

Bu anıt, üç yılanın gövdesinden oluşan sekiz metrelik tunç bir sütundur. Yüzyıllar sonra, MS 4. yüzyılda Konstantinopolis'e getirilir ve Hipodrom'a dikilir.

items.text: Here in İstanbul province stands a bronze column with a remarkable past: the Serpent Column, from 478 BC. The thirty-one Greek cities that beat Persia at Plataea cast it from captured weapons and dedicated it at Delphi. In the fourth century AD it was brought to the Hippodrome.
items.speech: Here in İstanbul province stands a bronze column with a remarkable past: the Serpent Column, from 478 BC. The thirty-one Greek cities that beat Persia at Plataea cast it from captured weapons and dedicated it at Delphi. In the fourth century AD it was brought to the Hippodrome.

items.text: Its story begins with a victory. In 479 BC, thirty-one Greek cities beat Persia at Plataea. From the weapons they captured they cast this monument, and the following year, in 478 BC, they dedicated it at the temple of Apollo at Delphi. Eight metres of bronze, formed from three entwined serpents. In the fourth century AD it was brought to Constantinople and set up in the Hippodrome.
